events.title: ‘The best address in Singapore’: Why Malaysia’s IOI Properties is betting billions on the CBD
events.summary: IOI Properties chief executive Lee Yeow Seng, who was among the speakers at the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore on Oct 7, says there is no better address and location than Marina Bay. - IOI Properties chief Lee Yeow Seng is betting billions on Singapore’s CBD, calling Marina Bay “the best address in Singapore” because of safety, prestige and limited land supply. - The group has bought major assets, including South Beach and Asia Square Tower 2, and may acquire One Raffles Place to grow its Downtown Core portfolio. - IOI plans more luxury homes, ultra-high-end hotels and a Singapore REIT to cut debt, while Lee urges land sales reforms to avoid rising property prices. SINGAPORE – IOI Properties chief executive Lee Yeow Seng is betting billions on Singapore’s Central Business District (CBD), which he regards as the best location for property investments in the country. “If you want to invest in properties, location is always the most important overriding consideration,” he told The Straits Times in an interview on the sidelines of the Forbes Global CEO Conference in Singapore on Oct 7. “There’s no better address and location than Marina Bay.” Underlying that bet is Lee’s belief that Singapore has established itself as a safe haven for high-net-worth individuals, whose presence in the Republic will support demand for prime offices, luxury homes and high-end hotels. “Rich people, when they look to park their money, the first thing they look at is safety,” he said. “I think Singapore has managed to brand itself very well as a safe haven for rich people. And probably now, after the Middle East conflict, there isn’t any country safer than Singapore.” The arrival of more rich people to the Republic would also draw multinational companies and create demand for the best property offerings. “When high-net-worth individuals come in, they want nothing but the best,” Lee said. “That is the segment I think is still very much underserved.” This explains IOI’s focus on the CBD, where it has assembled a portfolio spanning offices, hotels and luxury residences. These include IOI Central Boulevard Towers, which it built from scratch after acquiring the site in 2016; South Beach, which it fully owns after buying out City Developments’ 50.1% stake for around $835 mllion in September 2025; and Asia Square Tower 2, which it bought from CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust for $2.5 billion in April. According to The Business Times, IOI Properties and CapitaLand Investment are now conducting exclusive due diligence for the proposed acquisition of One Raffles Place, after jointly submitting a 50-50 bid to owners OUE Reit and UOB. If completed, the deal would broaden IOI’s exposure to the Downtown Core. One Raffles Place, which comprises two office towers of 62 and 38 storeys respectively, as well as a six-storey retail podium, also sits on an exceptionally long 841-year lease. The development has an indicative value of between $2.3 billion and $2.4 billion. Asked about his confidence in Singapore’s CBD, Lee said the limited supply of land, as well as the Government’s control over its release, gives property investors greater certainty. “You feel very secure investing in properties in Singapore because the supply is controlled and very limited.” He added that land for new Grade A office developments in the CBD has not been released for about 10 years. Lee is bullish on CBD offices despite the growth of flexible working and government efforts to decentralise jobs to commercial centres outside the CBD, saying companies and employees continue to value a prestigious downtown address. “If I’m a worker, I would still prefer to work in the city centre because it is much more glamorous,” he said. “You want to tell people that you work for a company that has an address in the CBD. You feel more proud and you feel happier working downtown because there are many more amenities and transport links.” IOI Central Boulevard Towers is within reach of several MRT stations and sits close to Marina Bay Sands, for example. The convenience and prestige has also allowed the development to command higher rents of close to $18 per sq ft, compared with about $8 psf a decade ago. The group has also raised rents at Asia Square Tower 2 since taking control of the property. “When we first purchased the property, the average rent was only about $11. Now we are getting renewals at $13 to $14.” IOI’s investments in the CBD extend beyond office towers. Lee said mixed-use developments allowing people to live, work and spend their leisure time in the same district represent both the present and the future of cities. “People go for convenience. They want access to a lot of amenities and to live, work and play near one another.” At Marina View, IOI is developing the 683-unit W Residences Marina View, which comes integrated with a W hotel of about 360 rooms.

events.title: AI chip boom pushes Samsung profits to record $80bn
events.summary: Samsung is also one of the world's biggest smartphone makers Published 8 October 2026, 02:31 BST Samsung Electronics says it expects a nine-fold surge in its quarterly profits compared with a year earlier, driven by surging demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) data centres. The tech giant estimates that its operating profit for the three months to the end of September will jump to 107.4tn won (£61bn; $80bn), its fourth quarter in a row of record earnings. Samsung is one of the world's largest memory chip makers alongside local rival SK Hynix and Micron in the US, which produce chips crucial for AI firms like Nvidia. Samsung, which makes the Galaxy Fold and S26 smartphones, is also expected to get a boost from its latest folding devices that were launched in August. The firm's full third-quarter earnings will be released at the end of October. Major South Korean companies tend to release previews of their earnings to advise investors ahead of more detailed reports. There has been huge global demand for computer chips that power AI development, helping to lift the earnings and shares of manufacturers linked to the technology. The surge in demand in recent years has resulted in a shortage of semiconductors globally, pushing up sales for firms like Samsung, with its stock market valuation crossing $1tn (£757bn) earlier this year . Investment in the industry has surged, with US tech giants including Google, Amazon and Meta pledging to pour more than $650bn into AI projects this year. In June, South Korea unveiled plans for at least $880bn in projects led by Samsung and SK Hynix to build out the country's chip manufacturing capabilities in the coming years. Rival Asian firms in Japan, China and Taiwan are also investing heavily in chip plants as demand for AI soars. A chip shortage driven by surging demand has led firms including Samsung to raise prices, making products such as smartphones and computers more expensive. events.title: Emails between Alan Jones and 17yo schoolboy read to court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Complainant denies deceiving Alan Jones for financial assistance, trial hears Veteran broadcaster Alan Jones denies all allegations against him. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Complainant A is giving evidence in the Alan Jones trial in the New South Wales Local Court on Thursday. The complainant, who is now an adult, is accusing Mr Jones of kissing him and touching his buttocks when he was a 17-year-old. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching related to five male complainants. A man accusing Alan Jones of kissing him when he was a 17-year-old schoolboy has denied he and his mother tried to deceive the veteran broadcaster to obtain as much financial assistance as possible before he came forward with his allegation. The now-adult, known as Complainant A, alleges Mr Jones kissed him, put his tongue in his mouth, and touched his buttocks when he visited the radio host at his farm on the Southern Highlands as a 17-year-old. The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to 21 counts of indecent assault and sexually touching relating to five male complainants between 2003 and 2020. Mr Jones is facing 21 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Complainant A said he first reached out to Mr Jones when he was 13 years old, sending the 2GB host a letter asking for help with his family's serious financial struggles. Emails read to the court showed Mr Jones had extensive correspondences with the young boy over a three-year period and used his influence to help the boy's mother re-negotiate a more favourable home loan, which included $600,000 being wiped off her initial debt. The trial heard Mr Jones also provided more than $100,000 of his own money to help with the completion of the boy's family home and to help with their legal fees. The court is hearing from Complainant A, who is the fifth and final male complainant. ( ABC News: Ethan Rix ) Under cross-examination, defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC raised an email sent by Mr Jones to the boy, three years after they started communicating with each other, and a year before the alleged indecent assault occurred. The court heard Mr Jones informed the boy in the email about how he had provided his family more than $100,000 in support, writing "enough is enough" and "there must come a point where I have to say, no more". Complainant A said he believed Mr Jones's email expressed frustration but told Ms Bashir he did not believe the email meant the end of the broadcaster's financial support to him and his mother. "Isn't it that the case that your intention was on obtaining as much financial assistance from Mr Jones as you possibly could?" Ms Bashir suggested. "That is not true," the complainant replied. "It's the case that your mother had the intention of obtaining as much financial assistance from Mr Jones as she possibly could?" Ms Bashir asked. "That is a lie," the complainant said. The court heard the boy replied to the email, writing that his family was "happy to make arrangements to make repayments", with Mr Jones's reply asking about when a legal matter would end and that "he was not a mobile bank". Ms Bashir questioned the complainant about whether he had drafted specific emails to Mr Jones or whether his mother also had some level of involvement. Complainant A repeatedly told the court he could not remember who may have drafted specific sections of emails but said there was certain information contained in correspondence that he would have only been able to obtain from his mum. "You were you trying to deceive Mr Jones about the author of the email when you sent emails signed off just from [your name] that your mother had input into?" Ms Bashir suggested. "I suggest that you were, what do you say to that?" Ms Bashir said "[I say] that you're wrong," he answered. The trial heard Mr Jones and the boy met in person on several occasions, including at his Circular Quay apartment, at the boy's home and alone at a pub. It is alleged that after many invitations over several years, the boy agreed to spend two nights at Mr Jones's Fitzroy Fall's property when he was 17 years old. Complainant A said the alleged indecent assault occurred on the second day at the property and that it left him feeling "violated". The court heard, the boy later wrote a letter to his mother saying, "something happened at Fitzroy Falls" and took his allegation to police the next year.

events.title: Oil gains as Middle East hostilities stoke supply worries
events.summary: NBC News reported that President Donald Trump and his national security team have talked about possibly restarting large-scale U.S. military operations in Iran in the coming weeks. The energy infrastructure remains threatened by Houthis' recent attacks on Saudi Arabia which included two attacks on the kingdom's airports in Jazan and Najran. Oil rose Thursday as Middle East worries keep markets on edge, with the U.S. reportedly considering large-scale U.S. military operations in Iran in the coming weeks. Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery gained 1.36% at $101.54 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November advanced 1.04% at $89.32 per barrel. President Donald Trump and his national security team have talked about possibly restarting large-scale U.S. military operations in Iran in the coming weeks, NBC News reported, citing sources. That also includes the option of strikes prior to next month's midterm elections. Meanwhile, tensions in the Middle East have been rising with Iran-backed Houthis recently targeting airports in Saudi Arabia, while Tehran has also been attacking tankers in the Hormuz Strait. " Looking ahead, crude is likely to remain tied to the security of Gulf export routes and infrastructure," said Inki Cho, a financial markets consultant at online trading platform Exness. "Any escalation affecting traffic through Hormuz or Saudi energy infrastructure would threaten physical supply and could lift prices further," Cho added.

events.title: Democrats sue US President Trump over taxpayer-funded ad campaign
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Trump has faced a bipartisan backlash over ads that critics say violate prohibitions on taxpayer-funded propaganda. The Democratic National Committee has filed a lawsuit against United States President Donald Trump over television advertisements that were publicly funded and allegedly used to promote his political policies. Ken Martin, who heads the Democratic Party’s leadership body, suggested in a statement on Wednesday that the ads were designed to bolster Republican odds in the upcoming November 3 midterm elections . list 1 of 3 US FCC head says controversial Trump ads do not raise concerns list 2 of 3 ‘We’ll decide’: Trump hints he may pay for US government-funded ads list 3 of 3 Most Americans oppose Trump’s taxpayer-funded ‘golden age’ ads: Poll “Donald Trump is misusing millions of taxpayer dollars to fund pure propaganda ads in a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November,” Martin said. Later that day, Common Cause, a democracy watchdog group, filed a second lawsuit over the same set of ads. It argued that the ads were “overtly political” and therefore ran afoul of laws that bar public funds from being used for political propaganda. “These ads are not public-service announcements,” Common Cause said in its lawsuit, citing a justification Trump has offered for the television spots. “They are personal publicity and political propaganda through and through.” Both lawsuits argue that, to create the ad campaign, Trump directed the White House to repurpose $20m in funds that Congress allocated for commemorative activities related to border security, including for those killed in the line of duty. That manoeuvre, they argue, violates the separation of powers established in the US Constitution. “The founders made clear more than 200 years ago that the executive can spend money only according to Congress’s direction,” Common Cause’s lawsuit said. The two lawsuits also point to a provision Congress includes in its appropriations bills barring the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda purposes”. Both complaints seek to have the ads declared illegal, and the expenditures stopped. They also call for steps to be taken to recover any money already spent on the ads. The Democrats’ lawsuit was filed in Washington, DC, while the Common Cause complaint will be heard in the Southern District of New York. Trump has faced mounting criticism over the ads, which began airing in September. So far, the advertising campaign has cost more than $12m to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. The $20m Trump tapped for the ads comes from a $175m package Congress assigned to the Department of Homeland Security as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda. Critics have pointed out that one of the ads appears nearly identical to a television spot Trump used in his 2024 re-election campaign. Three ads have aired so far. In one, a choir sings “love me” over a montage of Trump as he declares the US will “never be a communist country”. Another uses images of Mount Rushmore as Trump heralds a new “golden age of America”. The third is darker: Trump walks towards the camera in black and white, warning of a “final battle” against the “deep state” and other perceived enemies. On Wednesday, the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos released a poll showing the ads are highly unpopular . Some 86 percent of the Americans surveyed, including four out of five Republicans, said it was inappropriate for Trump to have used public money for them. Trump has defended the ads as “promotion for the country”, and he has argued they were similar to public outreach campaigns put out by previous administrations. But after a bipartisan backlash, Trump said on Monday that taxpayer funds would no longer be used for future ads . He did not, however, commit to paying back the money already spent on the existing ads. Members of Trump’s Republican Party have been among those speaking out against the ad campaign. Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said the advertisements resembled something former Hungarian leader Viktor Orban would put out. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, meanwhile, indicated he agreed with the message in one of the advertisements, but he emphasised that “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars”.

events.title: Yemeni government forces claim 1,860 Houthis ‘neutralised’
events.summary: Yemeni government forces said in a social media post that they carried out 2,103 “precise targeting operations.” Yemeni government forces said they have “neutralised” 1,860 Houthi fighters since launching a large-scale counter-offensive to retake territory under control of the rebel group. The spokesperson for the internationally recognised government’s army said in a social media post early on Thursday local time that they carried out 2,103 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi military positions across several fronts as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” operation. list 1 of 3 Yemen’s Houthis attack Aden airport; Saudi forces down missile near Riyadh list 2 of 3 More than 200,000 displaced as fighting escalates in Yemen, UN says list 3 of 3 Three killed, 36 injured in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports, Riyadh says Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced on Sunday the “Dawn of Yemen” operation to retake all Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group has controlled since 2014. Battles in Yemen have focused in recent days on areas around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz. Forces aligned with the Yemeni government launched an operation on Tuesday to capture strategic territory near the strait and around the city of Mocha, which the Houthis had captured in September. The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday it destroyed 82 Houthi military targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada, Hodeidah, al-Jawf and Marib. The spokesperson for the coalition said in a statement the targets included ballistic missile sites including “11 mountain-based ballistic missile storages in Saada, command and control centres, communication systems, missile and weapons storages”. The new operation followed Houthi attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport, according to the spokesperson. Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said the attacks on the two airports killed three people. One person was killed and eight wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport, and two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on facilities at Abha airport, the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement.

events.title: DBS Hong Kong and Manulife Hong Kong mark 10 years of partnership with HK$1 million donation to support healthcare workers’ wellbeing
events.summary: To mark their 10th partnership anniversary, DBS Hong Kong and Manulife Hong Kong are supporting enhanced round-the-clock digital mental health resources for approximately 90,000 Hospital Authority healthcare workers. [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] As DBS Hong Kong and Manulife Hong Kong celebrate the 10th anniversary of their bancassurance partnership, the two organizations are marking the milestone with a HK$1 million donation to Oasis – Centre for Personal Growth & Crisis Intervention, a centre under the Hospital Authority's Corporate Clinical Psychology Services. The milestone also reflects a decade of collaboration in helping customers protect their wealth and plan for their long-term financial needs. Over the past decade, the partnership has expanded substantially, with annual insurance sales, measured by annualized premium equivalent, increasing by more than 400%* since the partnership was launched. The figure is based on internal sales data from DBS Hong Kong and Manulife Hong Kong, verified as of August 31, 2026. Oasis has long been providing psychological wellness and mental health support to the Hospital Authority staff. The funding from DBS Hong Kong and Manulife Hong Kong will expand the resources available through myOasis, allowing staff to access additional support around the clock. Around 90,000 healthcare workers across Hong Kong's public hospitals are expected to benefit from the initiative. Beyond commemorating a decade of partnership, the initiative reflects the companies' shared commitment to creating lasting value for customers and society. Sebastian Paredes, Head of North Asia and CEO of DBS Hong Kong, said the partnership had helped customers protect their wealth and plan for their long-term financial needs over the past decade. As the two companies marked the anniversary, he said they also wanted to support the wellbeing of healthcare workers who care for the Hong Kong community. “Their dedication to caring for our community deserves our collective support, and we hope this contribution will help strengthen their resilience and wellbeing for years to come,” said Paredes. Wilton Kee, CEO of Manulife Hong Kong and Macau, said the companies had combined their strengths and shared vision throughout their decade-long partnership to deliver insurance and wealth solutions that help customers secure their financial future. events.title: Revolut to open new Singapore office; will invest $350 million and grow staff to 300 here
events.summary: Revolut Singapore CEO Raymond Ng said that the new office signals the company’s commitment to Singapore. - Revolut will open a new Singapore office at Collyer Quay Centre in early 2027 and invest nearly $350 million over five years. - The fintech plans to grow its Singapore staff from nearly 170 to over 300 in three years, with more hires in engineering, product, data and AI. - Revolut wants to move beyond travel services and become a daily app for money, with more digital banking, investing and AI tools for users and businesses. SINGAPORE – Revolut will open a new office at Collyer Quay Centre as a mark of its expansion plans in Singapore and the region , the London-headquartered fintech company said on Oct 8. It will also invest nearly $350 million in Singapore over the next five years, spanning product innovation, business growth and the expansion of its local workforce. Revolut, which opened in Singapore in 2019, now hires nearly 170 people here, but plans to grow its headcount to more than 300 over the next three years . It already nearly doubled its headcount in 2025, and is planning to hire more people for roles across engineering, product, data and artificial intelligence. The new office, which will occupy 8,880 sq ft of office space on the ninth floor of Collyer Quay Centre, is scheduled to open in early 2027. The company will also have its name on the building. Revolut currently operates out of co-working space WeWork at Funan. Revolut Singapore chief executive Raymond Ng told The Straits Times: “I think having our own space is very important not only for our staff, but also for our users, so they get more familiar with us and our logo. “We want to be their daily app, not a travel app, because our ultimate aim is to be all things money to our users.” He added that the new office also signals the company’s commitment to Singapore, and forms a base for expansion into the region. Besides Singapore, Revolut is already in Japan, India, Australia and New Zealand in the Asia-Pacific region, and it is on the lookout for more opportunities. It also has a tech hub in the Philippines. Ng said: “We are always looking at opportunities to go into markets. It’s all about timing, and it’s all about whether there’s a market fit. We need to look at the business case and talk to the regulators.” Within Singapore, Ng also wants to shed the image of Revolut as solely a travel app for Singaporean travellers to hold different currencies. Revolut already has a cryptocurrency licence in Singapore, and users can also make investments and trade on the app. Revolut announced its new office building in Singapore on Oct 8. It also offers tiered subscriptions where users can access wealth and lifestyle products, such as VPN services, AI services and travel insurance, according to their tier. Ng said: “In Singapore, we started off by doing travel-related services, but now we want to be used more for daily services, too.” He added: “We have many very sophisticated users here, and the way we are going now is that by giving them all these services, they will be using us more and more daily, and not only for travel.” The firm’s investment in Singapore is to scale its retail and business user bases, particularly because Singapore is a financial and logistics hub. He noted that many companies set up regional offices in Singapore, and they have immediate needs like remittances and doing financial transactions. That is where Revolut can enter to help small and medium-sized enterprises and cross-border companies that might be scaling up or looking for a more integrated financial operating system. When asked about whether Revolut is applying for a digital bank licence in Singapore, Ng said he is unable to comment at this time. Revolut already holds digital bank licences in markets like Britain, Mexico, France and Australia. Ng said: “We don’t think of the licence first. We think of what is needed in the market, get feedback from the consumer, then at the right time, we will apply for the right licence. It’s all about product fit. And we don’t want to be making any comment till we are ready.” He noted that the main difference is that institutions without a banking licence are unable to hold customer deposits, provide interest on the deposits or offer loans the way a bank can. But Ng also sees Revolut as a tech company first, then a finance one. “It is a very tech-driven company, and then we go into providing many financial services and lifestyle services,” he said, adding that the company has written its own AI model using internal data and in-house data scientists. He added that an AI-enabled interface will soon arrive on the app for users here, too, which includes allowing users to execute commands on the app using voice control or prompts. Ng said: “We can’t escape that everything is going to be very digital. The consumer is actually asking for more now...

events.title: Japan beer giants raided over alleged price-fixing cartel
events.summary: Japanese officials have raided the country's biggest beer makers over allegations they worked together to raise the price of their beverages. Asahi, Sapporo, Kirin and Suntory Spirits confirmed to the BBC that their premises had been searched by the Japan Fair Trade Commission (JFTC), adding that they would fully cooperate with the regulator. The four firms dominate Japan's beer market, with their drinks a common sight in supermarkets and convenience stores across the country. Asahi, Kirin and Sapporo all saw their share price fall after news of the investigation broke on Wednesday. Suntory is not publicly-listed. "I do not deny that an investigation is being conducted today, but I'd like to refrain from commenting on the details as a preliminary review is underway," JFTC Secretary General Iwanari Hiroo said, according to local media. The BBC has contacted the JFTC for comment. According to the Japan Times, the investigation centres on the companies raising their prices in April last year and in October 2022. All four companies announced increases, citing the rising cost of raw materials as well as other factors such as energy and transportation. Kirin Holdings said its subsidiary, Kirin Brewery Company, was searched "on suspicion of a violation of the Antimonopoly Act". It said it takes the matter "very seriously", adding it would "fully cooperate with the Japan Fair Trade Commission's investigation and any requests for cooperation". Kirin Holdings said: "At present, the impact of this matter on the company's financial results has not been determined. The company will promptly disclose any material developments as they arise." A spokesperson for Suntory confirmed "an on-site inspection" had taken place "in connection with a potential violation of Japan's Antimonopoly Act relating to domestic alcohol trade practices". The company said: "We sincerely apologise for any concern or inconvenience this situation may cause to our customers, business partners, and other stakeholders. We will cooperate fully with the JFTC's investigation." Asahi said it was "subject to investigation by the Japan Fair Trade Commission" and that it will fully cooperate with the regulator. It follows an investigation by the regulator in June over alleged cartel activity by some of Japan's biggest ice cream makers , including Meiji and Pocky maker Ezaki Glico. events.title: Samsung forecasts record third-quarter profit of $80 billion as AI boom fuels chip demand
events.summary: Samsung Electronics estimated its third-quarter operating profit topped 100 trillion won for the first time in the company’s history. It reported preliminary operating profit of 107.4 trillion won, with more detailed results due later this month. Samsung Electronics on Thursday reported third-quarter preliminary operating profit of 107.40 trillion won ($80.2 billion), surging past 100 trillion won for the first time in the company's history as booming demand for artificial intelligence continues to fuel its chips business. Projected quarterly operating profit is 782% higher from a year earlier. Revenue forecast of about 195 trillion won is up nearly 127% from the same period last year. Samsung shares, however, dropped 0.7% Thursday morning. "Samsung has delivered a record profit and still fallen short of expectations, which tells you just how demanding the AI trade has become," said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at investment platform eToro. "When expectations are so high for memory makers, the market doesn't hand out points for effort." With AI spending driving demand for memory and supply remaining tight, the larger story of the chip sector remains intact, Gilbert said, highlighting growth of AI agents that can consume far more memory than a chatbot answering a single question. "Memory buyers are also committing to multiyear supply agreements, giving Samsung greater visibility over demand in a business where investors have always worried about the next downturn," he added. In the second quarter, the company posted record revenue of 171.5 trillion won and record operating profit of 89.5 trillion won, driven by its memory business. The company has also stepped up investments and partnerships tied to AI. In September, Samsung announced a strategic partnership with French artificial intelligence startup Mistral AI, with plans to deploy the startup's AI models across its semiconductor operations. Samsung is expected to release its full third-quarter earnings, including a breakdown by business division, later this month.

events.title: How kidnappings are hitting Nigeria’s Borno families hard
events.summary: Across Borno, abductions are leaving families with depleted savings, missing loved ones and disrupted education. Maiduguri, Nigeria – When Musa Abdullahi Wakawa learned that his wife and seven-year-old son had been abducted, disbelief quickly gave way to fear. Then came the question confronting many families caught in Nigeria’s kidnapping crisis: How could he raise the ransom demanded for their release? For days, Musa searched for a way to bring his family home, confronting the financial burden imposed by the kidnappers. Across northeastern Nigeria, families sell livestock, seek loans, dispose of property and exhaust savings in the hope of securing the release of loved ones. In Borno State, kidnapping has become more than a security threat. Families are losing money, living with the trauma of abduction and, in some communities, keeping their children away from school. ‘Please just help me with your prayers’ Laraba Dauda, 45, still remembers the last conversation she had with her younger sister. Her sister was abducted on January 13, 2026, along the Biu–Buratai road, according to Laraba. Shortly after the abduction, the phone rang. Her sister was calling from somewhere in the bush. “Aunty, unknown people have kidnapped us and taken us somewhere in the bush. We don’t know where they are taking us. At this moment, Aunty, please just help me with your prayers,” Laraba recalled her sister saying. Months later, Laraba and her family still do not know where she is being held or whether she is safe. Laraba is calling on the Nigerian government to intensify efforts to rescue those still in captivity. “We need the government to come to our aid and help rescue our relatives who have spent more than six months in captivity,” she said. A journey that never reached Maiduguri For Anjikwi Hena, his son’s disappearance came just as the family was looking towards a better future. His son was abducted on March 30, 2026, according to Hena. He had completed his education and was preparing to travel to Maiduguri in search of work. His father encouraged him and prayed for his success. Instead, the young man disappeared into captivity. Hena said their close relationship has made the uncertainty especially painful. The kidnapping crisis is also threatening education in communities already weakened by years of rebellion. In Askira-Uba Local Government Area of Borno State, only 56 of 113 primary schools are currently functioning, according to Fasuma Askira, the local government education secretary. Before the May attack in Mussa, 76 primary schools were operating. The threat of violence subsequently forced authorities to close another 20, leaving only 56 functioning. On May 15, suspected rebel fighters attacked Mussa and abducted dozens of children. A register later obtained by news services identified 40 missing children, although figures provided by the community and government have varied. The Borno State government has more recently referred to about 44 children still missing from Mussa. Then, on June 29, armed rebels attacked the Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were taking National Examinations Council examinations. Some students were recovered shortly after the attack, but 36 students and a teacher have been reported as remaining in captivity. The attacks have deepened fears among parents and teachers already living with the threat of rebel violence. The education authority moved junior secondary students from Mussa to a government boarding school in Uba and advised the local government to deploy community vigilantes around schools. Soldiers have also been deployed in Mussa and Lassa alongside local vigilantes, according to the Askira. For families in these communities, keeping children in school now means weighing access to education against the risk of further attacks. Borno’s crisis reflects a national problem The situation in Borno is part of a wider kidnapping crisis across Nigeria. Amnesty International Nigeria says at least 1,100 people were abducted across the country between January and April 2026, while warning that the actual figure could be considerably higher because many incidents in remote communities go unreported. “Apart from killing people, gunmen are now on a rampage of abductions, largely for lucrative ransom,” said Isa Sanusi, director of Amnesty International Nigeria. “Some stay months at the mercy of gunmen in punishing situations.” Amnesty says victims can face torture, starvation and sexual violence, while families are often forced to raise money under extreme pressure. The organisation has also warned that fear of abduction is pushing children out of school, particularly in rural communities. Government says security and humanitarian measures are under way Borno State Commissioner for Information and Internal Security Usman Tar said the government was using both military and nonmilitary measures to confront insecurity.

events.title: US stocks slide as oil prices fluctuate over renewed Iran war fears
events.summary: Oil prices rose on fresh concerns about Middle East supplies, before falling over possible release of more reserves. US financial markets have been whipsawed as bond market fears grow, pushing Treasury yields to their highest levels in more than 20 years, and oil prices continue to fluctuate, despite the Nasdaq and S&P 500 hitting record peaks. Wall Street closed lower on Wednesday as oil prices rose then fell due to renewed concerns about disruption to Middle East supplies. list 1 of 4 Southeast Asia’s energy chiefs meet against backdrop of Iran war list 2 of 4 Is Iran charging a toll to allow oil traffic through Hormuz? list 3 of 4 What new measures is Iran taking to counter US economic pressure? list 4 of 4 Has Russia’s fuel crisis given Iranian oil an opening in Central Asia? Stocks fell after closing at record highs in the previous session on Tuesday, with yields on US government bonds climbing to 24-year highs as investors worried about the impact of high oil prices on inflation and interest rates. Oil prices initially climbed on Wednesday following a warning that Iran appeared to be stepping up attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, before closing lower after International Energy Agency (IEA) member states said they were ready to release more strategic reserves. IEA member countries said they stand ready to release additional oil from their reserves if necessary and will prioritise diesel due to tight supplies of the fuel, the head of the organisation said on Wednesday. G7 countries, in coordination with the IEA, agreed last Friday to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by fallout from the United States-Iran war. The latest announcement from the IEA calmed oil markets after prices had climbed on Wednesday following a report from UK Maritime Trade Operations. The maritime agency said on Tuesday that there had been nine attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz this month, representing half of the September total in the waterway and the Gulf combined. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, repeated Washington’s claims that it was in control of the strait and that oil flows were at close to normal levels. Oil exports from the Gulf have recovered significantly in recent days, despite a surge in attacks on ships around the Strait of Hormuz, maritime experts and trackers say. Gulf oil flows, excluding Iran, recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, while crude exports from the wider Middle East exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days during the month, maritime intelligence firm Kpler reported. However, the recovery has come as attacks on tankers increase and shipping companies face higher freight, insurance and security costs. On Tuesday, 12 crew members on a Panama-flagged tanker were injured in an attack by an unknown projectile while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement.

events.title: Amazon employees hit by fresh job cuts across several teams
events.summary: The Amazon headquarters in the South Lake Union neighborhood of Seattle David Ryder/Bloomberg via Getty Images Amazon had fresh job cuts across several teams on Tuesday. Fewer than 1,000 people were affected by the layoffs. The cuts follow roughly 30,000 job eliminations late last year and early this year. Amazon employees reported a new round of job cuts across several parts of the company on Tuesday. A group of employees wrote in an internal Slack channel that they had received emails telling them their roles had been eliminated, according to messages viewed by Business Insider. The channel, which had nearly 37,000 members, quickly filled with questions about severance, access to internal job postings, and whether further notifications were still coming. The messages suggest cuts across several business units, including customer service, marketplace support, and engineering roles in Amazon’s retail business, as well as in India and the UK. Fewer than 1,000 employees were affected in total, according to a person familiar with the matter. The new cuts show that Amazon's cost overhaul is still reshaping its corporate workforce even as the company embarks on its biggest spending binge yet. After eliminating roughly 30,000 jobs late last year and early this year to cut costs and flatten its organization, Amazon is now preparing to spend a record $220 billion on data centers, chips, and other infrastructure for AI. An Amazon spokesperson confirmed to Business Insider that the company eliminated “a small number” of roles on Tuesday, primarily in its Stores business. "We're always looking at our team structures to ensure we're best set up to move fast as we innovate for customers," the spokesperson said. "We've adjusted parts of our Stores business because we believe this structure will better enable us to deliver on our priorities. As part of these changes, we've made the difficult decision to eliminate a small number of roles, and we're committed to supporting affected employees through their transition." The layoffs followed months of anxiety among Amazon's corporate workforce over the prospect of another broad round of cuts, according to people familiar with the matter. Employees have been bracing for layoffs after prior reductions, and some leaders have scaled back planning for the next several quarters partly because they expected their teams or priorities could change, according to one of the people. The uncertainty left employees parsing leadership meetings, calendar invitations, and team changes for clues. In the Slack channel, workers asked whether all notices had been sent, how medical leave would be handled, and whether they would retain access to Slack and Outlook during their notice periods. Others wondered whether cuts would reach Mexico and elsewhere in Europe. For many employees, the immediate question was whether they could find another job inside Amazon before their employment ended. One post asked whether workers who received an outside offer during the 90-day notification period would have to forfeit severance if they left early. Amazon is not alone in pairing job cuts with a bigger AI push. Meta eliminated roughly 8,000 roles in May while shifting thousands of other workers into AI initiatives, and Microsoft cut more than 5,000 jobs across July and September. Amazon, meanwhile, has also been reaching out to former employees , including some laid off in earlier rounds, about open roles in AWS and its AI businesses. Have a tip? events.title: Russia dismisses reports of second plague case as ‘false information’
events.summary: Senior WHO official urges Russia to to provide more information on the suspected pneumonic ⁠plague case. What we know about Russia’s suspected plague case Russia has dismissed media reports of a second suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia, as the World Health Organization (WHO) urged Moscow to formally respond to its inquiry regarding the reports. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday that “the vast majority of what the media is reporting regarding this situation is false information”, in response to a question about reports of a second case. list 1 of 3 Russia plague quarantine following lab death: Should we be worried? list 2 of 3 Russia denies imposing anti-plague measures after lab worker death list 3 of 3 US CDC says it’s ‘aware of and closely monitoring’ Russian plague case Peskov said that information on the suspected cases should be derived from official statements by Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor. Russia’s health regulator said there were no infections detected among staff after a plague institute worker died from pneumonia. The origin of the illness remains unknown, prompting international concern that the case could involve the plague. Russia acknowledged on Sunday that a 28-year-old woman employed at a plague research institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk died after she was diagnosed with a “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, prompting global concern over a suspected plague case. The United States, the European Union and the WHO have all called on Russia to be transparent about the situation. WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Russia to clarify “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause” at the Irkutsk institute. “We have received information from two media outlets, one of them is Russian,” Tedros said in a briefing on Wednesday, adding, “We asked Russia to respond to that.” “We cannot ignore any reporting that comes,” the WHO chief said. WHO Director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management Maria Van Kerkhove said the UN agency does not know the “causative agent” behind the death in the first suspected case. In a briefing, Van Kerkhove said, “We don’t understand how she was infected.” “We need information in a timely way. We need regular information. We need answers to the follow-up of the questions that we have asked,” she added. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) described the risk to the United States from the suspected pneumonic plague case as “extremely low”. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said on Wednesday that the US agency is working with the departments of Homeland Security, State, Defense and other agencies to monitor people travelling from the area. The CDC has a health station at New York City’s John F Kennedy International Airport that can screen travellers coming from the Siberian region, she added. About 200 people per year travel from the Siberian region to the United States, a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson told the Reuters news agency. Direct flights between Russia and the US have been suspended since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022. “What we’re doing from a whole of government standpoint is we’re making sure that we understand exactly what that threat is,” Schwartz said at the Wall Street Journal’s The Future of Health event in Washington, DC. “At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC said in a separate statement.

events.title: Inside India newsletter: Food crisis, economic shock ahead as India braces for El Niño
events.summary: Between June and September, India received its lowest rainfall in more than a decade owing to the El Niño effect. India’s foreign minister has warned El Niño, coupled with fertilizer shortages due to wars, will lead to a major food crisis in the coming months. El Niño is expected to materially slow down India’s rural economy and lead to a sharp rise in inflation. Rural demand in India is key for major multinational companies such as HUL, Colgate-Palmolive, Nestle, and the automaker Maruti Suzuki. Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to the latest edition of " Inside India " — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy. India is one of the largest producers of farm products and ranks among the world's top exporters of rice and sugar. Its farms help to feed almost 1.5 billion people, keep supply-side inflation under check, and sustain 46.1% of India's workforce, driving consumer spending. But this crucial sector now faces the heat from the so-called super El Niño. This week I dig deeper to understand what this global weather event holds for India . Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team. This year is not getting any better for the world's fastest-growing economy. The super El Niño weather phenomenon is emerging as the latest headwind for India's growth, which is already facing global energy shocks, trade uncertainty with the U.S. and record exits of foreign investors from its equity markets. From June to September, a key season for its mostly rain-fed farms and reservoirs, India received its lowest rainfall in more than a decade , as per local media reports. It was the fourth lowest since 2001, and the 13th driest since 1901 , according to the India Meteorological Department. Reservoirs in the country were 28% short of full capacity at the end of September and posed a risk to winter crops, according to a report by Nomura on Monday. Several parts of key farm states such as Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, and Haryana are facing extreme "drought conditions," Nomura stated. India and other countries are contending with " significant fertilizer shortages " as key producers in the Middle East and Russia have been impacted by geopolitical conflicts, Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said at an event organized by the non-profit Asia Society in New York last week. Jaishankar warned that with the super El Niño added to the mix, "there is going to be a major food crisis" in the coming months. Energy shocks and the flow of money to safe harbors have been "very stressful" for economies of the Global South, he said. The Global South is a term used to characterize less-developed or emerging economies. Following Jaishankar's comments, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's political opponents blamed the government for not acting in time to avert the crisis . Inflation in India has been rising for 10 straight months, crossing the central bank's medium-term target of 4% in August, even as economic growth has been resilient so far. While the share of farming in India's economy is around 17%, it provides a livelihood to roughly 46.1% of India's workforce . Its produce is pivotal in curbing supply-side inflation domestically, and the country ranks among the top global exporters of rice and sugar. The rural economy, largely dependent on farming, is also an important pillar of consumer spending. India's " monsoon deficit appears to be larger than originally expected," the World Bank said in a report on Tuesday. "This is expected to reduce agricultural output and rural demand while increasing food inflation, adding to existing pressure from higher energy prices," the report said. Rural areas account for nearly 40% of sales of fast-moving consumer goods, according to data from consultancy Nielsen Consumer. Rural demand is key for major multinational companies in India such as Hindustan Unilever , Colgate-Palmolive India , Nestle India , and the automakers Maruti Suzuki and Hyundai Motors , per market data based on annual reports and earnings calls. According to Hanna Luchnikava-Schorsch, head of Asia-Pacific economics at S&P Global Market Intelligence, India's rural economy is likely to slow "materially" in 2026 and 2027, "as drought conditions, below-normal monsoon rainfall and depleted reservoir levels reduce crop yields and farm incomes." While broader indicators have remained resilient so far, Luchnikava-Schorsch told CNBC that "early signs of stress are already emerging," adding that tractor sales had slowed and "demand for rural employment support programs has begun to rise." Morgan Stanley estimated that the gross value added by India's agricultural sector will grow by 1.6% in the financial year ending in March 2027, much slower than the 3.5% growth seen over the past three years. S&P Global Market Intelligence Analysis forecast growth would cool to 1.9%.

events.title: Fuel prices added to Google Maps as petrol and diesel costs soar
events.summary: The prices will be displayed when people search for fuel, as well as listed underneath descriptions of forecourts Google Maps will now show fuel prices to help motorists find cheaper petrol and diesel in the UK as costs continue to soar. From Thursday, a search for forecourts on the app will display their locations as well as their pricing, using data supplied via the government's Fuel Finder scheme. It is a legal requirement for UK forecourts to add their prices to Fuel Finder within 30 minutes of changing them. It comes days after the price of diesel topped £2 per litre for the first time , which RAC policy head Simon Williams described as "a price threshold no one wanted to cross". There are multiple apps dedicated to finding the cheapest fuel around, but Google Maps is used by 77% of Britain's adult population for general navigation, according to Ofcom. Fuel costs around the world have been dramatically impacted by the US war with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine. Diesel price has since fallen by 2p but the AA says an average 55 litre tank of diesel still costs around £110, with the petrol equivalent coming to around £96. The feature is already part of the navigation app Waze, which is used by around 2 million people in the UK. Apple Maps does not show the price of fuel, although some third-party apps can link to its maps on iPhones. Some experts say Fuel Finder is not entirely reliable. "At the moment, we still have to supplement the Government's Fuel Finder feed with other data sources because, on its own, it does not provide the level of coverage and accuracy needed to deliver a complete and reliable service to motorists," said Clare Lafferty, director at the price comparison site PetrolPrices. "There are still sites that have not registered with the scheme at all, alongside sites that have registered but are not consistently updating their prices within the required timeframe." She said the firm identified 200 forecourts in September which it did not believe had updated its diesel prices in time. Sarah-Jayne Williams, director of product partnerships for Google Maps and Waze, said the firm would check the data independently, and would not display prices it believed were not up-to-date. "Accuracy is very important, so we will still show the petrol station and where it is, but you'll only see a price if we have high confidence that it's the right price," she said. The Retail Motor Industry Federation, which represents thousands of UK forecourts and petrol retailers, said its members were complying. Fuel Finder was launched in February by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who said at the time it could save households £40 per year. events.title: EU-China trade talks begin in Beijing amid escalating pressure
events.summary: Talks will focus on the €1 billion daily deficit and rare earth export restrictions. European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic has arrived in Beijing for talks on the European Union’s (EU) growing trade deficit with China. Sefcovic will meet Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao on Thursday and Friday after months of discussions over the EU’s trade deficit of more than €1bn ($1.12bn) daily, as well as Chinese curbs on exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. list 1 of 3 Has Russia’s fuel crisis given Iranian oil an opening in Central Asia? list 2 of 3 Coco Gauff says online racist abuse was ‘draining’ after China Open exit list 3 of 3 FBI arrests ‘Chinese foreign agent’ for spying on Taiwan president’s son Meanwhile, Chinese companies are increasingly challenging Europe’s top car brands. China rejected the EU request for voluntary curbs on Chinese hybrid car exports as the two sides enter negotiations, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. The European Commission now hopes to get Beijing to accept a unilateral EU measure to cap hybrid imports instead, the outlet said, citing two diplomats briefed on the plan. The two days of discussions come just as a majority of EU lawmakers called for a more assertive trade policy towards Beijing in a non-binding resolution on Wednesday. China vowed a “resolute response” to safeguard its industries if the European Union goes ahead with restrictions against Chinese companies or products, according to its commerce ministry. Germany and France propose rapid EU measure French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, leaders of the bloc’s two biggest powers, on Tuesday urged the EU to prepare a “credible instrument” that could be quickly activated to strike back against countries that harm the bloc economically. The new measure would not target any specific country. German officials said the EU needed a tool as powerful as the Section 301 tariffs imposed by the United States or China’s restrictions on critical-mineral exports. The proposed weapon – to be discussed at an EU leaders’ summit next week – would give the European Commission the power to respond to a trade aggression within days. China responded to the letter by urging Paris and Berlin to steer clear of “protectionist” measures. “We hope that France and Germany, as major economies in the world, will uphold openness, cooperation and free trade,” the commerce ministry said in a statement. “They should avoid going down the wrong path in the wrong way, only to ultimately suffer the consequences themselves.” G20 finance leaders, except China’s, agreed in September to act against “non-market” distortions that exacerbate imbalances. Beijing says that hyping up issues such as economic imbalances and overcapacity is a form of protectionism designed to exert pressure on and restrict China. EU and Chinese officials have been discussing trade imbalances since June. Sefcovic said he wanted “tangible results by October” as well as some form of commitment that can be put to EU leaders meeting in Brussels. Trade relations with China top the summit’s agenda next week, as ballooning debt has prompted auditors to warn about the next seven-year EU budget and has spurred protests in France. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament last month that the trade imbalance had reached a tipping point and that Europe would use every tool at its disposal to rebalance the relationship.

events.title: UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon says shots fired at Israeli border post
events.summary: The United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon said there were no casualties after small arms fire targeted a border post. The United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) says one of its posts on the Lebanon-Israel border was targeted by small arms fire, with no casualties reported. The UN force said the incident occurred on Wednesday morning with several rounds of small arms fire targeting a UNIFIL position near Kfar Shouba along the UN-drawn border with Israel, known as the Blue Line. list 1 of 3 Irish soldier killed in attack on UN convoy in Lebanon list 2 of 3 How and why UNIFIL failed to ‘keep peace’ in Lebanon list 3 of 3 French soldier serving with UNIFIL killed in Lebanon attack “Such deliberate attacks gravely endanger the lives of peacekeepers,” UNIFIL said in a statement, adding that it was investigating the incident. Under pressure from the United States and Israel, the UN Security Council decided earlier this year to set December 31 as the end of the mandate for the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon. UNIFIL was initially created to oversee the withdrawal of Israeli troops from southern Lebanon after Israel’s 1978 invasion, and its mandate has been renewed annually since then. The mission was expanded after the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah. Proponents say it remains important to maintaining a demilitarised buffer between the two sides along the volatile Israeli and Lebanese border. Israel has long accused UNIFIL of failing to prevent threats posed by Hezbollah and has increasingly pushed for the end of its mission since cross-border fighting escalated in the wake of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks on Israel and the start of Israel’s war on Gaza. UNIFIL currently has 7,500 peacekeepers from around 50 countries operating in Southern Lebanon. Last month, Lebanon’s Prime Minister Nawaf Salam pressed the UN on the need to “avert the vacuum” that would be caused by withdrawing the mission from the country’s south without a viable replacement. Violence has decreased since a ceasefire following a June memorandum of understanding in the US-Iran war. Lebanon and Israel concluded a US-sponsored framework agreement later that month. The Israel-Lebanon deal involves the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon’s south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region, starting in test areas known as “pilot zones”.

events.title: DNC sues to stop Trump's taxpayer-funded ad blitz
events.summary: The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration on Wednesday over its campaign-style ads . Why it matters: The DNC alleges the ads, which have drawn considerable backlash as they were originally paid for with taxpayer money, violate several federal laws. What they're saying: "These ads are a clear violation of the Congressional ban on the use of appropriated funds for 'publicity or propaganda purposes,'" the DNC's legal counsel wrote in the lawsuit . "The president has nationalized the midterm election, made himself the center of a two-day 'midterm convention,' and repeatedly directed voters to 'pretend that I am on the ballot," it added. "As the 2026 midterm election has approached, Republican poll numbers have plummeted in both traditional battlegrounds and typically favorable states, and Democrats are poised to take control of Congress, governors' mansions, and state legislatures around the country." Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom in: The lawsuit alleges the White House crafted the ads to boost the president's approval ratings and help Republican candidates. The complaint largely focuses on its allegation that the ads were paid for with money originally allocated for Customs and Border Protection that was rerouted for the TV spots. The DNC argues that the ads violate the Administrative Procedure Act, the Antideficiency Act, and the Purpose Act. The DNC asked a federal judge to step in, declare the administration's actions illegal and immediately block them from airing any more ads paid for with taxpayer money. It's not clear how the judge will rule, given President Trump said Monday that a Trump-affiliated super PAC would begin paying for the ads moving forward. A White House spokesperson confirmed Tuesday to Axios that the administration would not repay the government for the ads. Catch up quick: According to the suit, Trump personally hand-picked the ads that aired on television, which were broadcast to millions of Americans, including during NFL and college football games. The lawsuit says the ads aired "nearly 90 times across national television networks, including Fox, Newsmax, MS Now, and CBS" over four days in late September. Those spots likely cost around $337,000. In that same time period, the ads aired on local television stations at least 2,311 times and those placements cost around $1.4 million, the suit says. Advertisement tracking firm AdImpact estimates that over $2.5 million was spent on the ads the first week they were aired. Worth noting: Using public funds for campaign ads hasn't sat well with American voters. Nearly nine in ten voters said in a Reuters-Ipsos poll published Wednesday that using taxpayer money for campaign ads featuring a president or Cabinet member is inappropriate. events.title: Africa launches credit rating agency
events.summary: The News Africa’s long-planned credit rating agency launches in Mauritius on Wednesday, the continent’s most concrete answer yet to years of complaints that the world’s biggest agencies overstate African risk and drive up borrowing costs. The creation of the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) comes as global agencies face growing criticism for relying on offshore models that some African leaders and policymakers say misread local realities — a debate sharpened this year by Afreximbank’s public break with Fitch . AfCRA will rate governments, cities and companies, and it is meant to complement the three US firms, which control 95% of global ratings markets. The new ratings agency “ will add another opinion in the market place of opinions ,” said Marie-Antoinette Rose-Quatre, head of the AU body that incubated it. She called it “a very tangible outcome of our aspiration to build our own financial institutions”. Only three African sovereigns hold investment grade ratings, according to a background note from the AU’s African Peer Review Mechanism (ARPM). Thirteen are rated at very high risk or in default, and 23 have no rating from the big agencies, which cuts them from international bond markets. The AU has also said the continent’s external debt service costs climbed from roughly $60 billion in 2010 to more than $160 billion in 2024. Know More The launch is part of a wider push by developing countries, at the G20 and the UN, to change how global finance prices their risk. South Africa used its 2025 G20 presidency to put borrowing costs on the agenda. In an op-ed published in Africa Renewal, the UN magazine, Rose-Quatre and Ahunna Eziakonwa, the UN secretary-general’s special adviser on Africa, said unfair ratings cost Africa $74.5 billion a year — an estimate which was first published by the UN Development Programme in 2023. Key details of the new agency remain unclear. The APRM describes it as privately owned and self-funded but has not named its shareholders, chief executive, or board. Mauritius Commercial Bank and the pan-African lender Afreximbank took part in a 2025 meeting to raise support for the project. According to the APRM note, AfCRA “will require a licence” from Mauritius’ financial regulator. People close to the project say trust will take time. “Credibility in credit rating is accumulated rather than declared,” said Daniel Cash, a UK-based law professor who has advised the APRM on credit ratings. The real test, he told Semafor, will come when AfCRA issues a rating that a member state, “particularly an influential one” strongly dislikes. “Independence is demonstrated at the point of disagreement.” The launch also comes as global agencies expand on the continent. Moody’s owns GCR, the largest issuer of ratings in Africa, and in July S&P agreed to buy a majority stake in Nigeria’s Agusto & Co. S&P Global declined to comment, while Moody’s and Fitch did not respond to requests for comment. Tiisetso’s view For half a century, the cost of African borrowing has been set largely in New York by three firms that rate the 55 countries from a distance. AfCRA is the continent finally taking a seat at the table where its risk is priced. Every 10 basis points shaved off a $1 billion Eurobond saves an issuer $1 million a year. Twenty-three states have no rating from the big agencies at all, which locks them out of mandates that require one. That’s the prize. True, AfCRA has no track record and no named shareholders, but the quickest route to credibility runs through pain: an early, well-argued downgrade of one of the governments that cheered the launch. Room for Disagreement Critics question whether investors will trust any agency created by the governments it rates. David Lubin of UK think tank Chatham House asked whether AfCRA amounts to Africa “marking its own homework,” adding that fund managers compare African borrowers with the rest of the world and an African agency “does nothing” for them. Misheck Mutize, AfCRA’s chief architect, acknowledged that the agency’s main role would be to steer Africa’s $4 trillion savings into African assets rather than changing how foreign investors see the continent. “The challenge here is that this is the bare minimum disclosure required before international investors can even begin to take AfCRA seriously,” said Bright Simons, head of research at IMANI, a think tank based in Accra, writing on public policy platform Katanomics Society. Notable Nigerian President Bola Tinubu made the case for an African rating agency , arguing that the Big Three misjudge African risk and that a homegrown agency could spot progress early, which the global firms would later confirm.

events.title: Christa Pike was nearly taken off life support before waking, lawyers say
events.summary: Death-row inmate who survived execution by lethal injection is said to be ‘angry and confused’ about what happened. Lawyers for Christa Pike , the Tennessee woman who survived a botched execution attempt, have said that their client was nearly disconnected from life support before she awoke this week in a United States hospital. In a news conference on Wednesday, Randy Spivey, who represents Pike, described her as feeling “angry and confused” about what happened. list 1 of 3 Tennessee prisons official resigns after Christa Pike’s failed US execution list 2 of 3 Christa Pike lawyers say she is speaking one week after failed execution list 3 of 3 Christa Pike is awake after surviving execution: What happens now? “Monday night, our understanding was that Christa was brain dead, and life support would be removed the next day,” Spivey told reporters. But on Tuesday, he said, “Christa woke up and began talking.” Spivey added that Pike did not seem to recall the execution attempt itself. Upon waking up in her hospital room in Nashville, she reportedly asked those in the room, “Where am I?” and “Who are you?” Pike had been scheduled to die by lethal injection on September 30. But after receiving two doses of pentobarbital, she remained alive, becoming the first person believed to have survived such an injection in the US. The incident has renewed questions about the use of the death penalty in the country and its legality. Critics have long called such procedures a violation of the Eighth Amendment of the US Constitution, which prohibits “cruel and unusual punishments”. Prior to her execution date, Pike’s lawyers had also sought to have her sentence commuted, citing concerns about her mental health. She had been convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for participating in the murder of a classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. On Wednesday, her legal team described her as cooperating with Tennessee officials during the scheduled execution. “She was kind and polite as they worked for an hour, stabbing her arm with needle after needle, and then she felt the burn of the pentobarbital,” Spivey said. “And then she woke up in a hospital surrounded by people she didn’t know.” While the lethal injections were meant to go into Pike’s veins, experts have speculated that the pentobarbital instead pooled in the tissue of her arm. Her arms and hands remain heavily swollen and covered in blisters, Spivey added. It is unclear whether the state of Tennessee will attempt to execute Pike a second time. But Spivey has indicated he and Pike’s other lawyers will once more seek to have her sentence commuted, based on the suffering she experienced during the botched execution. On Wednesday, in anticipation of such legal proceedings, Nashville Judge I’Ashea Myles ordered the state to save evidence from the execution attempt, including drugs, syringes and IV lines, as well as recordings and any communication records between officials. Since the execution attempt, Tennessee’s Republican Governor Bill Lee has also ordered a halt to carrying out other death penalty sentences. Another execution had been scheduled in the state for later this year. “Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” Lee said in a statement. In the wake of the botched execution, the state’s top prison official, Tennessee Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, has announced he will resign this month. Pike’s lethal injection was not the only botched execution in Tennessee this year. Governor Lee granted a one-year reprieve to Tony Carruthers, whom officials attempted to execute in May 2026. But after an hour of trying, they could not find a vein to connect an IV for the pentobarbital, and the execution was suspended. Other states, however, have signalled they would proceed with carrying out death penalty cases despite the Tennessee incidents. A Texas court refused to halt the execution by pentobarbital of 46-year-old Jamaal Howard, scheduled for Wednesday, despite appeals from his lawyers citing Pike’s botched execution. Those opposed to the death penalty have argued that such executions can cause unnecessary suffering. In Pike’s case, she reportedly kicked a sheet off her body during the execution attempt and said she was feeling pain. Before her scheduled execution, Pike had warned authorities about the difficulty of finding veins in her arm and had even requested to be executed by firing squad.

events.title: Trump trade chief Greer reports higher cash holdings as law firm pay topped $650K
events.summary: U.S. trade representative Jamieson Greer reported roughly $1.17 million to $3.75 million in cash, retirement accounts and other investments in his 2025 financial disclosure. Greer reported $652,610 in salary and bonus from King & Spalding in 2025, while one bank account increased to $500,001 to $1 million. Greer received a $10,000 honorarium from Coupang in May 2024 and met with the company at USTR 11 months later, though public records do not establish that the meeting violated federal ethics rules. U.S. trade representative Jamieson Greer reported roughly $1.17 million to $3.75 million in cash, retirement accounts and other investments according to a CNBC analysis of his newly obtained 2025 annual financial disclosure. The 16-page filing from the Office of Government Ethics, offers a new look at the finances of President Donald Trump's top trade official after he left a lucrative partnership at the King & Spalding law firm to join the administration in February 2025. Greer reported receiving $652,610 in salary and bonus from the firm in 2025. In his nominee disclosure , he listed an anticipated performance-based bonus for work performed in 2024, valued at $250,001 to $500,000, that would be paid before he entered government. He had previously reported about $1.5 million in salary and bonus from King & Spalding. One of the clearest changes in the new filing is Greer's cash holdings. An account labeled "U.S. bank #2" jumped from $250,001-$500,000 in his nominee filing to $500,001-$1 million in the new disclosure. It generated another $15,001-$50,000 in interest. Federal disclosures report most assets in broad ranges, making it impossible to determine precisely how Greer's wealth changed. The asset total is also not an estimate of his net worth; his personal residence is not valued in the filing, while he reported a mortgage of between $1 million and $5 million at a 2.375% interest rate. Pete Hegseth reports at least $3.1 million in cash, investments and bitcoin Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reports more than $250 million in income last year NYSE CEO Sprecher, SBA head Loeffler’s husband, has ties to Trump Jr.-backed private club David Sacks sold $200 million in crypto-related holdings before taking White House job Beyond Greer's newest disclosure, CNBC's review of his finances and ethics records show a previously unreported timeline involving Coupang , the e-commerce giant often dubbed the "Amazon of South Korea." Coupang has become a trade flashpoint , with U.S. investors accusing Seoul of unfairly targeting the company after a major data breach — claims the South Korean government disputes. Greer's nominee disclosure shows that Coupang paid him a $10,000 honorarium in May 2024. Eleven months later, on April 24, 2025, he met with the company at USTR during a day of trade talks , shortly after meeting South Korean trade minister Ahn Duk-geun. Before taking office, Greer had pledged to avoid certain matters involving former clients for one year unless ethics officials cleared his participation. Public records reviewed by CNBC do not show whether USTR treated Coupang as a former client under that commitment or whether Greer received authorization to participate in the meeting. His nominee filing describes the Coupang payment as an "honorarium," while separately identifying other companies as legal services clients. USTR and Coupang did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
