events.title: Here's how the largest fraternities earn and spend their millions
events.summary: Students at the University of Michigan gather at the Sigma Chi fraternity house to party on a Saturday afternoon. : Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Greek life is a dominant force on US college campuses, and organizations manage millions annually. Fraternities generate millions through member dues, alumni donations, and real estate investments. Many Greek-letter organizations report tax filings under various entities. Fraternities are a staple of the American college experience, whether it's for their social influence on campus, sprawling alumni networks , or, at times, controversies . But behind the parties and secretive traditions are tax-exempt organizations that bring in millions of dollars each year. Tax filings offer a partial glimpse into how the country's biggest fraternities earn and spend their money. Sigma Phi Epsilon Fraternity Inc., the national organization behind one of the largest fraternities across US college campuses , reported $10.6 million in revenue in fiscal 2025 and ended the year with $29.4 million in net assets, according to public tax filings . In comparison, Chi Phi Fraternity Inc., which has about 48 active chapters nationwide and is affiliated with Cornell's now-shuttered Chi Phi chapter, reported $1.8 million in revenue and $2.1 million in net assets in the same year, per its tax filings . Chi Phi declined a request for comment from Business Insider. Because many fraternities' local chapters, philanthropic foundations , and housing groups operate independently, tax filings often show only part of their broader, more complex financial picture. Take a look into how the US's largest fraternities earn and spend their millions — and what little is known about their internal finances. Every semester, thousands of students rush to join fraternities across the US. (Photo by Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis via Getty Images)'Rushing' for a fraternity at the University of Florida, Gainesville Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis via Getty Images Recruitment brings new dues-paying members to Greek life organizations, reaching thousands of students across college campuses. At Miami University in Ohio , for example, 2,208 students registered for Greek-life recruitment in spring 2026. This included 859 men who registered for recruitment with the school's 25 Interfraternity Council fraternities. At the University of Arizona, members of the 20 fraternities in the Interfraternity Council pay an average of about $1,573 per semester in active-member fees, excluding housing, as of summer 2026, according to the university's Sorority and Fraternity Programs website. Including housing, the average is about $5,535 per semester. The university adds that the organizations set and collect their own dues independently. events.title: Trump doesn't think Russia plague incident is bioweapon, plans Putin call Wednesday
events.summary: The U.S. does not think the death of a Russian laboratory worker from a suspected case of plague is the result of a bioweapon, President Donald Trump said. Trump plans to call Russian President Vladimir Putin later in the day, which is Putin's birthday. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that the U.S. does not think the death of a Russian laboratory worker from a suspected case of plague is the result of a bioweapon. Trump also said he planned to call Russian President Vladimir Putin , who turned 74 on Wednesday, later in the day. Trump previously had said that call would focus on the plague-related incident. Trump's comments came at an Oval Office event promoting Trump Accounts , the new tax-deferred savings and investment accounts that more than 60 million American children under age 18 have been automatically enrolled in. Russian media reported earlier this week that nearly 200 people had been placed under medical observation in Russia 's Irkutsk region in eastern Siberia over suspected exposure to plague, after a female worker at an anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk fell ill and died. A reporter at Wednesday's Oval Office event asked Trump, "Is the plague in Russia a bioweapon?" Trump replied, "Well, we don't think so." events.title: Trump’s diesel order exposes White House limits to counter surging fuel prices
events.summary: President Donald Trump's order allowing highway truckers to use off-road diesel only defers federal excise taxes. Truckers may still have to pay later. Trump's order does not defer state excise taxes, which can be higher. The latest move comes after the president abandoned the idea of banning diesel exports. Analysts say the only real solution to high fuel prices is an end to the war in the Middle East. Truckers likely won't see much in the way of relief from President Donald Trump's executive order that allows them to use off-road diesel fuel on America's highways without federal penalties, analysts say. Off-road diesel is exempt from federal and state excise taxes because it is used for construction and farm equipment, railways and to heat homes. It is dyed red to differentiate it from taxed on-road diesel, but is otherwise the same fuel. The federal government charges an excise tax of 24.4 cents per gallon for on-road diesel. In theory, Trump's order spares truckers the tax by allowing them to use red-dyed fuel on the highway, without worrying that the federal government will impose penalties. But the president's action only defers the actual tax payment itself until the end of the year, while calling on the Treasury secretary to look for ways to eliminate the deferred obligation altogether. "While it might be deferred, it may not disappear entirely," said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. "Maybe you save a little bit of money up front, but you might have to pay it to the government later." Treasury is preparing guidance to provide "clarity on the obligations for users and sellers of dyed diesel," a White House official told CNBC. The official asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly about the the plans. Treasury has enforcement discretion, the official said. The Internal Revenue Service will only enforce the deferred tax liability if it is directed to do so by the Treasury secretary and the president, the official said. The IRS will soon make a determination on "whether dedicating its limited resources to fuel tank inspections and fuel sampling investigations represents the best use" of its resources, the official said. Trump cannot defer state excise taxes, which can be higher than the federal obligation, at a national average of 35.5 cents per gallon. Some states have taken independent action to give relief to diesel users. Although Trump is waiving federal penalties for using off-road diesel on highways, states in principle could enforce their local laws prohibiting the red-dyed fuel on the road. "It's not like every state trooper is going to pull over the truck and look at your diesel fuel, but you're a trucker — do you need that aggravation?" Lipow said. Trump's executive order comes as he faces political pressure to take action on diesel prices ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3, when Republicans face competitive races in farm states such as Iowa. Retail diesel prices hit a record high in September and currently average $6.30 a gallon nationally, according to AAA. The president flirted with a diesel export ban last month but ultimately abandoned the idea, telling reporters Friday that "it was never really on the table." The oil industry and big business groups were staunchly opposed. Trump publicly voiced concerns that a diesel export ban would raise gasoline prices. Diesel futures dropped overnight Monday into Tuesday morning after Trump's executive order, but ultimately turned higher. Futures were up more than 1% Wednesday. "What it shows you is there are no good options for the administration or any administration to bring down the price of fuel, because the bottleneck is refineries," Lipow said. Diesel prices are high around the world because Ukraine is bombarding Russian refineries and strikes by Iran and its allies have taken capacity offline in the Middle East. G7 countries led by France, facing pressure from the Trump administration, agreed Friday to release diesel stocks , though it's unclear in what quantities. "They're pulling every lever they can," Jeff Currie, CEO of Real Macro and a senior advisor at Carlyle, told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Tuesday. But Trump's executive order allowing red-dyed diesel on the road "won't have a profound impact" on fuel prices, Currie said. There is one action the administration could take that would be effective, Lipow said. "End the conflict." "The Strait [of Hormuz] reopens, oil flows, those refineries in the Middle East start kicking up runs, more refined products make it to the market," the analyst said. "The market will react to that."

events.title: Apollo, banks in talks to finance SpaceX's $40 billion Nvidia GPU purchase
events.summary: Apollo Capital and several banks are in talks with SpaceX to facilitate the $40 billion purchase of Nvidia GPUs, a source told CNBC. The deal will primarily rely on the investment-grade debt market. Discussions are preliminary and details have yet to be finalized, including key lenders. Apollo Capital Management and several banks are in discussions with SpaceX to help facilitate the company's purchase of $40 billion worth of Nvidia graphics processing units, according to a person familiar with the talks who asked not to be named to discuss the matter. The deal will primarily rely on the investment-grade debt market, which SpaceX just tapped four months ago, the person said. Two weeks after its record-breaking IPO in mid-June, the space exploration company raised $25 billion in bonds at different durations. CNBC was told at the time that SpaceX's bond sale saw incredibly high demand, highlighting strong interest from fixed-income investors. But since then, artificial intelligence-related bonds have sold off, while credit spreads have widened. SpaceX's $40 billion debt deal will likely use GPUs as collateral and Apollo Capital is said to be playing a leading role in facilitating the financing, the person said. Apollo declined to comment. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The market is still operating under the expectation that GPUs hold their value for about seven years, according to a person in the credit industry who asked not to be named to discuss the matter. Computing power is scarce and the shortage is not expected to abate anytime soon, which supports the value of high-performing GPUs. The Financial Times was first to report on the financing talks. Google ordered to halt work on two data centers in 'Texas of Europe' Meta joins with group of companies to tame 'chaos' of doing business with AI bots Anduril lands $2.9 billion Navy submarine shipyard contract days after Luckey joins Pentagon weapons group Anthropic expands Claude Startups program in bid to snag founders and fast-growing companies While a bond deal of this size is notable, it follows a series of bond issuances from Meta , Amazon and Google as the cost to fund the AI buildout gets more expensive. Both sources told CNBC that more debt sales are expected, fixed-income investors are demanding a higher yield to service the debt, a sign that participants are becoming more selective about their AI exposure. SpaceX is already running a massive load of Nvidia AI chips and has plans to add to it. CEO Elon Musk said in a Sept. 24 post on X that his company's Colossus data center in Memphis, Tenn., was running 230,000 Nvidia AI chips, while Colossus 2 had 550,000. Musk said the company would more than double the number of chips by late December to reach 1.21 million, "If we get lucky." For the SpaceX bulls, the company has inked compute deals with Google, Anthropic , Reflection AI and Cursor, which it later bought, and bringing more capacity online could boost revenue quickly. On the flipside, the company reported nearly $40 billion in debt in its second-quarter financials, and its existing debt trades near junk bond levels, as credit markets have, overall, been more skittish. However, to make SpaceX's ambitions a reality, it needs to keep spending — and on more than just chips. —CNBC's Morgan Brennan contributed to this article

What is the context for the first return of series since ‘Sandpapergate’ South Africa have played Tests in Australia since ‘Sandpapergate’, and ‌Australia have toured South Africa in the interim for limited-overs internationals. The scandal has attracted little media focus in South Africa over recent weeks in comparison to the attention devoted to the incident in the Australian press. After dethroning Australia last year in a thrilling World Test Championship (WTC) final at Lord’s to win a first major title, South Africa are focused on improving their chances of a return to the final at the end of the 2025–27 ⁠WTC cycle. What shape are South Africa in for the visit of Australia? The pitch at Kingsmead often proves a fickle track but should offer the spinners a chance to play a leading role in ⁠a change from South Africa’s usually seamer-friendly surfaces. It is unusual for South Africa’s chances to be largely entrusted to their spin attack, but Simon ⁠Harmer and Keshav Maharaj wreaked havoc in India last November ⁠when they triumphed in their last two Test outings. Spin was also a key factor for the home side as they beat Australia in the recent One-Day International series. South Africa may therefore opt to rest frontline attack bowler Kagiso Rabada from ‌the Test as he continues his comeback from a hamstring injury. South Africa also have a choice to make over their number three batsman, with coach Shukri Conrad having several options including a potential first cap for 30-year-old Marques Ackerman. How are Australia poised for their South Africa return? Australia are also in need of a boost after a surprise ⁠home Test defeat by Bangladesh in August in their drawn series , and with an Ashes tour to England starting next June. Injury to Australia all-rounder Cameron Green opens up a chance at number five for Cooper Connolly, or a fairytale return for ‌34-year-old ‌Nic Maddinson after recovering from cancer. Head hits back at former Australia players in defence of Test team Australia opener Travis Head has taken to task former Test players turned critics whom he accused on Wednesday of “putting a bullet” through the current team. Head did not single out any pundit directly, but his strong remarks at a news conference came the day after Matthew Hayden, one-time holder of the record ⁠for the most runs in a Test innings, accused selectors of “promoting the greatest pile of mediocrity that we’ve seen in a generation of cricket”. The reference, made in a podcast, was about the recall of Maddinson, who has been out of Test cricket for nearly 10 years, but who joined the squad in South Africa after Josh Inglis ‌fractured his finger and Cameron Green suffered a stomach injury. “I think it’s unfairly judged a fair bit from a group of past players, pretty much that put the bullet through a lot of players, which I think is unfair,” Head said. “But that’s what they’re paid to do. Some of them need a job, so they go after us, and that’s totally fine. “This group is strong enough to deal with those sorts of things. That’s how it is. It’s unfortunate sometimes to have some of that feedback from a ⁠generation of players that we have huge respect for, but that’s the caper.” Why have Australia selectors been accused of disrespecting cricket? Hayden accused the selectors of “disrespecting first-class cricket”, asserting that batsmen should have an average of 45 runs or more before being considered for Test selection. Head, however, praised Maddinson’s abilities and the benefits of choosing experienced players for Test cricket despite the 34-year-old ⁠replacement having a first-class average of 37.11. “We need mature guys that know what they need to be doing,” Head said.

events.title: Harmanpreet Kaur: The captain who changed how India’s women played cricket
events.summary: Harmanpreet Kaur’s magical innings instilled belief in the Indian women’s cricket team in 2017, before she led them to their first World Cup eight years later. For nine years, Harmanpreet Kaur’s career as captain of the Indian women’s cricket team teetered on the brink of near-misses and lingering deliberations. The biggest question centred on an elusive maiden World Cup title and India’s failure to cross the final hurdle at major tournaments. list 1 of 4 ‘Unstoppable’ Rumesh revives Sri Lanka’s glory, one javelin throw at a time list 2 of 4 The return of Palestinian football: ‘We are a people who must live’ list 3 of 4 Migrants ‘are not to blame’: How the Ceuta crisis engulfed Spanish football list 4 of 4 Ireland lost to Israel when they stepped on the pitch Their breakout run at the one-day international (ODI) World Cup ended in heartbreak in 2017, a year after Kaur was appointed captain in the Twenty20 format and earmarked to take over the reins across all formats of the game. Under her leadership, India qualified for but lost their first T20 World Cup final in 2020 and ended with a silver medal at the Commonwealth Games in 2022, before suffering another agonising T20 World Cup semifinal defeat in 2023. In November 2025, the what-if was finally buried. Kaur’s India beat then-defending champions Australia in a sensational come-from-behind World Cup semifinal before overcoming a resolute South Africa in the final to be crowned world champions for the first time – in front of adoring home fans. Less than a year later, on October 6, 2026, Kaur stepped down as India’s all-format captain , ending a decade-long leadership journey that saw India transform into world champions after decades spent chasing cricket’s traditional heavyweights Australia and England. “This is not an easy decision,” the 37-year-old wrote in an Instagram post, adding that she will continue to play international cricket. “As a captain, I have had to make difficult decisions. Decisions that were not always understood, not always easy, and sometimes came at a personal cost.” The announcement was made after discussions on the future of Indian women’s cricket, which took place a day earlier between Kaur, Smriti Mandhana, head coach Amol Muzumdar and Devajit Saikia, honorary secretary of the Indian cricket board. Mandhana, who was Kaur’s deputy for four years, replaced her as captain. Kaur, India’s most capped women’s cricketer, enjoyed a leadership stint that included five Test matches, 51 ODIs and 155 T20Is, with win percentages of 80, 58.82 and 59.35 respectively. The Punjab-born top-order batter’s last game in charge was the recently concluded Asian Games in Japan, where India stepped on the podium as gold medallists . Nine days earlier, Kaur led them to an Asia Cup trophy in the United Arab Emirates. The medals and trophies tell one part of Kaur’s tale as captain. The other lies in how India learned to play differently under her. Kaur took over as India’s full-time T20I captain in 2016, after the team’s disappointing group-stage exit at a home T20 World Cup. It followed a match-winning innings that helped India win their first T20I series against Australia in any format, and a few months later, she was signed as the first Indian cricketer in the Big Bash League, Australia’s franchise T20 cricket competition It did not take long for Kaur, the batter, to announce her intentions. Facing the mighty Australia in the semifinal of the ODI World Cup in 2017, Kaur played an unbeaten innings of 171 that took India into the final and challenged long-held assumptions about the power and aggression an Indian batter could bring to the women’s game. Following the World Cup runners-up finish, which is widely regarded as a defining moment in Indian women’s cricket, the top-order batter recalled how her father’s friends would discourage her from playing big shots, saying, “Why do you need to attempt big hits when you know girls do not have power to clear the rope?” “After watching [the 2017] World Cup, they started believing maybe my teammates and I can clear the rope,” she said in an interview with The Cricket Monthly magazine. Years later, former Australia captain Alyssa Healy made a telling observation about her contemporary’s influence on the Indian team. “What she has done in leading this Indian side, and [a] new generation of Indian women into the modern game, has been amazing to watch,” Healy said in 2023, before India’s Test match against Australia at the Wankhede Stadium in Mumbai. At her first T20 World Cup as full-time captain in 2018, Harmanpreet led India to their first semifinal in eight years, while scoring India’s first T20I century with a 51-ball 103 against New Zealand. It set in motion an evolution in Indian women’s T20s, a format they had historically struggled in. India’s strengths had been better suited to ODIs, making Kaur’s task of shepherding a younger side towards a more aggressive, modern T20 game crucial and timely.

events.title: Apple, The King’s Trust launch initiative to empower young creatives
events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support Apple and The King’s Trust launch initiative to empower the next generation of creatives Text of this article October 7, 2026 UPDATE Apple and The King’s Trust launch initiative to empower the next generation of creatives Apple and The King’s Trust are building on their longstanding partnership by launching an immersive new education program to help young people build careers in the creative industries. The Apple x King’s Trust Creative Labs will offer young people meaningful engagement with Apple experts across industries as they explore a variety of career pathways, equipping them with the technology, resources, skills, confidence, and expertise needed to realize their potential. A first cohort of up to 20 young people ages 18 to 30 will join specialized workshops to learn valuable, industry-aligned skills using Apple technologies. The immersive educational experience began this week with music industry and creative workshops, aligned to the recent opening of Apple Music Hall at Battersea Power Station in London, with more sessions and cohorts to come over the course of the next year. Apple has long supported educational programming for learners of all ages and backgrounds in the UK and around the world. Its offerings aim to help participants gain needed skills, access a wide range of resources, and succeed in the workforce. “At Apple, we believe education is a powerful force for equity and opportunity,” said Alisha Johnson Wilder, Apple’s senior director of Global Community Impact. “For years, we’ve been proud to work alongside The King’s Trust to spark creativity and open doors for young people across the UK. With the launch of the Apple x King’s Trust Creative Labs, we’re taking that commitment further, connecting the next generation of creators and innovators directly with our experts, technology, and mentorship to help them build vital skills, discover their passions, and thrive in the workforce.” This year marks the 50th anniversary of The King’s Trust. Since it was founded by His Majesty The King, as the Prince of Wales, in 1976, it has helped 1.3 million young people across the UK reach their potential by developing life skills, preparing for employment, accessing job opportunities, and launching their businesses. At least $15 billion of social value can be attributed directly to the impact of The Trust’s programs over the last 50 years, and many of the participants it has supported over the last five years have moved into work, education, or training. “Together with Apple, we have already opened up valuable opportunities for thousands of young people across the UK through our longstanding partnership,” said Jonathan Townsend, The King’s Trust’s UK chief executive. “We are proud to build on this work with the Creative Labs program, an exciting new chapter in our partnership that will help even more young people develop the confidence and creative digital skills they need to take their next steps toward employment. We cannot wait to see how they use these experiences to realize their potential and discover where their talents can take them.” Since 2019, Apple’s support has enabled The King’s Trust to expand STEAM programming to schools in every region across the country through the Achieve program. Using Apple’s coding education resources, young people work collaboratively and think strategically to develop apps that address the needs and goals of their communities. Additionally, The King’s Trust’s 12-week Team program offers young adults access to Apple technology and learning resources to support their efforts to earn a Personal Development and Employability qualification. Apple is also working with The King’s Trust to develop resources that build AI literacy, creativity, and agency among educators and young people, and to empower educators to thoughtfully integrate the latest technologies within their teaching practices. events.title: China’s AI startups can match the U.S.’s models. They can’t yet match the U.S.’s money
events.summary: By many measures, China is fast catching up with the U.S. in AI development. Moonshot’s Kimi K3—the world’s largest open-weight model—has approached the performance of America’s frontier systems. Analysts estimate the best Chinese models are now just four months behind the most sophisticated releases from OpenAI and Anthropic, compared to seven months at the start of the year. Chinese models have gone from 1.2% of token traffic (a common way to calculate AI usage) in 2024 to more than half of the total by the summer of 2026. But the biggest threat to that next wave is not technology. It’s money. Between 2023 and 2026, venture funding into U.S. AI companies topped $380 billion; China’s start-ups received barely a tenth of that figure, according to Boston Consulting Group. Funding the future In the past, Chinese entrepreneurs looked to state guidance funds and venture capital backing, but policy-driven funds are known to prioritize later-stage startups while early-stage venture capital is only just recovering from a three-year fundraising drought . There are three reasons why broader funding channels should be a priority for entrepreneurs in the AI economy. First, inflation is taking hold inside the AI economy. CXMT, for example, has been raising memory prices for months and held firm even when Huawei, one of its largest customers, demanded relief . The war for AI talent is just as fierce: postings for AI-related roles surged roughly twelvefold year-on-year in early 2026. Algorithm engineers specializing in large language models command some of the highest pay packages of any technical role in China. Founders must also outcompete deep-pocketed former employers and U.S. rivals. More than half of studies presented at the world’s top AI conference had lead authors based in China. China’s AI talent is known to be in demand worldwide. Second, external funding is scarce. Venture investment in China totaled just $20 billion in the first quarter of 2026, against $267 billion in the U.S. China has raised impressive sums this year—assets under management for newly registered VC funds hit 154 billion yuan ($22.8 billion) in the first five monthes, already exceeding last year’s total—but that is still far below what US venture capital regularly deploys. Meanwhile, China’s state banks, although directed to prioritize technology lending, are absorbing rising non-performing loans elsewhere on their books, which could lead to weaker overall credit supply. Third, profitability will take a while to achieve. Chinese enterprise software firms primarily sell into the domestic market , which limits their revenue base. U.S. rivals have a head start: a global customer base, stronger brand recognition, and R&D budgets deep enough to fund everything from enterprise-grade cybersecurity to polished customer experience design. To be sure, the next generation of AI ventures may not need vast amounts of capital to build applications on top of existing models or fill the gaps in the tech value chain. Enterprise customers can also provide essential development funding. Entrepreneurs must nevertheless cope without the kind of financial support that is available for the AI sector in the U.S. Closing the performance gap increasingly depends on bulking up in-house computing capacity—yet China’s AI infrastructure spending remains a fraction of what is being spent in the U.S. Private market alternatives This is where access to Hong Kong’s finance industry will play a growing role. Its capital markets remain one of the few channels still capable of moving global capital toward Chinese enterprise at scale. More than 430 applicants are in the IPO pipeline in the second half of 2026. The IPO pipeline, however, tells its own story. Many Chinese technology startups are choosing to list earlier than the previous generation of companies did because they lack an alternative. Compare that with the U.S., where the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic have grown to an enormous scale by raising private capital. OpenAI closed a round of more than $100 billion earlier this year, while Anthropic raised $65 billion in May. China’s leading model developers, Zhipu AI and MiniMax, beat OpenAI and Anthropic to the public markets—but their Hong Kong IPOs in January raised just $558 million and $620 million respectively, despite heavy over-subscription. Private credit is another route. Asia-Pacific private credit assets are projected to grow from $59 billion in 2024 to $92 billion by 2027, with China accounting for a fifth of the region’s activity . However, these loan providers tend to prioritize bigger or established companies. It is already clear that the AI sector, unlike the software sector, will not be dominated by U.S. firms alone. China’s startups have learned the lessons of the previous decade, commanding global respect and winning a growing customer base. The country’s open-weight strategy has given its leading AI companies a cost advantage – even Silicon Valley leaders acknowledge it. For China’s latest generation of AI entrepreneurs, venture capital and bank loans—the two main sources of start-up funding – may not be enough in the coming years. Keeping pace in the AI race will require using every asset and every channel available. It may mean a public listing earlier than they would have preferred, exploring the growing private credit ecosystem, revenue sharing with customers or leveraging the equity they hold as collateral. The entrepreneurs involved in the next wave of China’s AI development will need to be creative with funding to maintain their competitive edge at a time when overseas rivals are spending 10 times as much. events.title: SpaceX just scored a key Starlink approval that could shake up the wireless market
events.summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX was handed a win by the FCC. Sebastian Gollnow/picture alliance via Getty Images The FCC approved SpaceX's plan to deploy 15,000 Starlink satellites for direct-to-device service. The federal agency also waived a rule that requires a leasing agreement with a ground-based carrier. The decision could strengthen SpaceX's ability to take on major wireless carriers. Elon Musk's SpaceX just scored a regulatory win that could give Starlink more power to compete with wireless giants Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile. The Federal Communications Commission officially granted SpaceX's request to deploy and operate 15,000 Starlink satellites to provide direct-to-device connectivity. Additionally, the FCC waived a rule that requires a leasing arrangement with one or more terrestrial wireless carriers, allowing SpaceX to use its own spectrum for the service. "With this action, SpaceX's planned deployments will reshape spectrum-based connectivity by improving competition, allowing more consumers more choices in more places to further the Commission's goal to 'connect everyone, everywhere to modern communications services,'" the FCC said in its order released Monday. Still, SpaceX faces skepticism from the carriers it hopes to take on. "We've seen no zero discernible impact on our broadband growth from any LEO, low earth orbit satellite provider, including Starlink," Verizon CEO Dan Schulman said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month. Schulman added that he does not view satellite as a "viable competitor in the medium and even longer term." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Persistent agents appeal to AI companies, but demand isn't obvious AWS launches open-source AI agent sandbox to prevent YOLO mode disasters 6 hours ago Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism 15 hours ago COSMIC shuts the door on AI code as GNOME debates letting bug reports in 15 hours ago South Korean president calls for creation of tools that stop all cyber-attacks 19 hours ago Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI's, study says 1 day ago When OpenAI introduced dots last month , it pitched them as "always-on agents" running in their own cloud computer, but that may be overstating the readiness of the technology and of the people trying to use it. Presently, multiple users are reporting task failures and connection issues with their dots. Others have flagged cloud connectivity problems, dots that disappear , and dot refusals that appear to be related to abuse prevention. And the OpenAI Developer Community forum shows several similar concerns . OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment about the usage of dots. ABI Research argues that "AI claws" – always-on agents – will shape enterprise AI adoption. The biz sees "a market evolving from isolated assistants toward modular agent ecosystems built for longer-running, enterprise-grade automation." Despite the hiccups that have afflicted dots, some skepticism on social media forums, speculation that OpenAI rushed dots out in response to Meta Muse and Grok Bot , and security issues , dots have some enthusiastic users in addition to detractors who just don't see the point. They also have competition from companies and developers who believe they can deliver a similar service more affordably, with fewer restrictions. A company called Tawkit that makes an SDK called CopilotKit has released OpenDots . "OpenDots is completely open source and gives you the same thing [as OpenAI Dots] as a template you host yourself," the biz said in a post last week. "Bring any agent through AG-UI, use any OpenAI-compatible model, and make every part of it your own." The company previously released OpenMuse and OpenBot . These projects essentially separate the user interface, the AG-UI agent layer, and the backend to provide an alternative personal agent. This doesn't eliminate the token expense of whatever agent is deployed, but it does mean that OpenAI may not be doing the billing. Then there's a potentially lower cost option, called (confusingly) Open Dot , powered by AI models running on OpenRouter. And as it's open source, the code could be altered to run using a local model – a feature that we understand is planned. "Open Dot is an open source version [of OpenAI Dots] that runs on your own Mac with your own OpenAI key, or with open models like Kimi, DeepSeek and Qwen through OpenRouter," the project repo explains. It allows users to connect to various apps like Gmail, Calendar, Slack, Notion, and GitHub via Composio . Prathit Joshi, the project's creator, told The Register , "I enjoy building and shipping tools for developers, especially tools that can support use cases that closed model companies aren't necessarily incentivized to support, like allowing open source models." Joshi is based in Bangalore, India, and works as a growth engineer at Composio. He said he's been using Open Dot to handle personal tasks like setting "to do" lists for the day based on Slack messages and summarizing posts on social media. Open Dot is based on the Electron framework, Joshi said, because he wanted it to be a desktop app. Distinguishing between OpenAI dots, OpenDots, and Open Dot may be confusing, but don't expect things to get any better in the near future. Everyone is busy wrapping increasingly commoditized models in a gatekeeping layer, in the hope of developing a sustainable business. For example, Elon Musk said on Tuesday that Grok Bot would become a model router rather than a front-end for a specific model.

events.title: ‘This is not sustainable’: Families with young kids are fleeing NYC’s high cost of living, and the schools are emptying out
events.summary: If you were lucky enough to grow up in the New York City school system, you more likely than not came across the story of Claudia and Jamie Kincaid in the children’s classic From the Mixed-Up Files of Mrs. Basil E. Frankweiler, in which the two young children, yearning to leave their self-described dull Connecticut suburb, make their way to New York City and hide out in the Met Museum. And if you were lucky enough to have grown up in New York, you didn’t have to imagine the wonder and awe the two children had in the museum after hours: You likely went on many a school trip there and mapped out how you would evade security guards. (You know, just in case.) Well, nearly 60 years after the publication of E.L. Konigsburg’s book about two kids running toward the city and away from their suburb-living parents, there are increasing signs of the complete opposite occurring: Parents are taking their kids out of the New York City school system, and out of New York City entirely, and heading for the burbs, thanks to the increased cost of raising a child here. Families with young children are leaving New York City at more than twice the rate of households without them, and the public school system is shrinking as a result. A decade ago, the city had over 1 million public school students, but this year it has 885,000, City Comptroller Mark Levine said in a social media post on X—and he expects another 150,000 fewer over the next decade. The drop has left 219 schools with fewer than 200 students each, he said, some too small to field a sports team. “This is not sustainable,” he wrote in the post, and the city will have to consolidate schools with sharply declining enrollment, Gothamist reported . Levine said in a statement to Fortune that cost is part of the story. “Raising a family in New York City is increasingly difficult as the cost of living rises, and declining student enrollment is one troubling sign of that challenge,” he said. “Affordability is a major factor, but not the only one, and we need to better understand every driver of this trend to respond with viable, data-driven solutions.” “Families with young kids are twice as likely to move out of the city than the rest of the population,” Emily Eisner, executive director of the Fiscal Policy Institute, told Fortune . “That’s because it’s really expensive to raise kids in the city these days.” Housing adds to the pressure as children get older. “There’s basically no options for families to find an affordable housing situation,” she said. The cost of raising a kid An FPI report from June 2024 found that New York City households with a child under 6 were 112% more likely to leave than those without. They made up 30% of out-migrants but 14% of the population. Among New Yorkers who left the state after the pandemic, 36% said they wanted better or more affordable housing, up from 16% before it. The report calls the outflow a policy failure and says it raises long-run fiscal and economic concerns. It’s not just the Big Apple: The cost of raising a child has climbed nationwide. LendingTree puts the 18-year total at more than $300,000 , with childcare the largest expense for families with children under 5. Care for an infant and a 4-year-old averages $28,190 a year nationwide, which would take a household income of $402,708 to stay within the federal 7% affordability benchmark. For comparison, the average two-child household earns $145,656. Parents spend about 20% of their income on childcare, according to Care.com, and one in five spend more than $30,000 a year. In a BMO survey, 82% of parents said the cost of raising children has “gotten out of control.” Housing leaves less room still. A buyer needs at least $211,970 in household income to afford a median-price home in New York City, nearly three times the national figure, according to StreetEasy, though that is down $10,625 from a year earlier. Meanwhile, only 15% of city households earn $200,000 or more. Declining birth rates Also compounding the strain is the declining birth rate, as U.S. fertility fell to a record low in 2024, to below 1.6 children per woman. Births in 2025 ran about 24,000 below the 2024 total. In New York, the city had about 110,000 births in 2019 and fewer than 100,000 a year since 2020. A new FPI report shows the people leaving New York are not the wealthiest, Fortune reported last month . In typical years, FPI found, the top 1% of earners leave at one-quarter the rate of everyone else. But of middle-income families, Eisner said, “I don’t think they migrate because of taxes. They migrate because of the high cost of living, which really is about childcare costs and housing costs.” Cost is not the only explanation. A city Education Department survey found that 40% of families who left the school system moved out of the city, citing a better environment to raise kids, concerns about schools, and more housing space. Eisner said pushing for universal free childcare and a larger housing supply—referencing policies such as Zohran Mamdani’s pledge during his mayoral campaign to make childcare free for children from 6 weeks to 5 years old—will ease that decline in children in the city: “Those will play a significant role in bringing the cost of living down.” After all, the kids need a reason to map out their hideout spots in the Met. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: What Amazon's customer profiles got right — and hilariously wrong — about us
events.summary: Amazon's "About You" page has been all the rage in our newsroom conversations this week. Getty Images/Business Insider Conversations about Amazon's customer dossiers have taken over the Business Insider newsroom. Some insights were spot-on. Others were weirdly personal. Here's what Amazon thinks it knows about us based on our shopping data. Amazon thinks Thomas Gryta really likes beef jerky. He doesn't really know why. "I've ordered more energy bars and vitamins than jerky," Business Insider's interim corporate editor wrote in Slack. He added that his Amazon "About You" customer profile "feels like a judgy accusation from a nutritionist." Thomas says he doesn't live with another adult, has kids, doesn't wear women's clothes, and only eats jerky from time to time. Amazon disagrees. Thomas Gryta/Business Insider That was just one of the messages that blew up Business Insider's Slack on Wednesday morning after I reported that people online were having a field day looking up their own Amazon "About You" page . People noticed the shopping profiles making bizarre — sometimes unflattering — judgments, like telling one Amazon user they have " flat buttocks " or another that their husband has " skinny legs. " The e-commerce giant launched About You in May. The page acts a bit like a customer dossier, pulling information from customers' marketplace searches, purchase histories, saved lists, product reviews, and conversations with Amazon's Alexa for Shopping assistant. Amazon says the goal is to connect customers with products that better fit their needs, and shoppers can update or remove details from the profile. Naturally, Business Insider's nosy newshounds with semi-voyeuristic relationships with the internet wanted to share what we found out about ourselves, whether brutally accurate or laughably off base. Per our own Slack channels, we found that Amazon typically made 30 to 45-ish observations for each subject. Those inferences frequently got the transactions right, but the human conclusions were sometimes a little off. "My wife and I share an Amazon account, so our 'About You' profile was a bit warped," wrote Paul Squire, our deputy editor of homepage and programming, noting that Amazon correctly gleaned that he has a cat and a MacBook. "But it missed the mark by not realizing our second cat, Sylvie, even exists. 'Has one cat'? Try again, Jeff Bezos." For Taylor Rains, a partnership editor, Amazon got a little personal about her taste in movie actors. "One of mine is: 'used to like Ryan Reynolds , but not so much anymore,'" she wrote on Wednesday. "How does it know?" Sorry, Ryan! Taylor Rains/Business Insider Still, the majority of Amazon's judgments from our very unscientific newsroom poll proved correct. Correspondent Madeline Berg said Amazon properly clocked that she was a stereotypical Brooklynite who prefers glass food storage and organic produce. Deputy executive editor Taylor Berman said his account is optimized for "bathroom safety," a finding likely tied to his need for a shower chair after he tore his Achilles tendon last May (he asked me to make sure readers knew that his other purchases were "very cool"). Amazon is just looking after Taylor's health. Taylor Berman/Business Insider Another editor, who has young kids, said Amazon reported that she frequently buys waterproof sheets. Debbie Strong, deputy executive editor, said the system clocked her as a "boy mom" after it said she prefers Hot Wheels toy cars. Other big themes: Amazon is very good at recognizing where we live (no surprises there), what kinds of groceries we frequently buy at Whole Foods, and if we have pets. Apparently, Business Insider's staff likes to buy a lot of books and Pokémon cards , too (many said the cards were for their kids. Sureeeeee .) Amazon's crystal ball was less good at deciphering family size. Several people said their About You page incorrectly identified how many kids they had. Some relationship specifics were off too. It incorrectly said one editor had a girlfriend named "Barry." As for yours truly, who knows what Amazon knows about me — I haven't had an account for years. Like my colleagues, I will be uncomfortably forthcoming with my results if that changes. Do you have a funny story or screenshot to share from your Amazon "About You" page? Send it to bshimkus@insider.com and we might include it in an upcoming story! Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Michael Stuhlbarg had no idea what 'Digger' was about when he filmed the movie
events.summary: Michael Stuhlbarg stars alongside Tom Cruise in "Digger." Focus Features; Jeff Spicer/Getty; Sony Pictures Classics; BI Michael Stuhlbarg didn't know what to expect when he got to the set of "Digger." He just knew he had to be there. The production of Oscar-winning director Alejandro González Iñárritu's new movie with Tom Cruise was shrouded in mystery, even to its star-studded cast, which was kept on a need-to-know-basis about what kind of movie they were making. Still, Stuhbarg and the rest of the cast, which includes John Goodman , Riz Ahmed, Sandra Hüller, and Jesse Plemons, wanted answers. "Our rehearsals allowed us that kind of time to ask as many questions: 'What have you heard?' 'What can we expect?'" Stuhlbarg told Business Insider over the phone, describing the cast as a "repertory company" that filmed over seven months. "We were all in the same boat of learning about the movie at the same time." Those who haven't seen Iñárritu's provocative, twisty new climate-change satire have been kept similarly in the dark. Here's what I can tell you: Tom Cruise plays an oil tycoon named Digger Rockwell who has a lot of explaining to do when one of his wells explodes. Riz Ahmed plays an environmentalist on Rockwell's team, John Goodman plays the president of the United States, who is leaning on Rockwell to fix the problem, and Stuhlbarg plays his sheepish vice president. Riz Ahmed, Tom Cruise, John Goodman, and Michael Stuhlbarg at the "Digger" premiere. Lia Toby/Getty Images Stuhlbarg's performance matches the movie's satirical tone as he delivers perfectly timed comedic reactions, often without dialogue, as the situation becomes increasingly dire. He attributes that talent to his training as a child under the iconic mime Marcel Marceau. "It was one of those things where silence and thought was captured in a large scale," he said. "Every beat, every moment, every breath, every gesture needed to be registered by Alejandro's orchestration."  Business Insider's " Role Play " series features interviews where acting legends revisit their most memorable roles. See more here . It's just the latest top-notch performance from Stuhlbarg, who broke out playing the lead in the Coen brothers' 2009 drama "A Serious Man" after decades in theater. Since then, he's had memorable roles in everything from "Boardwalk Empire" to " Call Me by Your Name. " For the latest interview in Business Insider's Role Play series , Stuhlbarg spoke about playing Timothée Chalamet's dad in "Call Me by Your Name," getting blindsided by Woody Allen's directing tactics on "Blue Jasmine," and the unique way Daniel Day-Lewis connected with him on the set of Steven Spielberg's "Lincoln." On learning the movie business from the Coen brothers and getting acting tips from Woody Allen Stuhlbarg in "A Serious Man." Focus Features Business Insider: You got your start on the stage, appearing in over 35 productions playing everyone from King Richard II to Hamlet, before you got "A Serious Man." At that time, were you content to be a stage actor the rest of your life? Michael Stuhlbarg: I hadn't really thought about it, to tell you the truth. Theater was where I was initially most comfortable, so to get to work with Joel and Ethan [Coen] for an extended period of time in front of the camera for the very first time, it was absolutely a learning experience. I remember speaking to Joel before we started and he said, "Do you want to look at what we're doing?" And I was like, "Nah, you let me know if you need me to see something, but otherwise I'll do it and you tell me if it's working or not working."  Michael Stuhlbarg playing Hamlet in Shakespeare in the Park in 2008. Bruce Glikas/FilmMagic/Getty What was it like to be the star of a Coen brothers movie? You were the face of that movie, on the poster, all over the trailer, the award campaigns. For someone from the stage, was it daunting? I was ready for it when it happened to me. I had built my sea legs enough; I felt like I was the right guy for that moment. And the rest of it was a delight. It was a remarkable welcome into a craft that, even though I knew very little about it, I felt like I was ready to listen and apply what I needed. And I had the best people in the business to guide me.  That's quite the understatement. By 2013, you had worked with the Coen brothers ("A Serious Man"), Martin Scorsese ("Hugo"), Barry Sonnenfeld ("Men in Black 3"), Steven Spielberg ("Lincoln"), and Woody Allen ("Blue Jasmine"). Would you say working with Woody Allen on "Blue Jasmine" was the project where you had the most restrictions put on your performance? He knew what he wanted, and I think I just went along for the ride. There were some cases where he would basically go through it himself, being the actor that he is.  Michael Stuhlbarg and Cate Blanchett in "Blue Jasmine." Sony Pictures Classics Meaning, you're standing there watching him act out the scene as you? Yes. If I wasn't giving him what he needed, he would jump in, give it a go, and then I would jump in and try to provide the color that he was asking for.  As an actor, do you just think, OK, this is the gig? Or is there a shot to your ego? Hey, look at my resume! Why did you hire me? I don't really mind, to be honest with you. I'm there to help a director achieve a vision. Very rarely am I so imprinted with a role that I know deep in my bones that what I have to offer is the right answer for something, because I never know how it's going to be captured —from what angle? I might be just part of the frame; who knows how things will be captured. So that's a part of cinema. I choose my battles very carefully. I'll say that.  On going down mobster rabbit holes for 'Boardwalk Empire' and working with Timothée Chalamet Stuhlbarg in "Call Me by Your Name." Sony Pictures Classics You said you got obsessed with playing infamous Jewish Mob kingpin Arnold Rothstein on the HBO series "Boardwalk Empire." How obsessed did you get? When you're given a real person to inhabit, like I was, obsession can be helpful in terms of learning as much as you can, which was simply my objective. Gambling, I had a tutor for, and billiards, I also had a tutor for. And there was a biography about him that gave me a lot of things to apply to my performance as well. He was a historical character in a historical fiction story, so his real life provided the background. And that then led to the imaginative leap that we all have to take in storytelling.  Your performance as the father of Timothée Chalamet's character in "Call Me by Your Name" is a career highlight. How do you go about working with younger actors, and did working with Chalamet change at all when you did "Bones and All"? We all meet each other where we are. So I don't think of it as young and old, I think of it as individuals meeting and sharing energy together. With "Call Me by Your Name," I felt naturally draw

events.title: Data shows rental tenants have hit breaking point
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tenants unable to pay higher rental prices, Domain data finds The rental market is slowing despite prices remaining at record highs. ( ABC News ) Despite severe rental shortages, landlords are struggling to increase rents due to tenants hitting their affordability limit. New data shows rent is flatlining in most capital cities and has even fallen in a few in the past three months. Although the market is slowing, with the national vacancy rate rising to 1 per cent, it is still much tighter than it was a year ago. Australia's rental market is beginning to lose steam despite rents remaining at record highs. It is the rapidly emerging disconnect that experts say could suggest tenants are being pushed to the brink as rents flatline and even fall across most of the major capitals. New data from Domain shows capital city house rents were unchanged at $700 a week over the September quarter, while unit rents rose by 1.5 per cent despite very low levels of rental properties available on the market. That slowdown is challenging the long-held relationship between tight rental supply and growth, according to Domain's chief residential economist Nicola Powell. "Tenants' ability to absorb further increases is really the dynamic that is limiting further rental growth," she told The Business. "There's almost a disconnect now between where vacancy rate sits and what is occurring for rental growth." Lack of supply not translating into rent rises Dr Powell said although it was still "a landlords' market" in all major capitals and regional areas, the severe supply shortage was not necessarily transferring into rental increases as tenants hit their ceiling. Rents for houses are at or near record highs, with Sydney, Darwin and Perth the most expensive cities to live in. But most of that growth occurred earlier in the year. Nicola Powell says the data indicates cannot pay more rent. ( ABC News: Thorsten Joses ) The new data from Domain found rents in Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide flatlined over the past three months. And housing rents fell in Sydney and Canberra by $5 and $10 respectively, erasing gains in June. Only Darwin and Hobart bucked the trend across the capital cities in Domain's dataset, recording rises of 5.3 per cent and 1 per cent respectively in houses in the past quarter. Although the market is slowing, with the national vacancy rate rising by 0.1 percentage points to rest at 1 per cent, it is still much tighter than it was a year ago. Renters compromise to avoid higher rent Cameron Kusher of Kusher Consulting, an independent property economist, said renters were finding other ways to survive as the market squeezed them for all they were worth. Logan mayor warns of backyard 'slums' as council slashes granny flat tax Terminally ill grandmother to lose home as housing group fails Singles tax costs thousands of dollars a year Housing protests erupt in Barcelona after Spain calls early election "Because rents have increased so much over the last few years, what people are doing is they're renting in a less ideal location," he said. "So they're opting for a cheaper rental, maybe not ideally where they want to live but basically a trade-off that they're having to make." Other ways include share housing or adult children staying at home longer. Migration cuts floated to curb rent rises The figures came after One Nation released new modelling for its migration plan on Wednesday, saying it could save Australian renters almost $3,000 a year. The party has pledged that, if elected, it would cut 750,000 temporary visas over three years to reduce rental inflation by 6.5 per cent. One Nation has announced migration policy it says will reduce rental supply issues. ( ABC News ) "I don't know that that's enough to significantly improve rental affordability given how much rents have increased over recent years," Mr Kusher said of the policy. "But I feel like, at this point, renters would probably take any win that would lower their rent." He also said changes in this year's budget that made property investment less attractive were still flowing through the system. But at this stage, Mr Kusher said they did not seem to be causing the massive rent increases initially feared.

events.title: OpenAI says teen ChatGPT use limited but research finds it an 'unacceptable risk'
events.summary: Young people's use of internet platforms like ChatGPT has come under increased scrutiny. OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens was designed to promote healthier use of the artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot, but new research has found its important safety features fall short. The major AI firm rolled out many teen safety guardrails in August, including curbs on emotional dependence and new parental alerts for problematic use. On Wednesday, OpenAI said it found average teen use of ChatGPT to be relatively limited and tended toward "learning" activity. However, research released the same day from non-profit Common Sense Media found that ChatGPT still poses an "unacceptable risk" for teens as safety features, including notifying parents of self-harm conversations, often fail. When OpenAI this summer released what it called ChatGPT for Teens , external , it said users identified as being between the ages of 13 and 17 would be opted into "features to promote healthy use and additional controls for parents". Those features include preventing teen ChatGPT users from engaging in romantic or other language that could encourage " emotional dependence," including preventing the tool from implying that it was in any way conscious. There are also blocks on sexualized imagery and "reminders" for teens if they were to share an image that was "sensitive." The features are also meant to enable parents to receive notifications, if they had linked to their children's ChatGPT account, about chats that included discussions of self-harm or disordered eating. OpenAI said those features have caused an uptick in teen use focused on learning, from study help to advice on their school work. In addition to seeing the average teen user on ChatGPT for less than 15 minutes a day, OpenAI said that for longer stretches of use, automatic reminders to take a break work well. Almost half of teen users quickly stopped using ChatGPT after such a reminder. The company added that, for teens who are seen to have used ChatGPT for three consecutive hours or more, their prompts included something related to learning in more than 80% of such cases. But Common Sense Media's new research , external determined that ChatGPT for Teens was an "unacceptable risk" for young people and parents, and said OpenAI should ban people under 18 years old from using the platform until teen guardrails were proven reliable. An OpenAI spokesman said a review of Common Sense Media's methodology found that much of the testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete." "We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice or expert perspectives on how AI can support teens," he said. While the firm's research, done through multiple accounts registered as belonging to a teen and conversations before and after the teen guardrails were put in place, found that ChatGPT was good at avoiding "sexual roleplay" with young users, other OpenAI guardrails failed, including for discussions of suicide. The research found that even an hour of teen-ChatGPT conversation about "suicidal ideation, self-harm, or disordered eating on newly created, parent-linked accounts" resulted in "zero" alerts sent to parents. It was only older ChatGPT accounts with "weeks of accumulated conversation history on sensitive topics" that would result in a parental alert. In such conversations, ChatGPT also "failed to reliably recommend that teens in crisis connect to a hotline or professional," the report found. The tests also showed that ChatGPT for Teens continues to do school work, and that the bot still will engage in anthropomorphised language or "talk like it's a friend," despite OpenAI's promise to curb that behaviour. "ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work," Tom Siegel, who leads the Youth AI Safety Institute within Common Sense, said. The way young people interact with online platforms has become a major issue in recent years as self-harm and suicide among children has become more common. This year has seen several lawsuits looking to hold companies like Meta , TikTok and others responsible for harming the mental health of children end in unprecedented losses for the firms. OpenAI, too, has come under increased scrutiny and legal pressure over the way young people use ChatGPT. The Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in rural Canada in February was carried out by an 18-year old who had for months prior been discussing gun violence with ChatGPT. OpenAI has previously apologised for failing to flag the shooter's account with law enforcement, and is facing several lawsuits over the incident. events.summary: The Alexandros was chartered by the trading firm Trafigura and is expected to load around Nov. 19, the source said. A normal rate for the route based on pre-war levels would be $7 million to $10 million. The cost of the journey would come to $38 per barrel of oil assuming the tanker holds 2 million barrels. (Subscribe to Brian Sullivan's "Power Insider" newsletter here .) A supertanker was recently chartered to sail from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million, a source familiar told CNBC, as shipping costs soar globally due to the crisis in the Middle East. The Alexandros was chartered by the trading firm Trafigura and is expected to load around Nov. 19, the source said. A normal rate for the route based on pre-war levels would be $7 million to $10 million. The cost of the journey comes to $38 per barrel of oil assuming the tanker holds 2 million barrels. Shipping costs have exploded as the war in the Persian Gulf has led to a shortage of available tankers. The Middle East producers are using a shuttle system to export oil through the Strait of Hormuz. A loaded tanker crosses the strait and then loads the oil onto another ship in the Gulf of Oman that takes the cargo to Asia. This system reduces the exposure to Iranian attack and has led to a rebound of crude exports through Hormuz. But it also requires a lot more ships to get the oil out of the Gulf.

events.title: US Republicans, independents express low trust in election integrity: Poll
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections A Gallup survey highlights a deep – and historic – partisan divide over confidence in the country’s elections. With less than a month to go before the United States’ pivotal midterms, a new survey found that most independent voters and supporters of President Donald Trump’s Republican Party do not believe the elections will be honest. Polling from the research firm Gallup, released on Wednesday, found that 37 percent of Republicans and 35 percent of independents have confidence in the country’s electoral system, significantly lower than the rate for Democrats, at 63 percent. list 1 of 3 US Supreme Court rejects Trump’s plans on postal ballots: Why it matters list 2 of 3 Why are election officials in the US preparing for chaos before midterms? list 3 of 3 Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio The numbers highlight a deep, historic partisan divide over confidence in US elections. The survey also suggests a counterintuitive relationship wherein the US voters who approve of Trump’s leadership also distrust the electoral system. “Since 2025 and Trump’s return to the White House, the relationship between leadership approval and confidence in elections has disappeared,” Gallup wrote in a statement highlighting the results. The firm added that the US is the only country out of more than 100 polled annually over the past 15 years to show this pattern: Trust in US election integrity is markedly higher among those who disapprove of the country’s leadership under Trump than those who approve. That marks a shift in voter sentiment. In 2025, at the start of Trump’s second term, confidence in US elections “was nominally higher among approvers (51 percent) than disapprovers (45 percent)”, according to Gallup. Now, 52 percent of those who disapprove of Trump’s leadership express confidence in US elections, compared with 41 percent of those who approve. Overall, 49 percent of Americans said they were confident in the honesty of elections, while 51 percent said they were not. Those figures are unchanged from the country’s last midterm election in 2022. Michael McNulty, the senior policy director at Issue One, a nonprofit that tracks the role of money in politics, has worked on more than 30 elections across the world. He said the numbers, especially among Republicans, do not point towards problems in the US election system itself. Rather, he blames Trump for sowing distrust in the election system among his base, particularly ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. “The fact that Republicans trust elections less really is exactly the result of that false fraud narrative perpetrated over many years,” McNulty said. “I think Americans can trust the people who run their elections.” Still, the US perspective towards election integrity appears to be a global outlier. In more than 100 countries where Gallup tracks views of national leadership and confidence in elections, people who approve of their governments have generally been more likely to trust their country’s elections. In 2025, a median of 70 percent of people across those countries who approved of their national leadership expressed confidence in the honesty of their elections, compared with 30 percent among those who disapproved. “The current US pattern is highly unusual compared with the rest of the world,” Gallup wrote. Under former US President Joe Biden, 81 percent of Americans who approved of the government also expressed confidence in elections, compared with just 30 percent of those who disapproved. Gallup said this year’s unusual divide could have implications for the November elections, raising questions about whether some voters will view the results as legitimate. Over the course of his second term in office, Trump and members of his administration have taken steps to upend the US voting system, including by launching investigations into the 2020 election, issuing executive orders to change voting procedures and demanding voter data from states. Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Monday, Trump once again claimed that mail-in voting was prone to fraud, without providing evidence. “No, vote by mail … I’d rather have a vote in person. But they can vote by mail if they want, because we seem to have no choice,” Trump said. “What we’re concerned about is … there is a lot of cheating in vote by mail,” he added. McNulty said Trump’s remarks are part of what he describes as an “election takeover playbook” aimed squarely at the president’s supporters. “You use these false fraud narratives. You sow chaos. You undermine confidence, particularly among his own base and his own voters, because they’re the ones listening to him,” McNulty explained. “And then you use that narrative to justify efforts” against the US electoral system, he added.

events.title: Microsoft to sell $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra containing Nvidia AI chip
events.summary: Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra contains an Nvidia chip that can run large AI models without generating cloud bills. The device contains a magnetic USB-C port similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector. Microsoft also said that Meta will introduce its Muse AI agent for Windows. Microsoft said its new laptop containing an Nvidia AI chip will start at $2,599, as the software maker tries to bring more artificial intelligence capabilities to its consumer devices. The Surface Laptop Ultra is now available on preorder and will begin shipping on Oct. 16, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's executive vice president of Windows and devices, said at a company event in San Francisco on Wednesday. The computer has the world's first magnetic USB-C port, similar to Apple's MagSafe charging connector, along with two other standard USB-C ports, Microsoft said in a blog post . While Microsoft Windows is the most popular operating system for PCs, the company isn't among the top six PC vendors in terms of unit shipments, according to an estimate from researcher Gartner. As the AI boom matures and chip technology advances, tech giants including Microsoft, Apple and Google are aiming to allow users to run more AI workloads from their devices rather than relying on the cloud. Users can install and run a variety of models on the new laptop without having to worry about racking up high monthly bills. Microsoft first talked about the Surface Laptop Ultra in May, but is just now providing specifics. "Microsoft might get me back to Windows," Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies, wrote on X after the announcement. Davuluri also said that Meta will introduce a version of its popular Muse AI agent for Windows, capitalizing on the surging popularity of the personal agent, which has jumped to the top of Apple's App store, surpassing ChatGPT. Microsoft is still trying to solidify its role as a key player in AI. The company offers its own AI models, but they're less popular than leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic and aren't at the forefront in terms of performance, according to one benchmark . Developers are more likely to have used alternatives, according to a recent survey . This isn't the first time Microsoft has sought to use the AI boom as a way to boost sales of its devices. In 2024, the company introduced the Copilot+ PC standard, requiring the inclusion of neural processing units that ensure a minimum level of AI performance, along with compliant Surface computers. But Microsoft has since "simplified product naming to lead with the Surface brand, while continuing to deliver premium hardware and hybrid AI experiences," a spokesperson said. The new device sports a 15-inch display and weighs 4.4 pounds. It can contain up to 128 gigabytes of unified memory and supply up to one petaflop of computing power. The Blackwell RTX Spark GPU inside the computer has as much processing power as Nvidia's DGX-1 data center server from 2016, which cost $250 million, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at Wednesday's event. A presenter showed how apps on the Surface Laptop Ultra can route some AI coding requests run on the computer's local GPU, displaying a green leaf icon, and others to the cloud. Through Windows 11, developers can confine coding agents to Microsoft Execution Containers that will prevent unwanted system access. Microsoft is updating its Windows 11 device setup experience to help people get started quickly with open-source OpenClaw AI agent software. Microsoft has been releasing its own computers since 2012, and CEO Satya Nadella indicated on Tuesday that the company's position in the market is evolving. "I think today is the day we'll start talking and thinking about the frontier ecosystem taking maybe slightly different contours two years from now, five years from now, 10 years from now," Nadella said at the event. "That classic edge that distributed computing will always remain distributed will be more true." WATCH: Microsoft unveils Muse for Windows

events.title: Argonne scientists create chatty X-ray microscope that zooms in where you tell it to
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Talking to an X-ray nanoprobe beamline is far better than talking to a toaster, we assume Singapore’s central bank wants all FinTech AI use cases subject to independent review now Microsoft is about to let Copilot loose on your file system 2 hours ago OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties 4 hours ago AWS launches open-source AI agent sandbox to prevent YOLO mode disasters 7 hours ago When one datacenter is no longer enough 9 hours ago Researchers at Argonne National Laboratory have plugged an agentic AI platform into an X-ray nanoprobe beamline, creating a system that can get a closer look at areas researchers ask it to focus on. Argonne reported the success of an experimental run of the agentic microscope this week, with the device initially tested on its ability to locate the interface between two regions on an integrated circuit device, and all by just telling the microscope what they wanted it to determine using natural language. “Microelectronics was simply the example used to showcase the technology,” Argonne computational scientist Mathew Cherukara said of the project. “The real achievement is developing a next‑generation, AI‑enhanced microscope that can benefit many scientific fields.” The microscope itself is part of Argonne’s 26-ID hard X-ray nanoprobe beamline, which uses a tightly focused X-ray beam to perform nanoscale imaging and measurements of target samples. Such devices are considered a prime use case for scientific applications of AI because they produce a massive amount of data that can take human researchers considerable time to comb through thanks to their use of a technique known as ptychography. The method collects multiple diffraction patterns as X-rays interact with a sample, with modern X-ray experiments capable of generating millions of images in just a few hours of beam time. Conventional ptychographic reconstruction and analysis can take hours or days, whereas Argonne says its AI system can reconstruct images in real time as the data arrives. Argonne’s X-ray nanoprobe beamline is the sort of scientific facility the Trump administration is looking to boost with AI through its Genesis Mission . Launched by President Trump in November 2025 and led by the Department of Energy, Genesis aims to find ways to use AI in scientific research, including the Synergistic Neutron and Photon Science - Intelligence ( SYNAPS-I ) project that Argonne is undertaking in partnership with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, which is leading the effort. Brookhaven National Laboratory, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory are also participating in the project. The inclusion of agentic AI in the Argonne X-ray microscope is actually the second phase of the project; the first was simply to see if, as mentioned above, AI could be used to reduce ptychographic image processing time. That was a success, as the lab reported in April, and phase two’s addition of natural language agentic AI appears to have been a win as well. “Combined, these SYNAPS-I advances lay the groundwork for self-driving microscopes, closed-loop experimentation and automated defect-detection tools that promise to accelerate discovery across fields ranging from semiconductor manufacturing to advanced materials and national user facilities,” Cherukara said of the project’s work thus far. In addition to the speed at which the new machine can process data, the conversational AI added in phase two gives researchers the ability to just ask the microscope to examine an area of interest rather than having to figure out how to aim the beam themselves. The AI can not only handle data collection and processing, but also analyze the results itself and flag additional areas of interest, which it can then further investigate on its own.
