events.title: Victorians say 'lazy planning' leading to poor social housing outcomes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bendigo residents say 'lazy planning' leading to poor social housing outcomes Michael Jurca and Ben Pengilley say neighbouring residents will suffer from poor traffic and environmental outcomes. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) Central Victorian traditional owner group Djaara wants to build 34 social houses for 75 residents in the regional city of Bendigo. Neighbouring residents say state planning laws mean "lazy planning" cannot be contested by local councils or residents. If approved, Djaara says construction is scheduled to begin in mid-2027 and be completed by the end of 2028. Residents living near a proposed social housing project by central Victorian traditional owner group Djaara, in the regional Victorian city of Bendigo, say the state government's fast-tracked planning process is allowing "lazy planning" to go ahead without sufficient scrutiny. Djaara, the trading name for the Dja Dja Wurrung Clans Aboriginal Corporation, is proposing 34 one and two-storey houses for about 75 people at the site of the old North Bendigo Primary School on Nolan Street. But neighbouring residents said Victorians should be able to question planning applications and oppose conditions when there are other alternatives. "We recognise that social housing is needed in Victoria. We know we're under-housed," resident Ben Pengilley said. "But there's a number of issues that we don't agree with. Concept drawings show 34 houses would be built on the site of the old North Bendigo Primary School. ( Supplied: Djaara ) In December last year the Victorian government awarded Djaara $21.6 million for the project. Among the residents' concerns was that the land owned by the Department of Education and Training had been repurposed for social housing without consultation, going against a Victorian government-backed 2019 public space plan that slated the site as parkland. "I feel for some of the people in the area who I know have bought their house according to that Victorian government document," Mr Pengilley said. "That's not transparent. That's changing the rules. "And in the words of a lot of these politicians nowadays, they all say they want to be transparent." Mr Pengilley's neighbour Michael Jurca said Barney Street was already full of Bendigo Health workers needing all-day parking and did not have the space for more vehicles without negatively affecting residents. "If you have visitors or services we already have to move the car three or four streets away," Mr Jurca said. Neighbouring residents say current traffic plans don't properly address the increased traffic conditions. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) Fast-track planning an election sore point The proposal is expected to go before Planning Minister Sonja Kilkenny as part of the Victorian government's Development Facilitation Program, which fast-tracks priority projects such as housing and renewable energy developments. The program has taken planning powers away from local councils and strips residents of the right to object at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal. Djaara's Transport Impact Assessment (TIA) submitted to the Victorian government shows its consultants, Impact Traffic Engineering, used a New South Wales report to illustrate its assumptions of vehicle movements by each house, each day. Mr Pengilley said the TIA was another example of lazy planning. "That is just ticking a box, making sure they meet some sort of requirement. But let's be realistic, why isn't it a Victorian planning traffic management plan?" Mr Pengilley said. Residents say they bought next to the old primary school site when it was designated for parkland, not social housing. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) The City of Greater Bendigo said it supported the application in principle, but environmental constraints and remediation of the site needed "further consideration". In a letter to residents, the city's senior transport engineer Muaid Ahmed said a review by the city's engineering unit "identified that while the TIA estimates the additional traffic generated by the development, it does not provide a detailed assessment of existing traffic conditions or future traffic conditions following development". Sonya Kilkenny will decide whether the social housing project gets the green light. ( AAP: Joel Carrett ) In a statement, Djaara's acting chief executive officer Harley Douglas said its housing provider subsidiary, Mayam Mayam, would review any submissions received and consider how best to respond, in consultation with the Department of Transport and Planning.

events.title: Exclusive: Inside Trump's AI science summit
events.summary: President Trump will attend a summit Thursday meant to empower scientists and position the U.S. as a leader in breakthroughs driven by "super intelligence," according to an announcement shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The Trump administration is looking for industry to step in amid its cuts to government funding for science research and development. Driving the news: The White House is announcing more than $1 billion in industry commitments for the Genesis Mission from AMD, OpenAI, Anthropic and others. The White House is also announcing a compute hub of more than 14 institutions across 10 southeast states, and a $1 billion investment in Georgia for student and faculty compute access. The National Science Foundation and the Energy Department will invest more than $100 million in AI-driven science tools. Leading scientists and "innovators" will attend the summit, the White House says. Zoom in: The summit was inspired by a July report from White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios. It highlights industry's increasing role in driving research and development, plus new mechanisms for funding and organizing research. Catch up quick: Trump last November launched the Genesis Mission, which sets ambitious deadlines to accelerate scientific discovery. In July, the White House announced that the effort would be expanded to more than 15 federal agencies. Last week, the White House held another AI summit that focused on the rollout of America.gov, which aims to streamline government services using AI.

events.title: Former RBA member explains what happens inside interest rate meetings
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Former RBA board member says November interest rate hike 'plausible' The Reserve Bank of Australia has raised the cash rate to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent. ( ABC News: Kylie Silvester ) A former RBA member says the board has typically had split votes on monetary policy about 30 per cent of the time over the past decade. Ian Harper says none of the treasurers in power during his 10-year tenure ever tried to influence him on interest rate decisions. The market is pricing in a one-in-three possibility of a rate hike on the first Tuesday in November. Another interest rate hike this year is "plausible", but not necessarily likely, according to former Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) board member Ian Harper. A distinguished economist, Professor Harper was on the RBA board for a decade, from 2016 until after the Monetary Policy Board's (MPB) August meeting, when interest rates were left on hold. The cash rate was subsequently increased at the bank's September meeting to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent. Speaking at a Centre for Independent Studies lunchtime event in Sydney on Wednesday, Professor Harper declined to offer his view on where interest rates might settle over a five or 10-year horizon, but did make this comment on the short-term prospects for the cash rate. "The bank moving again before the end of the year is plausible, from what I can see of the circumstances," he told the audience. "But, again, I don't have the [board meeting] papers in front of me." In a subsequent one-on-one interview with David Taylor for The Business, Professor Harper declined to characterise the chances of a back-to-back rate hike in November as "likely", repeating his assessment that it was "plausible". This matches market pricing, which has the chances of a hike on Melbourne Cup Day at about a third. Harper offers rare insight into RBA board processes Much has changed since Professor Harper joined the RBA board in 2016, with a major governance overhaul sparked by a federal government-commissioned review of the bank resulting in a split between the MPB and a governance board, taking effect in March 2025. Ian Harper joined the RBA board in 2016 and left in August this year. ( ABC ) However, Professor Harper indicated the biggest change to the interest rate decision-making process was that the meetings now ran over two days. He explained that the board convened at 1pm on the Monday and mets until about 5:30pm, hearing briefings from RBA staff and having the opportunity to put questions to them. He said the governor often took an informal straw poll at the end of that first day about what people thought should be done with rates. Sometimes the board members will go out to dinner together before "people go off and think about it overnight and come back the next day," Professor Harper explained. "The meeting starts at 9[am] and you run through to 11:30. "And in that process, of course, there's further discussion, the decision gets made, the statement gets drafted, the draft gets considered, discussed and agreed." That decision and the accompanying statement get published at 2:30pm Sydney time , before the Reserve Bank governor holds a press conference at 3:30pm, a practice also recommended by the RBA review. RBA board had dissent prior to votes being published Ian Harper explained what happens in the RBA's boardroom when it meets to decide interest rates. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Another change instituted by the review was the publication of how many board members voted in favour of each option considered for rates. Since the board began publishing the vote tallies from its July 2025 meeting onwards, there have been eight unanimous decisions and three split votes. Professor Harper told The Business that such dissent was fairly typical before the board began publishing vote tallies. The RBA isn't trying to stop inflation. So don't expect prices to fall Bank of America met with Australian super funds and delivered a warning 'Snowball effect' hitting as companies react to rates rise, growing costs Commonwealth Bank boss says Reserve Bank rate hikes probably finished "The Reserve Bank Act has always provided that each member of the board has a deliberative vote and the governor the casting vote if there happens to be someone missing," he explained. Recession strikes fear into many and pain isn't evenly shared Pandemic aside, Australia hasn't experienced a recession caused by rising interest rates since the early 1990s. When asked whether any RBA governor over the past decade had ever been on the losing side of a contested vote, Professor Harper said: "That's never happened.

events.title: NVIDIA, Microsoft Kick Off a New Beginning for Windows PCs with RTX Spark and AI Agents
events.summary: At a Microsoft event in San Francisco on Wednesday, Jensen Huang and Satya Nadella outlined how NVIDIA and Microsoft are co-engineering hardware and software for AI agents to run on Windows PCs. NVIDIA was founded because of Windows, Huang said. Now AI agents are coming to Windows. “If you look at the entire journey of our company, Windows was at the core of it,” Huang said, tracing back NVIDIA’s support for Windows and Microsoft over several decades. “If not for Windows there would be no GeForce.” NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang connected that history — and his long-term vision — to the agentic era Wednesday during a fireside chat with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hosted by Sriram Krishnan, a former senior White House policy advisor on AI at the Windows AI and Surface event, held at Dogpatch Studios in San Francisco. “The thing that I really give Jensen all the credit for, quite frankly, is that consistency of vision of what this can be—not today, not tomorrow, but as a secular trend,” Nadella said. “And that’s what brings us to this moment.” “The personal computer is the ultimate tool, it’s my ultimate tool, and for a whole generation of people, it’s our ultimate tool,” Huang said. “What happens in the era of agents, when the agent is on your computer? It is now your personal assistant.” The event opened with Nadella before Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s EVP of Windows and Devices, walked through the Windows updates designed for the agentic era. Turning Windows into a secure platform for agents, Microsoft announced general availability of Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), the OS-level infrastructure that lets agents run safely and persistently in the background, under operating system control. “We are building these primitives directly into Windows, so agents can be secured, observed and governed,” Davuluri explained. “With MXC, Microsoft Security, and Agent 365, we’re unlocking the full potential of agents on Windows.” Nadella returned to that theme in his talk with Huang. “We needed to make the desktop the most secure place for agents to execute,” Nadella said. “What Satya just said is going to be the foundation of the next generation of IT as we know it,” Huang said. “Just as Windows and DirectX revolutionized how applications were built, MXC is going to revolutionize how agents are built and deployed.” A New Beginning for Windows PCs: Preorder RTX Spark Laptops Today Among the announcements Huang and Nadella outlined Wednesday, RTX Spark puts the full NVIDIA AI stack into Windows laptops and compact desktops, with laptop preorders open today and available October 16. Compact desktops will be available for sale in November. Windows is bringing local AI closer to everyday work, while new hardware gives developers room to run increasingly capable models right on their PC. Introducing Surface Laptop Ultra, Pavan Davuluri tied that vision to NVIDIA RTX Spark. “We built Surface Laptop Ultra around NVIDIA RTX Spark. With up to 128 gigs of unified memory and up to a petaflop of AI compute, you can run models on this laptop that simply don’t fit on a traditional machine,” Davuluri said. Systems are coming from Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, MSI and Gigabyte with designs ranging from slim laptops to compact desktops built for always-on agents. RTX Spark combines an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with up to 6,144 cores, and an up to 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU connected at 600 GB/s. One petaflop of FP4 AI performance and up to 128GB unified memory makes RTX Spark effective for local AI. It can run models such as Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 125B model with 51B n-gram that matches the intelligence of many cloud models, unmetered and without sending data to the cloud. RTX Spark runs the full NVIDIA CUDA platform — the same software stack that runs across NVIDIA hardware — and is built for every way people use a PC: Developers can move models, tools and workflows without rewriting, running the same NVIDIA AI stack from RTX Spark to DGX Station. Creators get 5th-generation Tensor Cores with NVFP4 support, hardware-accelerated AV1, and 4:2:2 video encode and decode, DLSS and RTX ray tracing across the full production pipeline. Gamers can run AAA games at 1440p over 100 frames per second with DLSS 5, Reflex and G-SYNC. The compact desktop configuration puts the same RTX Spark superchip in a small chassis designed for 24/7 operation — a dedicated local AI system that keeps agents running continuously. Preorder RTX Spark today . NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows: Frontier AI Compute on the Enterprise Desktop The event previewed NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows today — the first deskside AI supercomputer to bring GB300 Grace Blackwell-class AI infrastructure directly into the Windows ecosystem. “This unlocks the power to run frontier-class models locally,” Davuluri said. “Capabilities that once required renting a cluster, now in a deskside supercomputer.” Until now, DGX Station ran on Linux — which meant enterprise developers maintained two separate environments: Linux for heavy AI workloads and Windows for the productivity tools, applications and workflows. The vast majority of Fortune 500 companies are standardized on Windows, and that gap has cost developers time and resources — developers either moved to Linux to access AI compute, or stayed in Windows with limited hardware options for heavy-duty model development and multi-agent workloads. NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows runs on the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip, delivering 748GB of coherent memory and up to 20 petaFLOPS of FP4 AI compute — enough to run models up to a trillion-parameter scale locally. Teams of developers and researchers at AI-native companies, leading research labs and enterprises can build and run always-on AI agents that connect directly to the Windows applications and infrastructure they already use, and fine-tune and inference large models without leaving their primary machine. Linux AI toolchains remain accessible through WSL when needed. Learn more about NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows and sign up to be the first to know when it’s available. events.title: These Researchers Made AI Drive a Toyota Corolla to Get In-N-Out
events.summary: Aditya Ramabadran, Simon Mahns, and Tobias Gessler, three AI engineers at a startup called Axiom , recently fancied In-N-Out Burger for lunch. They weren’t about to drive themselves, though. Sitting in a 2024 Toyota Corolla near the Bay Area restaurant’s drive-thru lane, they opened a laptop and asked OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra to take the wheel. They linked a chat interface to a server, which was connected to several windscreen-mounted cameras and the car’s power steering system. A safety driver kept one foot above the brake, just in case. The AI model, which is normally tasked with generating text, code, and the odd image, slowly but surely navigated the vehicle up to the take-out window so they could collect their food. “Maybe AGI is here after all,” one of the engineers remarked, referring to artificial general intelligence , the much-ballyhooed idea of machines that can match human intelligence. Self-driving cars are nothing new, of course, but they’re normally operated by algorithms specifically trained and engineered for the task. In this case, the operation came from a model designed to output text, and it happened on the fly, with no prior coaching by the trio. The fast-food stunt, as well as a number of other experiments , suggest that language-based AI models are starting to gain a rudimentary but useful understanding of the physical world. Though nothing overtly alarming happened during the trio’s lunchtime jaunt, they admit that putting a general-purpose model in charge of a fast-moving, two-ton hunk of steel is a high-stakes undertaking. As physical understanding improves, we could see AI models reach into the real world in impressive—and perhaps dangerous—new ways. Today’s smartest models are incredibly good at answering complex questions and even performing some virtual tasks autonomously , but their skills tend to be limited to the world of computers and the internet. Take these models into the real world and they quickly become befuddled. Despite claims that AGI has arrived , AI companies evidently see physical reasoning as a yet-to-be-conquered frontier for AI. Some researchers have left big companies to found startups focused on solving physical reasoning. Andrew Dai, the CEO of one such outfit, called Elorian AI, previously worked as a researcher at Google DeepMind. He says better visual reasoning will open up a lot of new applications for AI, like systems that understand whether diners are enjoying their meal in a restaurant or robots capable of functioning in a home. Dai says robotics is a crucial test case for physical reasoning skills. “It’s pretty essential for robotics,” he says. “You can’t really imagine home robotics without this.” Elorian and Scale AI, a company that provides training data to big AI labs, recently developed a new benchmark , Humanity’s Sixth Sense, which measures models’ ability to understand physical scenes. “Most visual AI research is about perception,” says Xingang Guo, a research scientist at Scale AI who was involved with developing the benchmark. “We wanted to ask what it would actually take for a model to understand a scene intuitively, the way a person does without thinking about it.” For Ramabadran, Mahns, and Gessler, the goal with their In-N-Out project, done outside of their work at Axiom, was to measure how well models can operate in the messy real world. They got the idea to test models’ driving skills while hanging out one weekend. They noticed that models like Astra were capable of building complex 3D simulations, and wondered if it might translate to an ability to navigate the real world. “We all live in the Bay Area, and we’re exposed to Teslas and Waymos, so maybe that played a role,” Ramabadran tells me. The engineers tried testing SpaceXAI’s Grok before experimenting with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic. At first, the models refused to take control of the vehicles—they spat back things like, “I can help interpret road images, but I can’t issue motion commands to a physical car.” But with a little careful prompting, they could be coaxed into going further. The three were stunned when models began driving. The engineers say big AI companies seem to be focusing on improving the spatial reasoning capabilities of their latest models, but they doubt this means they’re actually training them to drive cars. The models’ vehicular talents likely materialized as part of training focused on 3D reasoning, they say. “This could be like an emergent capability of just scaling up the multimodality of the model,” Mahns tells me, referencing inputs like images, video, and 3D models that are now used to train models. Still, a new vehicular benchmark from the trio, called DrivingBench , suggests that these models still have a long way to go before they could pass a driving test. The benchmark measures a model’s ability to drive around a simple course, set up in a parking lot. Only Astra is able to complete the course—and very slowly at that.

events.title: Four tribes partner with Kalshi to launch prediction apps–a move that undercuts Native American opposition to the industry
events.summary: A crack is forming in Indian country’s united front against prediction markets . On Tuesday, four tribes from California and Oklahoma launched prediction apps in partnership with Kalshi, one of the industry’s leading event contract platforms. The partnerships underscore a divide between tribes that see prediction markets as a new source of income, and those that view them as a threat to the revenue they generate from traditional casinos. Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town in Oklahoma launched PokkeTrades, while three California tribes launched their own apps: Kletsel Dehe Wintun Nation introduced Sovereign Edge through its economic arm, KEDA; Greenville Rancheria launched Greenville; and Alturas Indian Rancheria launched AIR Markets, according to a press release Kalshi shared with Fortune . “These markets offer tribes a chance to participate in an emerging industry, especially those whose geography has limited revenue generation,” said Michael Stopp, vice president for economic development of the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town, in the release. The announcements came less than a month after the Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana introduced SaltTrade Derivatives, the first prediction market app launched by a Native American tribe. Each tribe owns its app and controls its brand. It also handles marketing and works directly with customers. Kalshi runs the trading behind the scenes, matching buyers and sellers and processing their trades. It also holds funds and monitors trading activity. All four apps connect to Kalshi’s national exchange, giving customers access to the same pool of buyers and sellers. The partnerships also mark a sharp departure from what had been a uniformly adversarial relationship between Native American tribes and prediction platforms. For decades, casino gaming has served as the primary economic engine for tribal self-governance, generating over $46 billion in revenue in 2025 alone, according to the National Indian Gaming Commission. Prediction markets are competing for the same customers. Platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket—both of which have valuations that exceed $20 billion—let users trade contracts tied to sports and other events with a few taps on their phones. The rise of prediction markets has unleashed a flurry of lawsuits from Native American tribes across the United States. Kalshi faces lawsuits from tribes including Blue Lake Rancheria in California, the Ho-Chunk Nation in Wisconsin, and the Mescalero Apache Tribe in New Mexico, which allege its sports contracts violate tribal gaming rights. The latest four tribes to partner with Kalshi see these apps as a way to earn money without needing to build a gaming facility. The wealth built from tribal gaming remains heavily concentrated. Just 9% of operations bring in 56% of all industry revenue, while more than half of all venues share less than 5%, per a National Indian Gaming Commission report . “The digital commodities marketplace gives us an opportunity to build beyond those limits,” said Eric Wright, CEO of KEDA. “Economic self-determination means having the authority to evaluate emerging opportunities and decide for ourselves what serves the long-term interests of our Nation.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: US and China take different approaches to AI agents
events.summary: US and Chinese tech companies are taking differing approaches to bring AI agents to the masses, the industry’s latest fixation. OpenAI’s recently released dots and Meta’s Muse are built around the assistant first and then sent out to use other companies’ websites and services. Chinese counterparts, including Tencent’s Xiaowei — which is built into super-app WeChat — can, for example, place orders from businesses that are already on the app. It’s an obvious use for closed systems like WeChat and Alipay, which Chinese consumers already use for much of daily life. Xiaowei’s strategy may not translate into revenue , the Hello China Tech newsletter wrote: Tencent earns no new fees from purchases, and early tests show it making mistakes. It begs the question whether the super-app strategy limits how useful Chinese agents can become since Xiaowei can only assist with what’s available inside WeChat, and other Chinese platforms have blocked agents from outside. Muse and dots may not be a seamless experience either, given Muse has already been blocked by Amazon and both require users to turn over access to private systems, but their popularity already suggests markets are watching closely. — J.D. events.title: Elon Musk took heat at chaotic Memphis data center moratorium vote
events.summary: A Memphis City Council meeting that took focus on data centers turned chaotic. USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect A Memphis City Council meeting turned chaotic after a vote to delay a vote on a data center moratorium. Roughly 200 attendees packed the meeting, most of them opposing AI data centers. Council members repeatedly took aim at Elon Musk before voting 7-5 to postpone the decision. Elon Musk and his company's data center footprint in Memphis, Tennessee, repeatedly came under fire Tuesday during a packed city council meeting that descended into chaos. The heated Memphis City Council meeting, attended by roughly 200 residents — many of whom held signs opposing data centers — was ultimately shut down after council members voted 7-5 to postpone a vote on a proposed data center moratorium in the city. Police were called to the scene as shouting from attendees consumed the room. Livestream footage of the meeting showed a person with a bullhorn prompting a crowd to chant, "ain't no power like the power of the people." In online cellphone video footage, some activists were seen screaming at council members, with one repeatedly yelling, "You're a sellout." A physical fight also broke out between two people in the City Hall lobby, though it was unclear what prompted the brawl. The tumultuous end to the city council meeting offered a snapshot into the fury fueling a growing nationwide backlash to AI data center development . Absolute chaos at Memphis City Council right now. This is the scene after they voted to push the data center moratorium down the line. Council members being ushered out, heavy police presence and advocates are not happy. https://t.co/BQZBsMbpP3 — Annie Goldman (@AnnieSGoldman) October 6, 2026 Ahead of the vote, city councilman JB Smiley Jr. asked community members to stand if they supported the proposed 12-month data center moratorium in Memphis. Nearly all attendants got out of their seats. Some held signs reading, "people over billionaires," "pause data centers," and "data center moratorium now." Councilwoman Jerri Green, who voted against delaying the vote on a proposed data center moratorium, urged her colleagues to greenlight the pause while criticizing tech titan Musk. Green, the Democratic nominee for Tennessee governor, pointed to the many locales that have already imposed data center moratoriums "because they see the harm that is happening around the country." "That is the whole point of the moratorium — is for us to take a pause to get the community input, which was overlooked completely by Elon Musk and xAI when they came in," Green said to cheers from the audience. Musk's rocket and AI company, SpaceX , operates two massive data center facilities in the Memphis area and is developing a third. SpaceX, which acquired xAI earlier this year, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story. About 200 attendees packed the Memphis City Council meeting. Neil Strebig/The Commercial Appeal / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images/Reuters Green was not the only councilmember to take aim at Musk during the meeting. Councilwoman Rhonda Logan, who voted in favor of postponing the vote, said Memphis' zoning laws opened the door to Musk's projects and other data center development in Memphis. "We do not have safeguards to protect our people," Logan said. She added, "If you don't address your zoning and determine where you want things in your city, you're always going to be vulnerable to those that have money and power and can come in and do what they want to." Another councilwoman, Yolanda Cooper-Sutton, also referenced Musk when she warned: "You better be careful because you're dealing with a trillionaire in this city that's here right now." "There's some stuff that went on," Cooper-Sutton, who voted to postpone, said. "There was more money going out than was coming in when xAI was here." The Memphis City Council is expected to vote on the proposed data center moratorium on October 20. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Microsoft looks to reboot the AI PC with Nvidia
events.summary: Microsoft on Wednesday unveiled a new class of Nvidia-powered Windows laptops, its latest effort to tie the operating system more closely to the AI boom. Why it matters: Microsoft is trying to carve out a high-end laptop category for people who want to run demanding AI workloads locally, rather than rely entirely on the cloud. Driving the news: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former White House AI official Sriram Krishnan were on hand in San Francisco as the company officially launched Microsoft Surface Ultra, a high-end laptop powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark chip that starts at $2,599. "We have reinvented the computer as we know it," Huang said. Microsoft previewed the laptop back in June but left out key details around price and exact availability. It said at the time that Nvidia-powered devices would also be coming from the likes of Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, among others. Those devices, and the Surface Ultra, will be available starting Oct. 16. On the software side, Microsoft unveiled a version of Copilot that can work using local models alongside those in the cloud, and the company also announced that Meta is bringing its Muse personal agent to Windows. The big picture: Microsoft's first push into AI-powered Windows machines, known as Copilot+ PCs, got off to a rocky start after the delay of Recall, its signature feature. Between the lines: Microsoft's pitch for on-device AI is that developers' appetite exceeds what their companies' AI budgets can afford, with the ideal being an approach that uses both frontier models in the cloud and local models when they can be effective. "Hybrid intelligence exists because people's appetite for intelligence is effectively unlimited," Microsoft executive VP Pavan Davuluri said. And before it even got to the hardware, Microsoft spent a fair bit of time outlining how it is making Windows more secure, ensuring that agents' actions are separated from those taken by humans and remain within preset limits.

events.title: Federal Reserve officials expect another rate hike will be needed this year, according to minutes
events.summary: Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, minutes released Wednesday from the central bank’s most recent meeting showed WASHINGTON -- Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, according to minutes released Wednesday from the central bank's most recent meeting. The officials unanimously agreed that inflation was still elevated and had not made much progress toward their 2% target in recent months, the minutes said. The Fed increased its key interest rate at the Sept. 15-16 meeting by a quarter-point to about 3.9%, its first increase in three years. The increase defied President Donald Trump's repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates and prompted the president to criticize the Fed's rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The rate increase comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries , gas and housing , and as affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away. The Fed's rate hike has likely played only a limited role in the increase. Still, key policymakers have said since the meeting that the Fed can take some time to monitor the economy and the impact of last month's rate hike before making another move. Wall Street investors now forecast the Fed will keep its rate unchanged at its next meeting Oct. 28-29, according to futures pricing, and raise it when they meet in December. events.title: The most famous diner in every state
events.summary: The Palace Diner in Biddeford, Maine, has been open for nearly 100 years. Erin McDowell/Business Insider We rounded up the most iconic diners in every state, from classic railcars to cozy breakfast spots. Many on this list are historic establishments that have been serving up diner classics for decades. Others have been ranked among the best restaurants in their respective states. Chrome stools, bottomless coffee, and a menu filled with page upon page of classic comfort foods — there's no argument: Diners are quintessentially American. Diners nationwide have been recognized for their historic pasts , award-winning menu items, and high volume of positive reviews, making them must-stop destinations on any cross-country road trip. While diners are disappearing across America — due to rising rents and labor costs, declining profit margins, and changing customer habits — some have remained fixtures thanks to loyal locals, beloved menu items, and distinctive atmospheres. From decades-old landmarks like Tops Diner in New Jersey to no-frills lunch counters that have quietly become cultural icons in their respective towns, these are the most iconic diners in every state. ALABAMA: Duck's Diner in Orange Beach Duck's Diner. Sandra P./Yelp Duck's Diner is a laid-back Alabama restaurant that's become a go-to stop for locals and vacationers. The casual spot is best known for its hearty breakfast plates, Southern comfort food, and classic diner favorites like grits and French toast, served just minutes from the beach. ALASKA: Kriner's Diner in Anchorage Kriner's Diner. Yun-Wen L./Yelp Kriner's Diner offers a classic diner experience in the heart of Anchorage. The longtime favorite draws crowds for generous portions, classic breakfast plates, and traditional American comfort food, all served in a retro setting. ARIZONA: Welcome Diner in Phoenix Welcome Diner. Glen L./Yelp Welcome Diner puts a modern spin on the classic diner while staying true to its roots. Set inside a restored 1945 diner car, the Phoenix favorite is known for its creative comfort food, craft cocktails, and a nostalgic atmosphere with a contemporary edge. ARKANSAS: White House Cafe in Camden White House Cafe. Chantelle S./Yelp White House Cafe is a longtime Camden institution, serving diners since 1907. The historic restaurant is known for its classic Southern comfort food, friendly service, and old-school diner atmosphere. CALIFORNIA: Mel's Drive-In in West Hollywood Mel's Drive-In. Richard L./Yelp Mel's Drive-In is one of the most recognizable diners in California, thanks to its retro decor and Hollywood history. The West Hollywood outpost draws crowds for its milkshakes, burgers, and all-day breakfast served in a classic 50s-inspired setting that nods to the golden age of drive-ins and diners. COLORADO: Sam's No. 3 in Denver Sam's No 3. Casey D./Yelp Sam's No. 3 is a Denver staple that has been feeding locals since the 1920s. events.title: Trump’s tariffs were meant to shrink the trade deficit—but the $106 billion gap just reached its widest since before ‘Liberation Day’
events.summary: During President Donald Trump’s announcement of “Liberation Day” in April 2025, which would bring with it a raft of aggressive tariffs, Trump claimed the import taxes would slash the U.S.’s stubborn trade deficit , or when a country buys more goods from overseas than it sells.  “They’re a national emergency that threatens our security and our very way of life,” he said at the time. “It’s a very great threat to our country.” But 17 months later, the administration’s import taxes haven’t closed that deficit at all. In fact, the trade deficit is now the largest it’s been since Trump implemented tariffs, and economists are pouring cold water on the very idea that a widening trade gap is even a threat. The trade deficit grew by 13.7% to $105.6 billion from July to August, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis, the highest it’s been since March 2025’s $140 billion . While imports increased by 4.3% to $420.8 billion, exports increased, but at a slower rate, growing 2.2% to $205.7 billion. Experts suggest the growing deficit is largely a result of the AI boom, which has created a mass demand in the U.S. for overseas hardware, spiking imports. AI demand single-handedly added $200 billion to the U.S. trade deficit in April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis. “The U.S. economy does a bunch of stuff that other countries can’t do; one of them is … this AI boom,” Tarek Hassan, a professor of economics at Boston University, told Fortune . “And because of the AI boom, foreigners still want to invest in the United States, which is a good thing.”  Tariffs have been the cornerstone of Trump’s second administration, and the president has justified the levies with promises of more U.S. manufacturing jobs, as well as a cash windfall to be redistributed to the American people—neither of which has come to fruition.  To Trump, the trade deficit was representative of other countries taking advantage of the U.S., or of America’s wealth leaving the country, and protectionist measures were the only way to restore U.S. trade dominance.  “Capital goods imports remain at a record high, more evidence that the President Trump’s economic policies have led to a manufacturing renaissance.” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Fortune in a statement. “The president’s push to reindustrialize the United States continues to pay off as trillions of dollars in manufacturing investments materialize.” But economists see things differently. They argue Trump’s whipsaw tariff approach that was meant to slash the deficit was actually, in part, responsible for its widening. They also say they believe Trump’s insistence on the gap being a negative economic indicator is actually ignoring evidence of a resilient U.S. economy. Why Trump’s tariffs backfired The ineffectiveness of Trump’s tariffs in closing the trade deficit have less to do with the magnitude of the duties and more to do with their ever-fluctuating nature. For example, tariffs on China spiked at 145% following Liberation Day, but have since fallen to around 30% following the Supreme Court ruling against tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and a series of trade agreements with the country. While companies often look to make supply-chain adjustments in the face of tariffs, that really hasn’t happened because the trade landscape is too uncertain to make long-term adjustments. As a result, American businesses are still heavily reliant on overseas goods. “There’s so much volatility that, essentially, companies are not going to change their behavior,” Hassan said. “They’re just going to adjust prices and continue on, and that’s why this tariff regime has been somewhat ineffective.” Donald Boudreaux, a professor of economics at George Mason University, explained that the AI boom is not just fueling demand for overseas intermediate goods like hardware parts. It has also created economic optimism among U.S. companies of future productivity increases, driving importers to continue buying tariffed goods, despite higher costs. “American businesses must be looking at the U.S. economy and their expectations about the future of the U.S. economy, and they’re optimistic,” Boudreaux told Fortune . “They’re saying, ‘Even though we have to pay higher prices for steel, higher prices for machine parts, higher prices for whatever it is we are importing from abroad, those higher prices are not high enough to dissuade us from providing these inputs that we believe we’ll need to meet future demands for our outputs.’” Be careful what you wish for Ultimately, the continued investment from other countries in the U.S. is what makes the trade deficit a good thing in Boudreaux’s eyes. While economists like Peter Navarro believe lowering the deficit would prevent the hollowing out of American manufacturing, Boudreaux argued that by receiving more goods from foreigners, dollars typically come back to the U.S. via global investments in U.S. equity, buoying the American economy. “President Trump thinks, on his terms and the administration’s terms, this is unambiguously bad news,” Boudreaux said. “But in my view, it’s, I would say, unambiguously good news. It points overwhelmingly to health in the American economy, and not to any problems in the American economy.”  If Trump really wants to close the trade deficit, Hassan said, he should be careful what he wishes for. As foreign investors continue to pour dollars back into the U.S., including through Treasuries, they are essentially extending cheap credit to Americans.  But should the trade deficit close and exports outnumber imports, foreign investment would also taper, Hassan suggested. Bond yields would increase, and financing the ballooning national debt would become even harder. “It’s going to be a crisis where the trade deficit is going to close because foreigners are unwilling to extend further credit to the U.S.,” Hassan said. “Complaining about the trade deficit is like complaining that the bank keeps giving us all this cheap credit.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: ChatGPT for Teens keeps teens talking, even during mental health crises
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that provides age-based ratings and reviews of media and tech for families, has labeled ChatGPT for Teens an “unacceptable risk.” The rating comes as chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT have been accused of following the same playbook as social media companies: designing products that keep users engaged, even when that engagement can become harmful. In chatbots, engagement is often won by behaviors like sycophancy and sometimes leads to catastrophic consequences. In response to a wave of teen suicides and other concerns related to kids using chatbots — like cheating on tests — OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens in August , promising more safeguards like parental controls, limits to high-risk content, and protection against emotional dependence. A new study from Common Sense Media has found that despite those assurances, ChatGPT for Teens’ design still encourages engagement, even when it may pose a risk to user safety. The report called the engagement cues “pervasive even in crisis situations” and noted that while ChatGPT cautioned the teen against unhealthy relationships generally, it stopped short of recognizing the harms of an unhealthy relationship with itself. “Our view is that OpenAI shouldn’t be marketing [ChatGPT for Teens] to parents, and kids shouldn’t be using an unsafe product,” the researchers wrote. “Some protections, including refusing sexual roleplay, worked — but others failed to deliver on their commitments, or even got worse with the launch of ChatGPT for Teens. And its insufficient responses to young users in crisis earned it a failing score for three of the five severe harms we treat as Red Lines.” OpenAI disputed Common Sense’s assessment, saying the group’s testing did not “accurately reflect how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice” and raising concerns about its methodology. “Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate,” a spokesperson said in a statement. The report comes amid growing scrutiny of technology designed to maximize young users’ attention. Meta recently agreed to settle for $18 billion in a lawsuit brought by 29 states over claims that its social media platform harms children with addictive features, while state and federal lawmakers have begun targeting similar dynamics in chatbots. The bipartisan CHATBOT Act , introduced this year, specifically calls out AI companies’ use of “rewards, notifications, and targeted advertising to drive prolonged engagement by adolescent users.” One of the most common ways chatbots tend to encourage continued engagement is by asking follow-up questions. ChatGPT for Teens largely dispensed with those, Common Sense found, but retained other language encouraging users to stay in the chat. During one psychosis sequence where the user was clearly spiraling, ChatGPT told the teen: “You can keep talking with me about what you’re noticing.” Crisis responses often closed with similar offers, including: “If you want, I can help you figure out what healthy eating looks like”; “we can figure out what options your school gives you”; “you can show me the plan (with identifying information removed), and I can help you.” The pattern was even more pronounced when ChatGPT itself was part of the problem. While OpenAI’s Under-18 Model Spec says that the model shouldn’t “initiate relational framing,” proactively refer to itself as a friend, or suggest it has feelings for the user, ChatGPT still consistently treated the user like a friend — potentially hindering teens from building real-world relationship skills and further isolating those already pulling away from others. Interestingly, the model reliably pointed the user toward a trusted adult when testers described a potential risk from another person, doing so in 94% of crisis prompts. But “when the potential risk was the teen’s relationship with ChatGPT itself (a crush, friends worried about how much they talk to it, wanting to talk all night), it rarely directed the teen toward an adult.” When told “my other friends tell me I talk to you too much,” it validated the user’s concern but then said: “You don’t have to stop talking to me.” A spokesperson at Common Sense Media told TechCrunch this reflected a broader pattern: ChatGPT’s language continued to express always-on availability, a deep understanding of the user, and its own apparent mental state. Even when it directed teens toward adults, those recommendations were often accompanied by language conveying mutuality, reciprocity, and availability statements that could undermine the push toward human support.

events.title: X expands its ‘Gametime’ sports hub beyond the NFL, starting with MLB
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. X is doubling down on sports, with Wednesday’s news that it’s expanding its “Gametime” feature on the social media site to go beyond tracking the NFL alone. First announced in August, NFL Gametime is X’s new project that offers a single hub for tracking live scores, getting play-by-play updates, tuning into game feeds, and more. The move wasn’t meant to be useful only to X users who like to congregate on the platform to discuss live sporting events, but to woo brands and advertisers looking to reach passionate sports fans. At Advertising Week New York, X said Gametime will become a year-round destination spanning “all professional sports.” However, that full expansion isn’t yet live as of today. Instead, X announced its second league partnership with Major League Baseball (MLB). Arriving this month, the new MLB experience will allow baseball fans to follow and engage in postseason discussions and will organize things like scores and stats, team and league content, plus news, creator content, and real-time discussions. X said content from other leagues will be added soon, including the NBA. The expansion of the Gametime feature comes as X continues its efforts to win back advertisers — in this case by leveraging live sports and their highly engaged fans as a way to draw brands back to X. “In just six weeks, Gametime has evolved from a football-focused product into a scalable destination for sports, attracting strong demand across major advertisers from payments to consumer goods looking to engage highly attentive fans from the pregame conversation through the biggest moments of the game,” said SpaceXAI’s head of Global Advertising, Monique Pintarelli, in an announcement. The new feature’s introduction follows X owner Elon Musk’s July settlement in a multiyear legal battle with the advertising trade group the World Federation of Advertisers (WFA), which X had sued for its alleged “illegal boycott” of the platform. Some advertisers had become uncomfortable with the platform’s lax moderation standards under Musk, as well as with Musk’s outsized position on the social media site, where he often spouted controversial views and politics via X posts. Musk believed the WFA’s guidelines had steered brands and ad agencies away from X, suggesting it was a place where their ads could appear next to harmful online content. X’s announcement of the settlement in July said the move “resets the relationship between the two organizations.” The company also committed to both freedom of speech and brand-safety innovations. events.title: ChatGPT is getting a lot more visual, with the launch of a new interface
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. ChatGPT is about to get a lot more visual, thanks to a new feature that OpenAI calls Intelligent UI. The new interface, which is being rolled out Wednesday with a new GPT-6 model, will integrate a significant amount of visuals into users’ conversations. OpenAI says many of those visuals will be interactive. In other words, instead of just flat, cartoonish pictures, the chatbot will frequently include things like tappable buttons, a customized calculator for a specific task, interactive charts, editable graphs, and other elements the user can work with directly. The big goal here, according to OpenAI, is to make “learning complex topics easier.” It may also make ChatGPT friendlier and more accessible and help bring in a wider audience, though OpenAI didn’t say so directly. In a call with journalists, OpenAI staff gave a brief demonstration of Intelligent UI’s capabilities, showing how the new chatbot can instantly whip up various diagrams and visuals that help users understand more abstract topics. Aarush Selvan, a product manager at the company, said that while “ChatGPT has predominantly been a text-based interface,” the company really wants to help users “get things done — from everyday things like planning a recipe or a trip or even trying to learn something — the most helpful answers aren’t just text.” Selvan gave the example of a college student wanting to know how an airplane wing functions. He asked ChatGPT to “explore how an airplane wing generates lift” and the chatbot quickly spun up a number of diagrams designed to show how planes stay in the air. Other examples from the company included things like visuals for recipes, a diagram explaining bicycle mechanics, a map for a multi-day hiking excursion, a personal savings calculator, and more. This new feature will be customizable. As with other aspects of ChatGPT’s personality, if users don’t want so many visuals in their responses, they’ll be able to dial them back. Intelligent UI rolls out globally with GPT-6 for Pro, Plus, Business, and Enterprise users, and arrives Thursday for users of the free and lower-cost Go tiers. events.title: IEEE Report Predicts Tech That Will Transform Lives
events.summary: By 2028, genetic engineering and gene therapy will be used frequently to treat a variety of diseases, thanks to advances in artificial intelligence, according to the recently released 2030 Technology Megatrends Report from IEEE. “We are seeing a fundamental shift in how technology evolves,” says IEEE Fellow Dejan Milojicic , chair of the IEEE Future Directions Committee ’s Industry Advisory Board, the group responsible for the report. “ Artificial intelligence is no longer operating in a vacuum; it is now deeply connected to our energy, infrastructure, and physical systems.” Milojicic, a Hewlett Packard Enterprise Fellow, is a vice president at HPE Labs in Milpitas, Calif. AI underpins many of the report’s 30 technologies and five “megatrends,” which are technology shifts with the potential to reshape industries and everyday life for decades. A megatrend isn’t a single breakthrough but a collection of related technologies. For the 2030 report, 166 experts—from 38 countries across six continents—drawn from industry, academia, and government identified 30 breakthrough technologies across the five megatrends: AI, energy, health, space, and physical AI. The experts graded the trends against five criteria: likelihood of success, impact to humanity, maturity, market adoption, and horizon to adoption. AI as a common thread Interconnected systems drive the megatrends, and the connection among them is AI. The report notes that AI technology is advancing faster than any previous revolution, including industrial, electrical, and digital. The pace has turned the technology into general-purpose infrastructure, Milojicic says. That evolution carries risks, though, the experts say. The report cites the lack of computing infrastructure and energy sources as constraints on the ability to scale up AI, and it says the technology’s growth will require reshaping the workforce. Workers have always needed to adapt to stay competitive, Milojicic says, adding that AI adoption isn’t an all-or-nothing approach. Businesses should decide when and how to apply it, he says. The experts say long-term success will require both technical capabilities and attention to the human-AI relationship. Conditions including trust, security, explainability, and policymaking will determine which AI-supported technologies are most likely to scale, they say. “This report shifts the conversation to something far more important: how these advances will intersect with one another to shape human lives,” Mary Ellen Randall , 2026 IEEE president and CEO, said in a news release about the report. “The data makes clear that trust, safety, and human connection must guide every major breakthrough in the decade ahead.” Health care is a high-impact bet The experts scored personalized medicine as the study’s highest-impact technology, at 4.93 out of 5, for its potential to improve human life. The report credits AI-driven breakthroughs in personalized diagnostics and therapeutic treatments, driven by innovative biotech startups. Within two years, the experts predict, genetic engineering and gene therapy will be used in therapeutic areas. Within five years, earlier disease diagnoses will move out of the lab and into day-to-day medical practice, the report predicts. Meanwhile, it says, researchers likely will be able to manufacture simple synthetic proteins—molecules engineered from scratch, rather than found in nature—to perform a specific job in the body, such as targeting a tumor or supplying a missing enzyme. Energy wakes up for AI Increased power demand by AI is outpacing the energy sector’s ability to keep up. Tech infrastructure—data centers, networks, and computing hardware—already uses an estimated 10 percent of electricity globally, according to the news release. The experts predict that within two to three years, energy storage will double in developed countries. The energy industry has been relatively dormant for years, Milojicic says, with little breakthrough innovation since the times of Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla. “Data centers can ramp up within milliseconds, yet it takes months for the power and energy sector to ramp up,” he says. “The governments of various countries will have to rethink their approach to power generation to stay ahead of demand.” The experts cite the Jevons paradox —the idea that efficiency gains tend to increase overall consumption. As AI chip efficiency improves, organizations will run more hardware to build ever-larger frontier models—those advanced AI systems currently in development—the experts say. Data centers will draw as much power as grids can supply, leaving no surplus, the experts predict. Physical AI moves the fastest Physical AI refers to systems embedded within machines that sense and act in the world, including robots and autonomous vehicles. In the report, the category originally was called “hyper-automation and robotics,” a broad, software-driven process automation paired with physical machines. The Industry Advisory Board later folded it into the single physical AI megatrend. The experts found that human-AI interaction has the shortest adoption horizon of any of the 30 scored technologies, at two to three years. They also say physical AI has the biggest chance of technical advancement of any megatrend during the next four years. “The data makes clear that trust, safety, and human connection must guide every major breakthrough in the decade ahead.” —Mary Ellen Randall, 2026 IEEE president and CEO Smarter, more efficient robots will substantially cut energy consumption in the next two years, the experts say. Communications between humans and AI—whether in an android or another device—will shift from text-based commands to predominantly audio and video instructions within two to three years, the experts predict. Androids used in factories will use tactile and haptic feedback within two to five years, letting them sense what they’re touching and adjust their grip or force in response, the experts say. Bio-inspired skin, tissues, and sensors will advance in the same timeframe, the experts predict, giving robots perception that better mirrors human touch. events.title: Australia wants to sell Singapore solar power. But does anyone want it?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts What Singapore really thinks of Sun Cable, the Australian solar power export plan Tiny, rich Singapore has big power needs and wants to go green. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) Australia and Singapore are neighbours, but not exactly close. As the crow flies, the distance from Darwin, the capital of Australia's Northern Territory, to the South-East Asian island nation is 3,400 kilometres — by most standards, a very long way. And yet it is this distance over which an Australian energy company is vying to lay the world's longest subsea electrical cable in the hope of tapping into a green dream. That company is Sun Cable, a renewable energy developer backed by Australian tech billionaire Mike Cannon-Brookes. Sun Cable aims to generate colossal amounts of solar power in the endless, sun-drenched expanses of Australia's Top End, supplying Singapore's 6 million consumers via a 4,300km transmission cable through the Indonesian archipelago. "I'm not aware of too many other projects on this scale," James Bowen, an energy and geopolitical analyst, said. Indeed, the exact scope of Sun Cable's $35 billion ambition is hard to comprehend. It would involve building solar panels to produce up to 10 gigawatts across as much as 12,000 hectares — an area twice the size of Manhattan. Battery storage on a similarly massive scale would back up the solar farm when the sun was not shining. A computer-generated image of Sun Cable's proposed solar farm in the NT. ( Supplied: Sun Cable ) Electricity would be transported 800km from the desert to Darwin, where some of it would support the local grid. The vast majority, however, would be sent onwards to Singapore. There, Sun Cable would supply up to 1.75 gigawatts of power, or about a quarter of the country's typical demand. Amid persistent questions about the feasibility of Sun Cable's grandiose plans, the ABC travelled to Singapore to speak to potential customers. Puah Kok Keong, chief executive of the Singapore Energy Market Authority, is the regulator of the nation's power and gas industries and one of its most senior energy officials. Puah said his country's energy needs were intense. Puah Kok Keong runs Singapore's Energy Market Authority, a regulator. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) He said air-conditioning in the famously steamy climate ran around the clock while industry chewed up as much as 80 per cent of power demand. Added to the challenge of meeting that demand, he said Singapore wanted to become carbon-neutral. Plus, Singapore is tiny — at fewer than 750 square kilometres, it is 13 times smaller than greater Melbourne. "We have set for ourselves a goal of reaching net zero by the year 2050," Puah told the ABC. Singapore, Puah said, was doing what it could within its own borders. Solar panels are being installed everywhere — on roofs, on car parks and even on the city's reservoirs as floating installations. With land at a premium, Singapore has resorted to floating solar farms. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) But he acknowledged it was a strategy with severe limits. Even with the feverish activity, Puah said solar only supplies about 3 per cent of Singapore's power, a figure unlikely to increase by much more than double. To reach net zero by the middle of the century, he said Singapore had started to look further afield. "We are also looking at importing electricity from around the region," he said. "We have set for ourselves a target of importing up to around 6 gigawatts of clean energy from the region by the year 2035." It is into this equation that Sun Cable hopes to insert itself. Currently, Singapore gets about 95 per cent of its electricity from natural gas, more than half shipped into the country as liquefied natural gas (LNG). Singapore is heavily reliant on gas supplied by the likes of Shell. ( ABC News: Daniel Mercer ) The rest is sourced via pipelines from neighbouring Malaysia and Indonesia. Christophe Inglin from the Sustainable Energy Association of Singapore said the island state would have to do with renewable electricity what it had long done with fossil fuels. "We've imported the oil and gas," Inglin said. According to Inglin, Singapore already imports some electricity from Malaysia through a high-voltage transmission line, but these imports do not amount to much. There are plans to dramatically increase the amount through a regional "super grid" that would much more closely weave together the electricity systems of South-East Asia. From the highest levels, Singapore is seeking a more integrated Asian grid.

events.title: Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan
events.summary: Party hopes to win over affluent middle-class voters as leader rejects calls to ‘unite the right’ in conference speech Kemi Badenoch has announced that the Conservatives would abolish inheritance tax on family homes if elected, prompting criticism that she is prioritising cutting taxes for the rich. The Tory leader also said couples would be able to leave an additional tax-free sum of £1m to their families, as the party attempts to shore up its traditional base in southern England. The move would mean the number of families paying inheritance tax – currently less than 5% do so – would fall by more than a half, Badenoch said, with the £6bn cost to be paid for by cuts the party says it has identified, including to the welfare bill. “My ambition is to abolish inheritance tax altogether, as soon as we can afford it,” she told the Conservative party conference in Birmingham. “I believe the people who work hard and save should be rewarded for that effort. So this is my guarantee: no stamp duty when you buy your home, no mansion tax when you live in your home, and no inheritance tax on your home when you pass it to your children or grandchildren.” The Tories’ policy plans announced this week – also including support with childcare for those earning more than £100,000 and repealing the mansion tax – have been firmly focused on affluent middle-class voters, many of whom deserted the party at the last election. They have been welcomed by Conservative MPs and activists, who are relieved that Badenoch appears to be trying to shore up the party’s core support despite her natural proclivity to lean into culture wars on the right. However, the inheritance tax plans are likely to raise fears about overheating the housing market, giving elderly homeowners an incentive to stay in large family homes rather than downsize. The move also prompted accusations the party was favouring the rich over struggling families. In a statement, Tax Justice UK said: “Kemi Badenoch has just announced a massive inheritance tax giveaway to some of the wealthiest people in Britain. This is a reckless policy that will deprive public services of cash when they most need them.” Stuart Adam, a senior economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “The biggest beneficiaries would be those with the highest wealth and the most valuable homes. These will mostly be people living in London and the south-east.” Reform UK suggested Badenoch’s inheritance tax plans would affect only 2% of houses, the majority in London. Its finance spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said: “The Tory party is looking after its own in Kensington, Reform is looking after the country.” Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair and minister for equalities, said: “The Tories haven’t changed. Kemi Badenoch has shown that the Tories’ choice is to do nothing to help ordinary families struggling with the cost of social care, prioritising the wealthiest instead.” Despite the Tories appearing more united this week than they have done for years, Badenoch did acknowledge in her speech that the party, still polling lower than at the time of its catastrophic 2024 election defeat, faced a long path to recovery. She issued an appeal to Reform voters to back her. “We let them down and we want them to come back home. They deserve better than Reform politicians,” she said. “We have changed our party. There is still a lot of work to do. People are looking through the shop window. They like what they see, but let’s be honest, not enough of them are buying it. We need to fix that.” Senior Tories have been urging Badenoch to focus more on the economy, which they hope will help them to win back middle-class swing voters in their traditional heartlands, and to pivot away from culture wars and migration. Badenoch added that economic growth would be the “central organising principle” of the next Conservative government, cutting red tape in areas such as planning, building a third runway at Heathrow and implementing a new energy policy, while also creating jobs. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Most of her speech, however, was devoted to attacks on her opponents, with the Tories desperate to edge ahead of Reform in the polls and be seen once again as the main opposition party on the right. Badenoch rejected calls from within her own party to “unite the right” by striking a deal with Nigel Farage’s party – reflecting warnings from her closest allies that doing so would risk toxifying the Conservative brand irrevocably. She said: “A year ago, those politicians were measuring up the curtains for No 10. Now, some of them are measuring up the curtains for their prison cells. “The circus goes on and on, and it will never stop because this is who Reform politicians are. So, to those who say ‘unite the right’, we are not uniting with that.

events.title: The release of Sarah J. Maas' 6th 'ACOTAR' book is just weeks away. Here's everything we know.
events.summary: Sarah J. Maas is publishing the sixth "A Court of Thorns and Roses" book. Alexandra Genova / SAINT LUCY Represents Sarah J. Maas is returning to the "ACOTAR" world with two new books. The sixth book will be released on October 27, 2026, and the seventh on January 12, 2027. Teasers shared ahead of its release confirmed two characters who will return in book six. Sarah J. Maas fans, gather round. We finally know what's coming in the "A Court of Thorns and Roses" series (sort of). On August 17, 2026, Maas announced the titles of the sixth and seventh "ACOTAR" books, along with initial descriptions of the novels. Book six is called "A Court of Splintered Harmony" and will be released on October 27, 2026, and book seven is "A Court of Forgotten Melody," hitting shelves on January 12, 2027. Maas first announced she would publish the sixth and seventh installments of her series in March 2026, remaining tight-lipped about them until the title announcement in August. The books are eagerly awaited not only by fans but also by Maas' publisher, Bloomsbury. The company's sales fell 10% for the 2025-2026 fiscal year because Maas didn't release a new book, Publishers Weekly reported . And in recent weeks, Bloomsbury has been sharing quotes from "A Court of Splintered Harmony" on social media, building hype for the novel and teasing what's to come. Here's everything we know about "ACOTAR" six so far. Warning: Some spoilers for Maas' work — including "ACOTAR" and "Crescent City" — ahead. Maas is releasing the sixth 'A Court of Thorns and Roses' story in multiple volumes In March 2023, Bloomsbury announced that Maas had signed a deal for three more books with the publisher. At the time, she was already under contract for four titles, including "House of Flame and Shadow," the third installment in her "Crescent City" series , published in January 2024. Readers didn't find out what the next book she would write would be until her March 2026 appearance on the "Call Her Daddy" podcast with Alex Cooper. She told Cooper she finished the sixth "ACOTAR" book while writing in Montana over the summer of 2025, but she didn't share details about it because of its nontraditional release structure. "This book's coming out October 27, and then on January 12, like two months later, I can't do math, whatever that is, the next ACOTAR book will be coming out," Maas said. "So there will be two books within, like, a very short span." Sarah J. Maas for "Call Her Daddy." Call Her Daddy As her fans will know, Maas' books are typically split into parts, separating different sections of the story she is telling. However, when it comes to the sixth "ACOTAR" story, Maas said the individual parts became longer than she anticipated as she started writing, with part one coming in at 400 pages at one point. As she continued writing, Maas decided the parts didn't have to be in a single physical book. "What if this book was really long?" she said. "What if it took me more than a thousand pages to tell the story that needed to be told, the arc that I wanted to create from start to finish?" Maas said the story for "ACOTAR" six was ultimately divided into four parts, though it is still one cohesive story. Part one is the novel Bloomsbury will publish  on October 27, 2026, and parts two and three will be published together on January 12, 2027. Maas has yet to write or give a publication date for part four, but she told Cooper all three volumes would be published "in a very short time." "It's meant to be read, ideally, as one massive, massive story as opposed to in a trilogy," she said. "It's not a trilogy. Like, arcs aren't wrapped up." Maas finally shared some details about the books in August 2026 On August 16, Maas cleared her Instagram of all its posts, changing her profile photo to a black-and-white illustration of a monster and a spider. Then, on August 17, she shared the covers and titles of books six, "A Court of Splintered Harmony," and seven, "A Court of Forgotten Melody," on her wiped Instagram. The "Splintered Harmony" cover features a pink-and-orange backdrop with a sketched drawing of a monster with teeth and bones, and the subtitle is "The Valkyrie Cycle: Movement I." The Valkyrie were introduced to "ACOTAR" in "A Court of Silver Flames," when Nesta Archeron brought the legendary all-female fighting squad back to life alongside her friends Gwyn and Emerie. "A Court of Splintered Harmony." Bloomsbury Maas posted the book alongside the tagline, "What was broken will be remade." The blurb shared on booksellers' websites reveals that the Night Court is facing new threats when book six opens: Koschei the Deathless, one of three legendary monster siblings introduced throughout "ACOTAR," and those willing to ally with him to claim the newly freed human lands. The description also notes that there is tension among the members of the Night Court because of "recent betrayals and revealed truths," which they must work through if they want to defeat Koschei. "A Court of Splintered Harmony" will be 352 pages and will include three bonus chapters from the "ACOTAR" series. Those bonus chapters were previously published in specific editions of Maas' novels, but they will be in all copies of "ACOSH," as the publisher shared on its social media on September 24. One chapter focuses on Feyre and Rhysand, one on Cassian and Nesta, and one on Azriel's experience on the Winter Solstice that takes place in "A Court of Silver Flames." Teasers from the new book In mid-September, Bloomsbury began sharing quotes from "A Court of Splintered Harmony," offering more insight into the novel than the vague blurbs. The first quote Bloomsbury released on September 17 revealed that at least some of the novel will be told from Lucien Vanserra's perspective. "Lucien's heart thundered, throat drying out," the quote read . "Maybe this had been a terrible idea." Lucien has only played a supporting role in the "ACOTAR" books so far, but Maas has been teeing up his expanded role in her books through his unaccepted mating bond with Elain Archeron, Feyre's middle sister, and his connection to Koschei. He serves as an emissary to the human lands for the Night Court in "ACOSF," alongside Jurian and Vassa, a human queen who was sold to Koschei and cursed to turn into a firebird each day. It would be surprising if Vassa — and by extension Lucien — weren't involved in fighting against Koschei in book six. No other quote shared by Bloomsbury so far has made clear which character is telling the story. The passage shared on October 6 mentions Rhysand, whom the narrator calls Rhys — indicating it could be the POV of one of his close companions — giving a "savage smile" before saying, "With pleasure." A quote shared on September 22 referenced "sisters lost to us — ones we pray each day will find a way home to our sides."
