events.title: AWS launches open-source AI agent sandbox to prevent YOLO mode disasters
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Strands Box is the latest open source AI control tool from the cloud giant; like its predecessors, it promises tighter reins on autonomous agents OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties 4 hours ago Attackers hijacked top-level domains, minted fake security certs for Google and other orgs 5 hours ago US states sue popular kitmaker TP-Link over China risks 7 hours ago Poetry is the new AI security threat as PoeLLM malware infects 3K+ servers 9 hours ago FortiBleed still a bleeding nuisance as FBI confirms ongoing attacks 14 hours ago AWS has offered multiple open-source strategies for holding AI agents accountable, and now it’s adding a full-on sandbox to this stack. Dubbed Strands Box , the new solution uses OS-level isolation and some of AWS’ other recent open-source AI control tools to, ostensibly, retain greater control over autonomous AI agents’ behavior. “Agents increasingly run in ‘ YOLO mode ,’ approving every action without human review,” the AWS team explained in its announcement. “The usual solution to this problem is a sandbox … but access is only part of what we want to control.” The problem with containers and microVMs typically used to isolate AI agents, as AWS explains it, is that their strong isolation doesn’t come with contextual rule enforcement. In other words, when a containerized or virtualized agent gets hold of a tool, there may be no stopping it from doing whatever it wants - like deleting a production database, or gaining access to the internet and doing dog knows what . That’s where the other open-source tools inside Strands Box come in: It uses the Dogwood Local Engine to give the policy engine in Box temporal awareness, so tool calls can be checked against not only what the agent wants to do, but what it’s already done. As one example, AWS noted that an agent could be allowed to post status updates to Slack, but no more than three times every ten minutes to prevent it from spamming its human operators. An AWS spokesperson further explained that Box could be used to control when an agent can perform a Git push, or it could be used to put a cap on API calls that could end up costing a small fortune. Additionally, Strands Box includes Strands Shell and Monty for Python, which expose shell and Python operations to the same Dogwood policy engine and event history, making agentic actions clearer to developers and allowing policies to account for what an agent is trying to do. AWS VP and distinguished engineer Marc Brooker , one of the folks behind Dogwood and Strands Box, explained to The Register that the interpreters are a key part of making agentic behavior more intelligible, which allows for devs to write more precise policies to prevent agents from taking bad actions. “Box’s Shell and Python interpreters expose operations such as file deletions, while its gateways expose API requests and tool calls,” Brooker told us in an email. “Policies can then account for the action being attempted and earlier activity.” Box, Brooker added, enforces those rules without trusting or relying on agents to actually follow instructions, which should ideally prevent them from running roughshod over their operators’ wishes. As for the reason behind AWS’ push to develop open-source tools like Dogwood, the Dogwood Local Engine, and Strands Box, Brooker said that AWS wants to find the right balance between boundaries and policies that prevent agentic AI disasters of the kind we regularly report. “Box enforces the policies developers configure, deterministically, and the agent can't talk its way around these rules,” Brooker explained, though he added that, even with properly configured permissions, an agentic action can still produce an unwanted result. “Developers remain responsible for deciding what access to grant and where human review is needed,” Brooker added - in other words, don’t let your YOLO mode go too YOLO. A bit of human oversight is still necessary.

events.title: Americans don't want taxpayer dollars funding campaign ads: poll
events.summary: Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Nearly nine in 10 voters say using taxpayer money to pay for election-related ads featuring the president or Cabinet members is inappropriate, including 80% of Republicans, according to a recent Reuters-Ipsos poll . Why it matters: The administration's decision to spend millions of taxpayer dollars on Trump-fronted ads weeks before the midterms is facing an uproar and overwhelming public opposition. While the administration insisted the ads were actually PSAs, Trump later announced that a super PAC affiliated with him would foot the bill for future ads (but not reimburse the taxpayer dollars already spent). Friction point: New polling suggests the TV spots, which the White House said "are a reminder for Americans to love their country," might not get much love from voters. The poll of 4,506 adults found that just 9% of Americans find it appropriate to tap taxpayer funds for election-related television ads featuring the president or cabinet members. Zoom out: A majority of Americans also panned other actions Trump has taken: 68% say it's inappropriate to block media outlets from entering the White House, and 72% say the same about naming federal institutions and buildings after a sitting president. Data: Reuters/Ipsos ; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Zoom in: A White House official contended in a statement to Axios that the "PSAs are clearly not political," saying Trump "is not on the ballot and the ads don't have a call to action." But one is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad, using the same footage and narration, with the campaign sponsorship tagline replaced with a disclaimer: "Paid for by the U.S. Government." Earlier this month, Democrats called on the Government Accountability Office and the U.S. Office of Special Counsel to investigate the use of taxpayer money to produce and air the ads. Between the lines: Axios' Alex Isenstadt scooped late last month that the ads released so far were "just the beginning" and that Trump himself — pleased with the war-room-style social media posts his digital team regularly pumps out — was hand-picking the ads himself. And it's not just the White House that's gotten in on promotional hype that blurs the lines with campaign content: The FBI's rapid response account released a video Tuesday applauding director Kash Patel — and criticizing Democrats, including Senate candidate Abdul-El Sayed. The bottom line: As an election approaches where cost-of-living concerns are paramount, Americans have strong feelings about how their taxpayer dollars are spent. events.title: Greenairy is building smart plant towers to clean the air in your office
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. How clean is the air in your workplace? That’s the question Tanvi Thombre and Lakshya Saraf began investigating when they were engineering students who worked in their university makerspace. In fact, Thombre said via email that, while working in the space, they were “unknowingly exposed to toxic fumes from laser cutters, 3D printers, and soldering irons,” but they didn’t realize it until Thombre’s best friend fainted and had to go to the hospital. After that, Thombre said, “We began investigating indoor air pollution and realized it was an invisible but dangerous health risk — especially in schools, offices, hotels, salons, and any commercial buildings where air-conditioning prevents windows from being opened.” Those issues persist even when a building is equipped with air purifiers, as their makerspace was. The problem, according to Saraf, is that although purifiers are good at cleaning out particulate matter like dust and pollen, they are less effective at removing toxic gases such as carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, and benzine (many of which are classified as volatile organic compounds, or VOCs — chemicals that evaporate easily into the air). Thombre said that VOCs are linked to chronic disease and “ sick building syndrome ,” a condition in which occupants experience health effects and discomfort after spending time in a building, even though no specific cause or illness has been identified. She also pointed to Harvard research showing that improving indoor air quality improved cognitive function and productivity as well. That’s why the pair is targeting toxic gases in the workplace with their startup Greenairy , which will be part of Startup Battlefield 200 at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt . Greenairy’s approach centers on building plant towers that are supposed to draw in air, break down toxic gases, and then release the purified air. As Saraf put it, “A plant in a pot cleans air slowly. But, when we change the conditions around the plant, it cleans air much faster and better than these conventional methods.” Saraf also said that while some air purifier filters can remove “a narrow range of VOCs,” those filters need to be changed frequently to be effective. In contrast, plants are “a natural solution, no harmful by-products are formed, and no filter replacement is required.” Greenairy has already conducted short-term pilots at locations around Singapore. Saraf said that in the startup’s own testing using RESET-certified air monitors, it compared three offices: one with Greenairy plant towers, one that had a medical-grade ionizer (a device that uses an electrical charge to make dust and other particles clump together and fall out of the air), and a third with a HEPA air purifier that traps very small particles. “Our tower had the lowest VOC levels and removed VOCs the fastest,” she said. “The office staff also grew fond of the natural ‘fresh’ aroma of the tower and the natural vibe it brought.” Thombre added that they saw an “immediate” improvement within regular office hours, with a 50% reduction in both the daily VOC average and peak levels. She said the results improved even more “as the plants and microbes mature and the gases are prevented from accumulating.” Greenairy has also had its results validated by the German testing and certification firm TÜV SÜD and will be publishing them soon. (Results are available upon request in the meantime.) The pair plans to begin large-scale manufacturing after the results are certified. The startup’s founders are currently based on opposite sides of the world, with Saraf in Berkeley, California, and Thombre in Singapore. It’s an arrangement that Saraf said “works well at this stage,” allowing one founder to focus on testing in Singapore while the other can fundraise in the Bay Area. “If things go to plan, both of us will be in Singapore by the first half of 2027,” she added. “That’s when we expect to launch our first mass-produced towers and install them for our first customers” in Singapore. Join us October 13-15 at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco to learn more about the company and the dozens of other teams pitching to VCs at Disrupt. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. He lives in New York City. You can contact or verify outreach from Anthony by emailing anthony.ha@techcrunch.com . Get 50% off a second pass The Disrupt experience is meant to be shared. events.title: US states sue popular kitmaker TP-Link over China risks
events.summary: The attorneys general of Florida, Iowa, Montana, and Nebraska have sued ubiquitous networking and smart home tech maker TP-Link, alleging its security claims were misleading and it hadn't properly disclosed ties to China. The company has a large presence in US retail and the tech channel, especially in consumer routers, with stats from Circana asserting it had around 36.6 percent US market share by units and 31 percent by dollars in 2024. The complaint [PDF] accuses California-based TP-Link Systems, whose brand originated in Shenzhen, of deceptive and unfair marketing practices concerning its routers' security and its connections to China. It cites exploitation of TP-Link devices by Chinese and Russian state-backed hackers. The suit also claims TP-Link allegedly concealed facts about its "past and ongoing ties to the People's Republic of China," accuses it of having a supply chain that's reliant on PRC players, repeated firmware vulnerabilities, and being subject to Chinese laws that force companies to cooperate with state intelligence. According to the states' attorneys general, the hardware vendor still relies on Chinese companies for research and development and manufacturing operations, despite previously claiming to have moved into Vietnam after severing ties with China. The complaint alleges that only 0.5 percent of components used at TP-Link's Vietnamese plant, measured by value, are bought in Vietnam, with "all other inputs" imported "from or through China." The complaint also claims that a US-designated Chinese military company carried out construction work at the Vietnamese factory, challenging TP-Link's assurances about its supply chain's security. The complaint cites 2025 testimony [PDF] from former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce that TP-Link's share of the US retail market for Wi-Fi systems and small-office/home-office (SoHo) routers at at least 60 percent. Lawyers pointed to various snippets from TP-Link's marketing materials. These included claims that its HomeShield product "covers all security scenarios" and, on a version of its website available in November 2025, provides a "100 percent safeguard" for network security. The complaint argues that TP-Link's security assurances were misleading because its routers contained critical vulnerabilities. It further cites Joyce's that TP-Link routers were among the brands exploited in the China-linked Volt Typhoon and Flax Typhoon campaigns. The complaint also alleges that TP-Link's privacy policies permit it to collect customer data and share it with affiliates without disclosing how its Chinese connections and China's intelligence laws could expose that information to Chinese intelligence agencies. "Iowans' sensitive data and our national security is at risk because of TP-Link and their connection to the communist Chinese government," said Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird. "TP-Link tells Iowans its routers are safe, our personal data is secure, and that they have no ties to China. They are not telling the truth. It's time to hold China and China-backed companies accountable." "TP-Link's false statements and deceptive advertising are a violation of Montana law," said Attorney General Austin Knudsen. "As a result of their nefarious practices, millions of Americans have unknowingly invited a foreign adversary into their living rooms and put their personal information at risk. "I will do everything I can as Attorney General to hold TP-Link accountable and protect our privacy and security." Steve Kovsky, corporate affairs officer for TP-Link Systems Inc., said the lawsuits were based on false premises, did nothing to advance national security, and unfairly penalized a US company. Kovsky added that the company has spent months providing officials with clear documentation showing that it is not owned or controlled by any foreign government and that its devices sold in the US are manufactured in Vietnam. "Any claims that our products present a threat to user security or grant unauthorized network access to foreign governments are baseless," he said. "TP-Link Systems is a US company that complies with US privacy and data protection laws. We perform comprehensive security testing and rely on trusted third-party security labs for additional scrutiny to ensure our products meet the highest security standards and are recognized as among the most secure on the market. "We meet or exceed all industry best practices for monitoring and preventing vulnerabilities and actively support our customers to mitigate any issues that occur as they are identified. We do not, and will not, share customer network data with foreign governments or unauthorized third parties. "We stand fully behind the security of our products, the integrity of our company and our people, and our commitment to serving the best interests of our customers in the United States and globally. We look forward to refuting these baseless allegations in court." The allegations echo those made by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose office sued TP-Link earlier this year over its Chinese connections and router security. US officials began weighing restrictions on TP-Link router sales in 2024. In March 2026, the FCC imposed broader restrictions [PDF] on new foreign-produced router models, barring new equipment authorizations unless an exemption is granted. Previously authorized models were not automatically banned. ®

events.title: 10 things we want to see in season one of HBO's 'Harry Potter' show
events.summary: The new "Harry Potter" trio: Arabella Stanton, Dominic McLaughlin, and Alastair Stout. Warner Bros. Pictures The "Harry Potter" TV adaptation will premiere on HBO this Christmas. It will cover the first book, " Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone " — or the Philosopher's Stone. There were a few cuts from the book in the film adaptation that we want to see in the TV series. It seems that every other week, we're getting a new cast announcement for the "Harry Potter" TV series that's hitting HBO — most recently, Kit Harington was announced as Gilderoy Lockhart in season two. But we're getting ahead of ourselves. Season one of the show, which is set to drop on December 25, will cover the events of JK Rowling's first wizarding book, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone," which was first published in 1997. If you live outside the US, you'll know it as "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone," which HBO is going with this time around. Since HBO's CEO Casey Bloys promised that each season will "dive deep into each of the iconic books," Potterheads expect the TV series to include details that had to be cut from the films for time constraints. Here are the 10 biggest things we want to see included in season one of "Harry Potter." The first chapter from Vernon's POV Vernon Dursley. Warner Bros. Pictures The first chapter of " Harry Potter " begins not from Harry's perspective, but from his obnoxious Uncle Vernon's. The first chapter follows a typical day in the life of Vernon — except this day isn't typical at all, as it's the day that Lord Voldemort was defeated by his baby nephew, Harry Potter, though he doesn't know it yet. This first chapter sets the tone for the book series, as it explains how the wizarding world (sort of) blends in with the Muggle world, establishes how bigoted the Dursleys are toward their magical relatives, and shows just how famous Harry is in the wizarding world. In comparison, the movie begins with Professor Dumbledore and Professor McGonagall rolling up to the Dursleys' house and dropping Harry off. Speaking of that scene … More of Harry's life pre-Hogwarts Harry Potter and his letters. Warner Bros. Pictures A not-insignificant chunk of the " Sorcerer's Stone " book is spent explaining what Harry's day-to-day life in the Muggle world is like, including the unexplainable things that happen to Harry, like his hair growing out after a particularly bad haircut or how he somehow jumps up onto the ceiling of his school to avoid bullies. Also, hilariously, when Harry starts receiving letters addressed to the Cupboard Under the Stairs, the Dursleys, fearing that someone is aware of their abuse, let Harry move into the second bedroom, which had once been occupied by Dudley's toys. There's also supposed to be a very awkward month between Hagrid's first meeting with Harry and taking him to Diagon Alley, and then the Dursleys dropping him off at King's Cross , which would add some comedy to the proceedings. A little Sirius Black foreshadowing Gary Oldman played Sirius Black in the films. Warner Bros. Pictures In the film (and the book), Harry gets dropped off by Hagrid, the kind half-giant groundskeeper at Hogwarts, who scoops him up from his parents' house and brings him to the Dursleys via a giant, flying motorcycle. In the movie, Dumbledore asks if there's been any trouble, and Hagrid just replies that Harry fell asleep over Bristol. However, in the book, Hagrid mentions that he borrowed the bike from "young Sirius Black." This is a small detail, but one that will pay off in two seasons from now, since, of course, Sirius is Harry's godfather, which we don't learn until " Prisoner of Azkaban ." Seeding Sirius' name early on in the TV show is a fun Easter egg for devotees and a little thing to chew on for newbies. Harry and Draco's first meeting Draco, played by Tom Felton, and Harry, played by Radcliffe. Lox Pratt will play Draco in the show. Warner Bros. Pictures In the movie, Harry meets Draco for the first time at Hogwarts, right before the sorting ceremony, and he coolly tells Draco he can tell who the "wrong sort" of people are for himself, after Draco tries to befriend the famous Harry Potter. In the book, this takes place in Diagon Alley, when the two are shopping for robes. They have a brief conversation, during which neither introduces themselves, but Draco insults Hagrid. They meet once more on the Hogwarts Express, which is when Draco learns who the boy he spoke to at Madam Malkin's was — and they have the same "wrong sort of people" conversation. Harry's first meeting with Draco is important for a few reasons. One: It makes the reader and Harry nervous that everyone at Hogwarts is a major snob, so it's a huge relief when Harry meets Ron. Two: It's effective exposition, showing us that there are hierarchies within the wizarding world based on blood status. Three: It helps Harry and the reader understand just how much Harry doesn't know about this world he's entering — crucially, this is when he learns about Quidditch. More of the friendships between Harry and his classmates Harry (Radcliffe) and Seamus Finnegan, played by Devon Murray. In the show, Leo Earley will play him. Warner Bros. Pictures Since the movies are pressed for time with all the plot they have to get through, the friendships Harry forms outside Ron and Hermione take a back seat. But in the books, Harry is relatively popular — at least, in the first book. He's good friends with the other Gryffindor boys, Seamus Finnegan and Dean Thomas, and is protective of Neville Longbottom. He also has strong bonds with the Gryffindor Quidditch team. We hope that the TV show is able to expand upon the other students at Hogwarts outside the core trio. Peeves Peter Serafinowicz is set to play Peeves. Danny North/Comic Relief/Getty Images This might be a little bit of a cheat, since Peeves has already been cast (Peter Serafinowicz will play him in the series), but the omission of Peeves from the entire film series, not just the first movie, is probably one of "Potter" fans' most disliked choices. This devious poltergeist takes pride in messing with students, professors, and ghosts alike, but when it comes time to protect the residents of Hogwarts from truly evil forces, Peeves is up to the task. Also, as the series gets darker, it's always nice to have some comic relief from Peeves. All the Norbert drama Hagrid, as played by Robbie Coltrane, and Norbert. Nick Frost will play Hagrid in the show. Warner Bros. Pictures Hagrid acquiring a dragon egg, raising Norbert, and then having to give him away, is a memorable, but truncated plot in the film adaptation, and we don't get to see what happens to the dragon — Hagrid tells the gang that Dumbledore arranged for him to be sent to a dragon colony in Romania. events.title: Is my HBO safe? What the Paramount-WBD merger means for the future of CNN, movies, and more.
events.summary: HBO Max and CNN will operate as is for now under David Ellison's Skydance. Illustration by Omar Marques/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images; Noam Galai/Getty Images for Paramount; Bloomberg/Getty Images Skydance's mega-merger is complete, giving David Ellison control of HBO and the Warner Bros. studio. The combined company also includes Paramount Pictures, Paramount+, Pluto TV, and CBS News. Here's what the Paramount-WBD deal means for HBO Max and CNN. What's going to happen to all my favorite TV shows and movies? Paramount has joined forces with Warner Bros. Discovery , prompting questions about what the mega-deal means for the likes of HBO and CNN. Skydance, David Ellison's new entertainment giant , is now home to HBO, HBO Max, CNN, CBS, Paramount+, Pluto TV, the Warner Bros. studio, Paramount Pictures, and cable networks like TNT and HGTV. That portfolio of assets is poised to make Skydance a powerhouse that could challenge Disney and Netflix in streaming while boasting the premium, historic IP that Google's YouTube doesn't have. Below is a breakdown of what Skydance has said about how it will approach movies, streaming, traditional TV, and news — both publicly and in private meetings with employees. Streaming: An HBO-Paramount super app is coming, eventually Although Ellison has said that HBO Max and Paramount+ will eventually become a unified service, that won't happen immediately. Skydance will build a tech platform that supports both streamers "as quickly as we possibly can," Ellison told employees in a town hall on Wednesday, since he said operating multiple separate streaming stacks is "inefficient and just not the best way you'd want to build it." "That allows you to build better personalization systems, better recommendation systems, allows you to monetize better," Ellison told staffers. It's unclear what this supercharged streamer would be called, or how much it would cost a month. The standard ad-free version of HBO Max costs $18.49 a month compared to $13.99 for Paramount+, while the ad versions are $10.99 and $8.99, respectively. While Skydance builds its streaming super app, it will create a bundle that lets consumers get both services at a discount, similar to how Disney offers its Disney+ and Hulu bundle . Ellison talked about creating a "mutual ingest bundle" that would make HBO Max and Paramount+ content available to bundle customers in both apps, which he said would be a "really, really powerful" offering. "Because the Paramount-WBD deal was financed with a massive amount of debt, it's hard to imagine that streaming price hikes aren't in Skydance's future," said media analyst Mike Proulx of Forrester. Skydance must pay down about $80 billion in debt. Skydance's streaming business will be run by Casey Bloys, the HBO chief, after Paramount streaming head Cindy Holland stepped down . News: CNN and CBS will be separate brands, for now Ellison seems set on keeping CNN running as a separate brand, despite speculation about a merger with Bari Weiss' CBS News . CNN CEO Mark Thompson is staying at the network, and Ellison said at Wednesday's town hall that he won't interfere in news coverage. He said the network will have "complete editorial independence." Ellison told employees Skydance wants to help CNN "scale and transition the business digitally." The news giant already offers a $6.99-per-month subscription for a live TV feed and full access to its site. When asked by CNN's Anderson Cooper at the town hall how CNN and CBS could work together, Ellison said he's still figuring out the details but suggested the two news networks will come together in some way, whether by sharing resources or talent. "You can only be so smart from the outside looking in," Ellison said, adding that "within, usually, 120 days," new leaders should "be able to start to make those decisions." Movies: There will be a steady stream of films in theaters Skydance seems set to keep film output steady. Ellison's company has promised to put 30 movies in theaters in both 2027 and 2028, and 32 films a year in 2029, 2030, and 2031. About two-thirds of those movies must be wide releases, as part of Skydance's settlement with the 12 states suing to stop its deal, and at least four a year must be independent films. Warner Bros. has 15 films on its theatrical schedule this year, as does Paramount Pictures. That's compared to 11 and eight in 2025 for Warner Bros. and Paramount, respectively. Skydance has also promised not to sell the Warner Bros. or Paramount Pictures lots until at least 2032. Ellison said on Tuesday that one lot could host film production, while the other could host TV production. Skydance wants to "cherish and celebrate" its film studios and "keep their identity very strong," co-CEO Ynon Kreiz said at the town hall. TV: It's business as usual for the next few years When settling the lawsuit from the states, Skydance promised to separately negotiate rates for its cable channels and those of WBD through 2031. Otherwise, it could be forced to divest assets like BET. That pledge should help maintain the status quo in the pay-TV world, since the combined company won't be able to gain as much leverage on distributors like Comcast, Charter, or YouTube TV. Without that clause, Skydance could have tried to secure higher rates for Paramount channels like MTV, Comedy Central, and Nickelodeon by threatening to withhold WBD networks like CNN, TruTV, and The Food Network. events.title: She's lost 2 teeth and 25 pounds. Now Nicolás Maduro's wife says she should get out of jail for a heart procedure.
events.summary: Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, in Venezuela before their capture by the US military. Jesus Vargas/Getty Images Nicolás Maduro's wife, Cilia Flores, is experiencing health issues while awaiting trial in jail. The doctors in her Brooklyn jail recommended a diagnostic procedure to address her heart condition. She asked a judge to let her out of jail and allow her to stay in a private home to recover. In a jail in Brooklyn, Cilia Flores — the ousted first lady of Venezuela — has not been feeling well. She has lost two teeth. Her weight has dropped by 25 pounds. Her heart condition has gotten worse, her lawyers say. Now, as she awaits trial on drug-trafficking charges alongside her husband, the toppled Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, attorneys for Flores have asked a federal judge to release her from jail. They want her placed under house arrest, where she can recover from a procedure recommended by the doctors in her Brooklyn jail. Prosecutors haven't disputed that Flores has health issues. But they say that she has refused to take doctor-recommended diagnostic tests unless she is released, meaning she "effectively created a medical hardship that she now relies on to seek release." The 92-year-old jurist overseeing the case against Maduro and Flores, US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, scheduled a hearing for Thursday to decide the matter. If Flores is allowed to leave jail, it could mean that the federal government would no longer have direct oversight over every aspect of her life. Flores' doctors have recommended that she get a cardiac catheterization, a diagnostic procedure in which doctors would thread a tube through blood vessels and into her heart. Flores has been happy with the medical care she has received while incarcerated in New York, according to a person who has spoken with her. But the 69-year-old is afraid of going through the medical procedure and then waking up from anesthesia handcuffed to a bed or surrounded by dozens of other inmates, the person told Business Insider. "She's very afraid of waking up and then getting thrown into some situation that she has very little control over, and something happens," the person said. Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, stand with their attorneys at a court hearing in June. Jane Rosenberg/REUTERS Her lawyers are proposing that she move to a private home — the proposed location isn't disclosed in public court filings — with 24-hour monitoring from armed security teams. The arrangements would be overseen by a firm led by Louis Milione, a former narcoterrorism special operations agent and second-in-command at the Drug Enforcement Administration. The attempt to stay in a private residence while seeking medical treatment and recovery is "an attempt to leverage her wealth to receive special treatment," prosecutors say. Prosecutors noted that judges have rejected similar moves in other high-profile cases, including in criminal cases against Sean "Diddy" Combs, Ghislaine Maxwell, and Jeffrey Epstein. Living with roommates in New York Until her capture on January 3, Flores' life looked very different. As Maduro's wife and former leader of Venezuela's legislature, she was part of the country's ruling elite. Then, US special forces descended on the fortified compound in Caracas where she and Maduro were staying, and seized the couple. They were flown to New York City to face federal charges . The former first couple of Venezuela are now living in a federal jail between a pier and a cemetery in a not-yet-gentrified Brooklyn neighborhood. After arriving at the jail, Flores had her own cell for six weeks, according to the person who spoke with her. Afterward, she was moved to the female general population area, where according to a jail spokesperson, there are now about 35 inmates. There is a barracks-style area where beds are arranged in rows in one big room, as well as another area where they can hang out. "It's not uncomfortable by the standards of prison," said the person who spoke with Flores. Do you have a tip or a question about our reporting? Contact this reporter at jshamsian@businessinsider.com or on the secure messaging app Signal at JacobShamsian.07. Here's our guide to sharing information securely . Male and female inmates are completely separated, and the jail doesn't offer any way for Flores and Maduro to see each other. Fights occasionally break out between inmates, creating additional health risks for Flores, her lawyers have said in court filings. The effort to get Maduro's wife out of jail because of her health issues is one of many side-plots that have emerged from the criminal case against the former first couple. The two won't see a jury anytime soon. Maduro and Flores face a slew of drug-trafficking and gun-running allegations. Their lawyers have only just begun what's expected to be a long series of legal challenges to the Justice Department's criminal charges. In September, their defense attorneys filed motions arguing that the couple should be entitled to sovereign immunity. Maduro remains Venezuela's rightful head of state, and Flores holds official roles as Venezuela's first lady and as a leader of the country's legislature, they said in court filings. Maduro's 60-page brief cites the 2024 US Supreme Court decision that granted Trump broad immunity from criminal prosecution. Whatever conduct American prosecutors had an issue with, the lawyers say, could be considered an "official act" as part of their government roles. Since Maduro's capture, the country of Venezuela has asserted head-of-state immunity for Delcy Rodriguez in American court proceedings, but not for Maduro. And then there is the question of why this case is happening in the United States at all. Maduro's lawyers also say the top charge against him — engaging in a narcoterrorism conspiracy by trafficking drugs to US-designated terrorist groups, including the FARC and the Sinaloa Cartel — involves alleged actions that are beyond the reach of American courts. It likely won't be until next year that Hellerstein will decide those motions. events.title: Boots sold in £7bn deal to Canadian billionaire family
events.summary: Boots, the High Street pharmacy and retail chain, has been sold in an $8.9bn (£6.7bn) deal to Canada's billionaire Weston family. Wittington Investments, the holding company, confirmed it had agreed to buy the 177-year-old retailer on Wednesday from US private equity firm Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family. Boots started as a simple apothecary in Nottingham but has evolved to become a stalwart of the High Street, expanding its business to sell a vast range of health and beauty products, meal deals and travel accessories. The chain has performed well in recent years despite challenges from rivals and changing shopping habits. Its stores have seen lower footfall as people switched to working from home rather than visiting town and city centre offices every weekday. It has closed hundreds of branches across the UK in recent years, leaving it with about 1,800 stores and 51,000 employees, but remains a familiar British brand. In its most recent annual results, Boots generated £7.5bn in sales - a 3.2% increase on 2024. Retail expert Catherine Shuttleworth, chief executive of savvy marketing, said shoppers were unlikely to see much change to stores in the coming months, but added what they can "expect over time is an improved shopping experience as the new owners invest in the business". She said health and beauty was a "massive area for growth", and fresh investment from its new ownership would help. The last two decades has seen several changes of ownership under discussion and sometimes completed. Sycamore only owned the retailer for 18 months, and Shuttleworth said the chopping and changing of owners had been "an unhelpful distraction". Boots gets new US owner in multi-billion dollar deal Published 7 March 2025 The company was established by John Boot, who opened the first herbalist store in Nottingham, offering an affordable alternative to traditional medicines in 1849. It has since expanded over the decades into selling various products, but health products have remained a key part of its business. As well as vaccines, it offers eye and hearing tests, providing much needed health care support in everyday moments as well as at times of national crisis like the coronavirus pandemic. It launched its loyalty scheme in 1997, the Advantage Card, which became hugely popular and a move repeated by various retailers since. Galen Weston, the chairman of Wittington, will become chairman of Boots. He signalled the new owners had fresh plans for the chain, including shop upgrades and an expansion of healthcare services. "We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come," he said. The Weston family will be buying Boots' retail operations in the UK and Ireland, Boots Opticians, No7 Beauty Company and its Thailand and franchised businesses. It is set be completed in early 2027. The Weston family owns the Canadian grocery chain Loblaws, pharmacy business Shoppers Drug Mart, and previously owned the London department store Selfridges from 2003 to 2021, before selling it for $4bn. The separate UK branch of the Weston family is the majority owner of Associated British Foods, the parent firm of Primark. The Westons were ranked fifth on this year's Sunday Times Rich List with a combined fortune of almost £19bn. Wittington will have operational control over Boots, it has secured ownership in partnership with Fairfax Financial Holdings, a Toronto-based holding company. Sycamore Partners, in partnership with Stefano Pessina and his family, will retain ownership of The Boots Group's Farmacias Benavides in Mexico and Alliance Healthcare Deutschland in Germany. events.title: Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense | Heather Stewart
events.summary: Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit makes no economic sense The Tory leader’s proposal to slash the tax would shovel £6bn of taxpayer money to the already-wealthy Kemi Badenoch’s inheritance tax gambit is a Conservative classic. After all, it was George Osborne’s high-profile pledge to “take the family home out of inheritance tax” in 2007 that put Gordon Brown off calling a snap general election. In practice, Osborne’s plan involved a £1m threshold for inheritance tax – and given the global financial crisis had blown a hole in the public finances by the time the Conservative-Lib Dem coalition came to power in 2010, it never came to pass. But the promise was grabby enough to change the political conversation – and contributed to Brown’s fateful decision not to go to the polls early. So politically, Badenoch’s flagship policy may have merit. IHT, as policymakers call it, is notoriously unpopular. Families never likely to be liable nevertheless fret about their kids having to paying it, while a cacophony of highly paid tax advisers offer to help them avoid it. The furious response to Rachel Reeves’s reform of the inheritance tax regime for family businesses and farms, with tractors streaming down Whitehall , underlined how unpopular it is. But whatever its political logic, the Tory plan makes little economic sense. First, it’s worth pausing to underline how very wealthy the beneficiaries of this new policy are likely to be. The latest data from HMRC shows that less than 5% of estates – the wealthiest 5%, that is – were liable for any inheritance tax at all in 2023/24. And under current rules, by combining their tax-free allowances, a married couple can already pass on a property worth up to £1m to their children or grandchildren, without them being liable to pay a penny in inheritance tax. Badenoch’s new, much more generous regime would permit a couple to pass on the entire family home, however valuable, without paying any tax on it at all; and for good measure an additional £1m in other assets. And the more valuable the property, the bigger the gain. Clearly, in a sluggish economy where resources are stretched, there’s a question about whether that is the best use of the £6bn of taxpayers’ money the policy is reckoned to cost – compared with, say, investing in infrastructure where there might be the prospect of a return. Total revenue from IHT is forecast to be about £9bn this year, rising to £15bn by 2030-31 – Badenoch’s plan would wipe out about half of that. Worse than that though, it will create perverse incentives for older homeowners to do exactly what the economy needs them not to do, and hang on in a valuable property, for fear the proceeds of downsizing would be grabbed by HMRC . Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters The Tories claim they’ll also abolish stamp duty, helping to oil the wheels of the property market and encourage downsizing; but for the most valuable homes, the benefits of not paying 40% inheritance tax above the current threshold would be likely to more than overwhelm the boon of a tax-free move. And that would be likely to mean far fewer family-size homes coming on to the market in the places up-and-coming buyers most need them to be available. As Arun Advani, of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation at the University of Warwick, points out, the biggest beneficiaries would be in areas where housing is expensive. He says: “‘Where housing is expensive’ mostly means ‘where lots of people want to live’, usually because there are good jobs. Reducing housing sales here will make it harder for young working families trying to upsize. By staying put, they will in turn make it harder for school leavers and university/college graduates to move to the area for work. This is bad for growth,” he said. Indeed, he points out there would even be an incentive for those who can afford it to “upsize” – moving to a larger house, which would then effectively shelter the asset from inheritance tax. If Badenoch and her party want to shovel an additional £6bn of taxpayers’ money to the already-wealthy in the hope of winning back votes in the stockbroker belt, so be it – but she should not be able to claim the policy would be anything but bad for economic growth.

events.title: AI video startup Higgsfield launches tool to build custom AI influencers
events.summary: There’s a new kind of AI influencer flooding social media feeds — and they’re not even pretending to look like real people. Higgsfield — which recently announced it hit a $1 billion run rate , and which boasts 30 million users — has updated its AI influencer tool, making it easier for users to insert a character of their own creation into existing videos. The characters are peculiar: They look realistic, but not quite of this world. Many have geometric haircuts, elongated necks, or other extreme bodily proportions that make clear they’re artificial. That’s by design. “A flawless face is the fastest way for a character to read as generic AI,” a Higgsfield spokesperson told Semafor. This odd aesthetic plays to AI’s strengths: Creating uncanny characters is a better use of the technology than trying to pass as human. It’s a more transparent way to create content that doesn’t deceive the audience the way deepfakes can. Some of these AI-generated influencers have racked up millions of views and thousands of followers across platforms (some users are already using them to promote memecoins). — Jake Angelo

events.title: No child should have to learn in a cold classroom - children's commissioner
events.summary: Chris Quinn has criticised the suggestion that children should have to wear more clothes No child should be expected to learn in a cold classroom because of budget pressures, according to Northern Ireland's commissioner for children. Chris Quinn was speaking after it emerged that staff and pupils at schools across Northern Ireland have been told to "wear more clothes" to cut heating bills. Schools have been told by the Education Authority (EA) that increasing costs will affect school energy bills and to reduce heating and lighting "wherever possible". Quinn said: "Children should not be left to pick up the pieces of a problem that they did not create". The EA has said that school gas and electricity bills are set to rise by about £8m by March 2027. But principals have told BBC News NI it is not straightforward to cut heating costs, with one describing her school's energy bills as "ferocious". Rising energy costs are already affecting households across Northern Ireland. The impact of the US-Israel war with Iran is one of the factors behind the increase. The letter from the EA to head teachers said that "recent geopolitical events are expected to have a substantial impact on energy costs... during the 2026/27 financial year". It said that total school gas bills were expected to go up by 60% from £10.7m to £17m by March 2027. Meanwhile, total school electricity bills are expected to rise from £23.8m to £25.1m in the same time period. "Given the scale of the anticipated cost increases, we are asking all schools to review their energy usage and identify opportunities to reduce consumption wherever possible," the EA said. Among the measures suggested to schools are cutting heating use by an hour a day and switching off classroom lights to use natural daylight instead. Quinn told BBC Radio Ulster's Evening Extra programme that the department and EA had a "duty to properly fund schools and not to pass this burden onto children". Quinn said he had visited schools where young people were already wearing extra jumpers and teachers were buying heaters to keep pupils warm and in extreme cases, some pupils were using hot water bottles as well. "Learning in a cold classroom will have a detrimental effect on the child's ability to learn but also, their health," he said. He said the burden of savings were being put on the wrong people. "That line about wearing extra clothes, in no other industry, in no other workplace, would you expect that people put on an extra jumper or wear a coat in doors", he said. Kirsty Logan-Hall says her school is in an older building which presents energy efficiency challenges The principal of Tullygally Primary School in Craigavon, Kirsty Logan-Hall, said that the school was "committed to promoting responsible energy consumption and regularly reinforce good practice with staff and pupils". "However, our ability to achieve significant reductions in energy usage is constrained by the nature of our estate," she said. "The school operates from an older building which presents inherent energy efficiency challenges. "In addition, our site is particularly spread out due to the accommodation and operational requirements associated with our specialist provision. "This necessitates the heating, lighting and ongoing use of multiple areas across the site throughout the school day to ensure appropriate learning environments, accessibility and pupil welfare. "It is important to recognise that there is limited scope for reducing energy consumption without adversely impacting the quality of provision, staff working conditions or the wellbeing of pupils, including those with additional needs." Claire Robinson says heating can't just be "turned off" in some parts of the school Meanwhile, the principal of Holy Evangelists Primary School in Dunmurry, Claire Robinson, said that energy costs were "ferocious". "We can't play around with the heating." Parts of the school are relatively new and have underfloor heating. "Our classrooms can't drop below a certain temperature so we have to keep the heating on. "We can't just turn the heating off in some areas of the school." Robinson said that although the school was relatively new it had been given an energy efficiency rating of D due to the costs involved in running the heating system. Brian Guthrie is principal of Ebrington Primary School in Londonderry Brian Guthrie, principal of Ebrington Primary School in Londonderry said asking children to sit in a class wearing extra clothes is "ridiculous". "I'm not going be asking children and staff to put coats and hats on during the winter time. "We will be running the heat as we need it but we do look at all other energy saving costs as we can," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme. Guthrie said his school building is around ten years old and is, at present "very energy efficient". The installation of 100 solar panels last year, he added, should "have paid itself back" over the next five years.

events.title: Burnham, take note: water shareholders have their uses – they can be squeezed for cash | Nils Pratley
events.summary: Burnham, take note: water shareholders have their uses – they can be squeezed for cash Owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its investors for £550m after sewage spills South West Water owner taps investors after sewage spills W ater is “a service where the shareholders never lose and the public never win,” Andy Burnham, the prime minister, told the Labour party conference last week , reflecting the popular feeling towards the industry in England. And, of course, his big-picture point is familiar: the £80bn, or thereabouts, that has been paid in dividends over the past 35 years represented over-the-top rewards for investors in many cases. It is easy to agree the public was taken for a ride. But the idea that shareholders never lose is not correct – and has been out of date for a while. For starters, the current owners of Thames Water have been wiped out. Their shares are worthless whatever the outcome of the interminable talks over whether to put the company into administration or opt for a recapitalisation by the creditors (who will get a sharp haircut on their debt in all circumstances). Meanwhile, the owners of Southern Water have been obliged to shove in cash on dilutive terms. Now comes something similar at Pennon Group. The owner of South West Water, Bristol Water and Bournemouth Water is tapping its shareholders for £550m via a rights issue to fund, in effect, the cost of clearing up past failures. The new-ish Pennon chief executive, Keith Haslett, outlined an extra £1bn of capital investment on top of the existing £2.6bn in the current five-year period. Of the new £1bn, only £400m represents spending on new infrastructure that can be charged to bills (an extra £10 a year for South West customers if Ofwat gives a thumbs up). The other £600m hits shareholders directly and is the catch-up cost of fixing things that should not have gone wrong in the first place. Reading between the lines, Haslett seems shocked by what he found. The rights issue document talked about sustained improvement requiring “a fundamental change in how we plan, deliver and maintain our assets” and how previous efforts have been “held back by the way accountability sits within the organisation and gaps in the capability”. Mr Fixit is not saying it’s an overnight job. All the biggies of water companies’ performance – pollution, leaks and supply interruptions – got a mention as items in need of improvement. The plan is merely to reduce regulatory penalties by 50% in the current period. Haslett’s hope is that, come 2030, Pennon will be closer to earning a few rewards via Ofwat’s incentive mechanism. The point is that none of this will feel like a case of “shareholders never losing” if you’re unfortunate enough to own Pennon’s shares. Anybody who bought at virtually any point in the past five years has lost a packet. The price was £13.30 in July 2021. Now it is 361p, down 20% on Wednesday with the rights issue to a 22-year low. For good measure, the dividend is being cut by 30% on a per-share basis to reflect the new equity issuance. Reality has arrived at Pennon. Burnham might reflect that private investors can have their uses: the capital has to come from somewhere and shareholders can sometimes be forced to swallow some financial medicine. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning One could take the view that those investors deserve something even sourer, such as outright nationalisation. It’s a point of view but, since Burnham has pretty much ruled it out for water as a blanket policy (we wait to see what happens at Thames), the argument feels academic at this point. If Burnham, despite it all, is going to live with a privatised system, he could do everybody a favour at this point by hurrying up and deciding what he means by his “public control” overlay. Keir Starmer’s water bill, based on Sir Jon Cunliffe’s 2025 review of the water sector and including a stronger regulator, would have been published about now. Instead, we’ll get Burnham’s “strengthened” version some time next spring, according to the Westminster whisper. Given that it could take 12 months to become law, that will be four years for the Labour government to reform the water sector. That is shockingly slow. As Pennon’s fundraising demonstrates, even the current rickety system is moving faster.

events.title: The 35 colleges that produced the most US presidents, ranked
events.summary: Barack Obama went to Harvard University, the undergraduate alma mater of five US presidents, for law school. Eduardo Munoz Alvarez/Getty Images/Steve Rosenbach/iStock Some US colleges have alumni who have reached the highest office in the country. The Ivy League, the US Military Academy, and some liberal arts colleges have produced US presidents. Harvard University leads the ranking, with five former presidents among its ambitious alumni. Some US colleges stand out for being highly selective schools , for having some of the highest-earning graduates , or for their surprising sticker prices . But some have bragging rights to a different metric: multiple  former US presidents  among their alumni. The oldest school in the country leads the pack in producing the most commanders in chief. Harvard University has taught five US presidents at the undergraduate level, more than any other school in the country. A number of other schools also helped shape the minds of the 45 men who have served as president throughout the nation's history, including Ivy League institutions , small Christian colleges, and state research universities . However, presidents didn't necessarily graduate from all of the schools on this list. Some future leaders, including William McKinley, John F. Kennedy, and Jimmy Carter, bounced between institutions during their undergraduate years for financial reasons, health difficulties, or changing preferences. But US presidents did study at an undergraduate level at all of these colleges. Many also went on to attend law school and pursue graduate studies , although this list does not include those institutions. Other presidents, including George Washington, never attended college at all. Here's a look at which colleges' undergraduate programs have produced the most US presidents. Fordham University: One president wdstock/Getty Images President: Donald Trump Donald Trump attended this Bronx-based Jesuit school before transferring to the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. According to "The Trumps: Three Generations of Builders and a Presidential Candidate," the president's sister, Maryanne, said that Trump chose to attend the college because "that's where he got in." University of Delaware: One president Joe Biden is the only US president to attend the University of Delaware. MANDEL NGAN/AFP via Getty Images President: Joe Biden During his college years at the University of Delaware in Newark, Joe Biden "was more interested in football, girls and late-night gab sessions than in his studies," The New York Times wrote in a 2008 profile. Biden's school transcript  showed that he earned mostly C's and D's during his first three semesters. Biden quit the football team after receiving a warning from his parents to focus on his grades and after meeting Neilia Hunter, who would become his first wife,  The Daily Pennsylvanian  student newspaper reported. Occidental College: One president Jim Brown/Getty Images President: Barack Obama Before attending Columbia University, Barack Obama studied for two years at Occidental College in Los Angeles. Columbia University: One president peterspiro/Getty Images/iStockphoto President: Barack Obama Obama transferred to Columbia University as a junior. There, he studied political science with a specialty in international relations, as well as English literature. Georgetown University: One president chemistkane/Getty Images/iStockphoto President: Bill Clinton Bill Clinton received scholarships to attend Georgetown University, where he was class president in 1964 and 1965. Eureka College: One president Dirck Halstead/Getty Images President: Ronald Reagan Ronald Reagan attended this nonprofit Christian college, originally founded by abolitionists in 1855. Georgia Southwestern State University: One president John Bazemore / POOL / AFP President: Jimmy Carter Jimmy Carter bounced around before transferring to the US Naval Academy. He began his undergraduate journey at Georgia Southwestern College before transferring to the Georgia Institute of Technology. Georgia Institute of Technology: One president Aneese/Getty Images President: Jimmy Carter After leaving Georgia Southwestern State University, Carter attended this public research university before transferring to the US Naval Academy. United States Naval Academy: One president SeanPavonePhoto/Getty Images/iStockphoto President: Jimmy Carter As a young man, Carter had always dreamed of attending the US Naval Academy. He achieved that goal in 1943. University of Michigan: One president Dirck Halstead/Getty Images President: Gerald Ford Gerald Ford attended the University of Michigan, where he was a star player on the Wolverines football team. Whittier College: One president photojohn830/Shutterstock President: Richard Nixon Richard Nixon attended Whittier College. He had received a grant to attend Harvard, but he remained in his hometown of Whittier, California, in order to help his parents care for his tuberculosis-stricken older brother and run the family grocery store.  Texas State University: One president BackyardProduction/Getty Images President: Lyndon B. Johnson Lyndon B. Johnson enrolled at the Southwest Texas State Normal School, now known as Texas State University. There, he became editor of the student newspaper and honed his debate skills. London School of Economics: One president formerly Her Majesty's Land Registry Building President: John F. Kennedy John F. Kennedy briefly studied at the London School of Economics before being forced to return to the US due to health reasons. Stanford University: One president CravenA/Shutterstock President: Herbert Hoover Herbert Hoover entered Stanford University in 1891, the first year the school admitted any students. He later claimed to be the university's first student, having sneaked into its unfinished dormitories and slept there before anyone else. Amherst College: One president Boston Globe/Boston Globe via Getty Images President: Calvin Coolidge Calvin Coolidge sharpened his debating skills at Amherst College, from which he graduated in 1895. Ohio Central College: One president Nicholas Klein/Getty Images President: Warren Harding Warren Harding attended Ohio Central College, where he founded a student newspaper: The Iberia Spectator. The college, founded by the Free Presbyterian Church, ceased operations by the end of the 19th century. Davidson College: One president marlin goodwin/Shutterstock President: Woodrow Wilson Woodrow Wilson's time at Davidson ended in 1874 after he fell ill. He later moved on to study at Princeton. Allegheny College: One president Jacob Boomsma/Shutterstock President: William McKinley William McKinley attended this Pennsylvania liberal arts school before withdrawing. During his time at the school, he was a member of the Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity. University of Mount Union: One president MohammadMKS/Shutterstock Presid

events.title: I made Ina Garten's easy apple spice cake. It's the perfect dessert for fall.
events.summary: I made Ina Garten's apple spice cake and found the perfect fall dessert. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I made Ina Garten's fresh apple spice cake, her most fall-friendly dessert.  Garten used to make the cake all the time at her Barefoot Contessa store in the Hamptons. The cake features rum-soaked raisins, Granny Smith apples, cinnamon, nutmeg, and pecans.  From her delightfully bright breakfast cake to her "outrageous" brownies , Ina Garten's repertoire is full of delicious desserts . The temperatures have barely dipped this October, but I still wanted to find a sweet treat that embodied autumn. And Garten's fresh apple spice cake sounded like the perfect candidate. Garten demonstrated the cake on an early episode of "Barefoot Contessa," revealing she used to make it at the Hamptons food store that helped launch her cooking career .  "We used to have all kinds of cakes like this out on the bakery counter, and you could come buy a whole cake, but you could also buy a piece," she said. "It's not fancy, just really delicious and earthy, and you always want to come back for more."  Ina Garten's apple spice cake features classic fall flavors. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider To make Garten's apple spice cake, you'll need:  1 ½ pounds of Granny Smith apples, peeled, cored, and ¼-inch diced  3 extra-large eggs, at room temperature  2 ½ cups of all-purpose flour  1 cup of chopped pecans 1 cup of golden raisins  1 cup of granulated sugar  1 cup of dark-brown sugar, lightly packed  ½ cup of dark rum (Garten recommends Mount Gay)  ¾ cup of vegetable oil  2 teaspoons of pure vanilla extract  2 teaspoons of grated orange zest (2 oranges)  2 teaspoons of baking powder  ½ teaspoon of kosher salt  2 teaspoons of ground cinnamon  ½ teaspoon of ground nutmeg  ½ teaspoon of ground ginger  ⅛ teaspoon of ground cloves  Vanilla ice cream for serving  Caramel sauce for serving  Before the baking began, I needed to preheat the oven and prep my pan. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I preheated the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit and greased and floured my 9-inch by 13-inch baking dish.  Garten has a few tricks for getting the best flavor from her ingredients, including the pecans. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten explained in the "Barefoot Contessa" episode that toasting the pecans "crisps them up and brings out the flavor."  "I want everything to taste as good as it can possibly be," she added.  I placed my chopped pecans on a sheet pan and toasted them in the oven. Garten recommends five to 10 minutes to get them lightly toasted, so I took my pecans out after eight minutes. She also has a hack for the rum-soaked raisins. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I combined the rum and raisins in a small bowl, then covered it with plastic wrap and popped it in the microwave for 60 seconds.  Garten says this helps the raisins plump up and absorb the rum.  I also chopped my apples and zested my oranges. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Within a few minutes, my prep was done. It was time to start the batter. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I threw the granulated sugar, dark-brown sugar, eggs, vegetable oil, vanilla, and orange zest into the bowl of my electric mixer fitted with the paddle attachment.  Garten explained during the "Barefoot Contessa" episode that she uses vegetable oil instead of butter because it keeps the cake really moist.  I mixed my wet ingredients for three minutes. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten said the mixer should be set to medium speed for this step. Then I prepped my dry ingredients. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I sifted the flour, baking powder, salt, cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, and cloves into a medium bowl. I slowly added my dry ingredients to the mixer. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider I added my dry ingredients while the mixer was on low until everything was just combined. Then I drained my raisins. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten said there's no need to save the extra liquid. I folded the raisins, pecans, and apples into the mixture before spreading my batter onto the prepared pan. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider "Make sure everything is really well folded in because you want every bite to have raisins, pecans, and apples in it," Garten explained during the episode.  Garten recommends baking the apple spice cake for 35 to 40 minutes. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider It took my cake 45 minutes to fully bake. Then, per Garten's instructions, I set it aside to cool.  I cut my cake into squares and served each slice with vanilla ice cream and drizzles of caramel. It looked — and tasted — like an absolute delight. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten recommends enjoying her fresh apple spice cake with a cup of tea in the afternoon for a snack, or with ice cream and caramel for the "perfect dessert."  I opted for the latter for my first taste of the cake, which was a flurry of fantastic fall flavors. The nearly caramel flavor of the rum-soaked raisins brought some sweetness to the Granny Smith apples, while the pecans added some crunch. The cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, and cloves infused the cake with warm, nutty flavors, while the orange zest added balancing brightness to each bite.  The cake's texture was also deliciously moist, and eating it warm with some ice cream and caramel on top felt like such a treat. Since the flavors aren't overwhelmingly sweet, you can also enjoy the cake for breakfast without the ice cream or caramel, which is what I did the morning after I baked it.  Whether you're hibernating for fall with Nora Ephron flicks or starting your annual "Gilmore Girls" rewatch, Garten's fresh apple spice cake is sure to warm your heart, stomach, and soul. events.title: CIA officer admits to creating fake top secret government program to steal over $190M, including gold bars
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. A now-former officer with the Central Intelligence Agency has pleaded guilty to stealing almost $200 million, including hundreds of gold bars, as part of a fraudulent scheme masquerading as a top secret government program. The U.S. Department of Justice on Tuesday confirmed that David J. Rush, a Virginia resident, admitted to one count of wire fraud linked to running the fabricated operation and defrauding the government while he was a CIA officer. In a statement, prosecutors said that Rush lied about his education and military experience to gain a position at the CIA, and used his access as an employee to set up the top secret and highly compartmentalized program with the intention of using it to funnel U.S. government funds into his possession. During his arrest, law enforcement found more than $46 million worth of gold bars in Rush’s house linked to the long-running fraud scheme, along with cars, watches, and over $2 million in cash. The plea deal means that Rush escapes trial, as much as the U.S. government likely avoids having to explain in open court how Rush evaded vetting scrutiny to join the U.S. intelligence agency, and how actions went undetected for more than a year. Rush was until recently a senior CIA officer who, according to earlier reports , worked for a division of the CIA since 2010 that develops hacking tools and techniques for carrying out espionage. Per court filings , Rush had significant authority over government intelligence programs and spending. Over the course of 2025, Rush used his position to fabricate a so-called special access program, which are surveillance or intelligence-gathering operations so sensitive that only a few people are read into them. Special access programs, or SAPs, require special clearance that not even the most cleared individuals in government are granted access to. According to The Washington Post , Rush constructed the compartmentalized program under the guise of a fake “continuity of government” plan, aimed at keeping the government functioning in the event of a war, natural disaster, or some other destructive catastrophe. As part of the scheme, Rush used the program and fake government contract to trick an unnamed defense contractor into buying large amounts of gold that Rush then pocketed. According to The Post, the case astounded officials as Rush’s duties at the CIA involved work with one of the government’s “most sensitive intelligence-gathering programs,” with details so sensitive that only a few senior U.S. intelligence officials and lawmakers know of its existence. The Post withheld details of that program from publication as its disclosure could “jeopardize ongoing intelligence-gathering operations.” Court filings said that by virtue of his position, Rush “effectively acted as his own approving official, enabling him to expend substantial amounts of United States government money without meaningful scrutiny.” Rush is scheduled to be sentenced in late January 2027 and faces up to 20 years in prison. events.title: Changing Your Career Isn’t Easy
events.summary: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum ’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written i n partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free! When I changed careers at 30 to become a software engineer, I expected it to be hard. I expected to struggle to fit in, and I expected to bomb a lot of interviews (I did). What I didn’t expect was how few people would support me. As a parent, I get it now. A career change is a risk, and the people who care about you tend to project their fears onto you. They don’t want to watch you struggle or fail, so they discourage you or just don’t offer much enthusiasm. Right now is a strange time to be in engineering, or knowledge work in general. Plenty of us are excited about what AI means for our jobs. More of us are nervous, and I think that fear is justified. Employment for entry-level software developers has fallen nearly 20 percent since late 2022, according to Stanford’s 2026 AI Index , and it can feel like the knowledge we spent our careers building is being commoditized. Lately I’ve seen a flood of social media content telling software developers to go into the trades. YouTubers are telling you to become a plumber or a goat herder. But before you do that, I want to warn you, there is no EASY path. Even if you want to become a goat herder. I’ve changed careers once so far, but my business has forced me through several pivots that felt a lot like career changes—new audiences, new skills, new identity. Here’s what I’d tell anyone considering a change, whether you’re moving into engineering, leaving it, or finding a new speciality. Find someone who’s done it and ask how This is exactly what I told my oldest son, who’s getting ready to enter the job market full-time. Outside of the primary social media feeds, the internet is full of free and paid communities on Facebook, LinkedIn, and other sites. Reddit works, too, if you can stomach the trolls, because there’s valuable information buried in there. Many of these spaces are flooded with people trying to break in, so look for the ones full of people who already do the work and talk openly about what is and isn’t going well. Then find one or two people in your own circle who’ve done it and ask what the job takes. You’ll often find the degree matters less than you assumed. Indeed Hiring Lab found the share of U.S. postings requiring a bachelor’s degree fell from 20.4 percent in 2019 to 17.8 percent in early 2024, and more than half listed no education requirement at all. Build proof of work, even if it’s unpaid Yes, you’ll probably need to do some work for free, or at least far cheaper than you’re used to. I’ve had to do this in my business over and over. Nobody cares that I’ve been a software engineer for 12 years. They want to know whether I can do the thing they need. When I started pitching businesses, I offered to build something for free as a case study, then used it to land clients who paid well. You can copy this in most fields. Say you want to get into marketing: Learn how Facebook ads work, find a friend or small business that needs help, and run the campaigns at a low price. Now you’ve picked up the jargon, and you have something concrete to show a hiring manager. Stability is a myth It may be corny, but change is the only constant. If you’re a software engineer, you could argue you’re in the middle of a career change already, whether you opted in or not. Programmers in the 1990s had the same experience when the web showed up and they had to quickly learn new tools just to stay relevant. If you’re looking for stability, you’re in the wrong place, and I think it will get scarcer as AI and other forces reshape work. The best move is to build a strong foundation so you can adapt when the ground shifts. I wrote about the foundational skills to focus on if you’re interested. —Brian Barbara Mazzolai Wants to Build a New Field of Robotics Roboticist Barbara Mazzolai is a prime example of someone who advanced her career by switching fields—and now, she’s helping to create a new one. events.title: The West’s open-source AI race kicks into high gear
events.summary: J.D.’s view The race in the West to become the top open-source AI model shifted into higher gear this week, as both Nvidia-backed Reflection AI and French lab Mistral unveiled new models they hope will break China’s open-source monopoly. The challenge looming over Beam and Le Chonk ’s debuts (immediately my new favorite model name) is that they lag the top Chinese models and the leading closed systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on prominent benchmarks. But Reflection and Mistral boasted in their announcements that they do beat other open Western models, such as those from Thinking Machines and Nvidia, suggesting the companies care just as much about the race against each other as the one with Beijing — despite US and European companies’ shifts to using more Chinese models over the past year. Reflection CEO Misha Laskin told me his goal isn’t necessarily to dismantle the foothold Chinese models have achieved among developers and large companies. Instead, he sees a market in entities that can’t or won’t use Chinese models — think heavily regulated industries and governments — and might otherwise have no choice but to pay for closed American AI. The timing of that pitch is opportune: Many businesses are heading into year-end budget reviews with eye-popping AI spend figures to account for. Governments are also bracing for sticker shock as $1-a-year pilot deals expire. New data from Ramp suggests companies are switching which AI providers they use more than ever. The question that will determine the fate of these and other Western open-source players is whether businesses and agencies will tolerate less advanced models for some tasks in exchange for affordability and control. Notable Businesses are finding it hard to budget for AI because the number of tokens a task will consume is hard to predict, The Wall Street Journal reported.
