events.title: Democrat rolls out AI liability proposal
events.summary: A leading House Democrat is rolling out draft legislation to clarify liability for AI developers when their agents cause harm in direct response to the rogue AI hack of Hugging Face earlier this year. According to an announcement shared first with Semafor, Massachusetts Rep. Lori Trahan’s “CLAIM Act” would make it easier for third parties to sue AI developers while clarifying questions around intent related to AI agents’ conduct. “When someone breaks the law and hurts you, you can take them to court. That shouldn’t change just because the wrongdoer is an AI agent,” Trahan said. Trahan, who previously joined Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., in a bipartisan push to draft AI regulations, is framing the liability push as a way to incentivize AI developers to embrace safety. The legislation would also set a federal floor, rather than preempt state laws.

events.title: Progressive groups lay out AI demands for candidates
events.summary: The Scoop A coalition of nearly 40 labor, progressive, faith, and AI safety groups is laying out demands for AI legislation in Congress, warning lawmakers that any bill that crosses their red lines will face “active, mobilized opposition,” according to a letter shared first with Semafor. The letter is spearheaded by Guardrails Action, the nonprofit affiliated with Guardrails Alliance, the super PAC launched in June as a counterweight to pro-AI election groups. The group is calling for “independent, transparent government oversight with real enforcement power” and “a mandate that addresses human impacts from safety to economic disruption.” They also want to ensure that “AI models are not making final decisions such as denying people health care or benefits, firing or disciplining workers, or deploying weapons,” and that AI is a “universal benefit” to society. In 2028, Guardrails will be organizing a coalition around a “populist demand for AI-related policy” but for now, the principles will serve as a floor for what the group and its broader coalition want to see in AI legislation, said Maya Handa, a senior adviser at Guardrails and former adviser and campaigner for democratic socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “We want members of Congress and 2028 candidates to know that it’s not enough to come to the table with half measures, and they need to be ambitious,” Handa said. Know More Handa likened the push for AI regulation to progressive calls for Democrats to support Medicare for All and the Green New Deal. “We want them to be forced to weigh in on what the New Deal for AI looks like in this transformative moment. And what they should say is: that they are not beholden to billionaires,” she said. Other key groups that signed onto Guardrails’ letter include the American Federation of Teachers, the P Street Project, progressive and civil society groups, and the new group Who Decides run by Alex Bores, the former New York congressional candidate who faced a deluge of attack ads from pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future. The group is not specifically endorsing or looking to knock down any specific bills in Congress yet, Handa said. The associated PAC Guardrails Alliance announced today an ad spend of $1.2 million opposing candidates backed by the Leading the Future in California, Montana, and Arizona.

events.title: Guyana: The tiny country with big ambitions fast emerging as a global oil producer
events.summary: A tiny South American country is emerging as a reliable oil supplier globally as flows from the Middle East face disruptions and European nations seek alternatives to Russia. Guyana's rapid increase in crude production, from zero in 2019 to about 900,000 barrels per day in the first half of the year, is catapulting the country to one of the world's fastest-growing economies, lifting thousands of people out of poverty with newfound wealth. The non-Opec country's oil output is expected to reach 1 million barrels per day (bpd) imminently, with the country targeting 1.7 million bpd by 2030. “With disruptions in the Middle East, Guyana’s oil is becoming strategically more important to global markets,” Stephanie Rivera, research analyst at S&P Global Energy told The National. “Guyana’s light-to-medium, low-sulfur crude is not exposed to Middle Eastern shipping chokepoints, providing refiners with an attractive option for diversifying away from Middle Eastern supply. As the conflict in the Middle East continues, Guyanese crude can help enhance energy security in an increasingly tight market.” The Middle East conflict, which broke out on February 28 after the US and Israel attacked Iran, has roiled global markets, with prices jumping to an intraday high of about $120 per barrel in April. Tehran carried out retaliatory strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure leading to curtailment of production, with 10 million bpd of Gulf output remaining shut as of August amid heightened security risks, according to the International Energy Agency report last month. The Strait of Hormuz, through which more than 20 per cent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies used to pass before the war, has been a restricted route since the war began, raising supply concerns. Europe focus Countries in Europe, North and South America have been the main importers of Guyana’s oil, but the Middle East crisis has also prompted some Asian countries to look towards Guyana for oil. Europe imported up to 57 per cent of Guyanese crude between March and August this year, Kpler data shows, with the Netherlands, Sweden, Germany, the UK, Italy, Poland and Spain being the main buyers. The Americas took about a third, while Asian nations, including China, Thailand, Singapore and Indonesia, imported about 6 per cent of Guyanese crude during the period. Turkey bought roughly 5 per cent. Another factor that is contributing to a rise in demand for Guyana's crude is the Ukraine war. European nations are looking for alternative sources of supply as they seek to reduce dependence on Russian crude and squeeze off Moscow’s oil revenue as it continues to wage war against Ukraine. Guyanese crude is also highly valued for its low sulfur content, high yields of middle distillates such as diesel and jet fuel, and competitive break-even costs of $30–$40 per barrel that "make it particularly attractive to refiners, especially in Europe", Ms Rivera said. Investment of $60 billion An oil boom is a recent phenomenon in Guyana, with production starting only seven years ago following the discovery of oil in 2015. An ExxonMobil-led consortium – including Chevron, and China’s CNOOC have been dominating production, with total investment estimated at between $55 billion and $60 billion at the Stabroek Block. The group hit a milestone last month by producing its billionth barrel of oil at Stabroek less than seven years after production began in 2019. “With an estimated resource base of just under 11 billion oil-equivalent barrels and plans for up to eight offshore developments by 2030, the Stabroek block is helping meet demand across the Americas, Europe and Asia, contributing to global energy security and market stability,” ExxonMobil said in a statement last month. More projects are expected to come online, with Uaru expected to start up by the end of 2026, Whiptail expected to start up in 2027, and Hammerhead expected to begin production in 2029, it added. Last year, France’s TotalEnergies, QatarEnergy and Malaysia’s Petronas also signed an agreement with the Guyanese government to explore a shallow block off the coast of Guyana for oil production. Economic boost Oil revenue, spurred by a rise in production and higher prices, has transformed Guyana from a small, agriculture and services based economy into one of the world’s fastest-growing economies. From an annual growth rate of 5.4 per cent in 2019, when it first started producing oil, the country’s economy expanded by 43.5 per cent in the following year, 20.1 per cent in 2021, 63.3 per cent in 2022, 33.8 per cent in 2023, 43.8 per cent in 2024 and 19.3 per cent in 2025, International Monetary Fund data shows. The country's GDP is projected to grow by 16.2 per cent this year, the highest rate globally, as oil revenue continues to increase due to higher production and rising crude prices. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, is currently trading at about $100 per barrel. "The economic outlook [for Guyana] remains highly favourable," the IMF said in July. "Oil production is expected to continue expanding, and the non-oil economy is projected to grow by about 7 per cent on average over the next five years as the government continues its ambitious plans to address infrastructure and developmental needs."

events.title: Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism
events.summary: Last month at Rails World 2026, Ruby on Rails creator David Heinemeier Hansson gave a relentlessly optimistic keynote in which he suggested AI has all but eliminated the need for developers to manually write code. But perhaps DHH, as he is known online, shouldn’t delete his code editor quite yet. On Sunday, DHH posted about a test in which he had frontier agents implement and optimize his company’s Campfire group chat app in three languages: Elixir, Go, and Rust. He then compared the runtime performance of those versions with the original Ruby on Rails implementation. DHH’s post includes data that seemingly demonstrates the efficiency of the Rust programming language, and AI agent coding itself. But many observers came to another conclusion: Don't trust DHH’s benchmarks. As of press time, the post and accompanying chart garnered over 900,000 views. It showed the Rust rewrite of the chat app outperformed others by a wide margin on five tasks, including searching or posting a message. DHH did not say which AI services he used for these rewrites, but noted that each rewrite took only a few hours, as the original code itself, largely written in Ruby, is relatively compact. Many observers, notably advocates of other languages, quickly surmised from the source material that DHH had optimized the Rust results but didn't do the same for the other languages he tested. Whither high-level languages? Rewriting applications in Rust, often with the help of AI agents, seems to be a popular undertaking these days, with Microsoft's Copilot runtime, the pnpm JavaScript installer, and the Bun JavaScript toolchain all getting the Rust treatment. In DHH’s test, the Rust implementation handily bested the others across all five workloads, sometimes by a wide margin. To serve a “room page,” for instance, Rust knocked out 36,260 requests per second. In contrast, Ruby on Rails was only able to fulfill a paltry 241 requests, while Elixir delivered 722 requests, and even runner-up Golang only knocked out 3,860 requests a second. Rust executed the other tasks with similar alacrity, easily besting the other languages DHH used. The takeaway was obvious to DHH: Rewriting an application in Rust, or better yet having AI agents do the job, may very well result in major performance improvements for an app. DHH suggested that many factors go into choosing a programming language for a particular job, and execution speed is not the sole criterion. Rust can be agonizingly slow to compile, and for many, writing or even reading Rust code is an arduous job. DHH himself began developing Rails in 2003 while building Basecamp in the then relatively obscure Ruby programming language to ease the developer experience. He doesn’t seem to mind that Ruby ranked the slowest in his own tests. “I didn't care about [performance] when the pay-off was huge in terms of productivity and developer joy.” But AI agents don’t give a hoot about joy. “You really have to bury your head in the sand not to see that when agents write the code and validate the output, we need to adjust to a new reality,” he wrote. Chips on the table DHH’s ad-hoc test was quickly met with skepticism, criticism and outright mockery, especially on X. (It’s as if DHH’s conservative views on immigration and his work to bring yet another Linux desktop into the world didn’t give him enough headaches). “What worries me about the future of programming is you see this and don’t immediately know there must be something wrong with the results or what you actually measured,” wrote prominent Google engineer Jaana Dogan in an X response to DHH’s tests. Dogan did not elaborate on the test’s shortcomings, but many others, especially advocates of other languages, were more than happy to provide details. One Elixir advocate called DHH’s implementation “moronic,” while a couple of others actually rewrote the Elixir code to make its performance comparable to Rust’s. After that rewrite, the Elixir version of the app bested Rust’s performance on some tasks, despite further third-party Rust optimizations. DHH expressed surprise that others would assume a high-level language like Elixir or Ruby could even compete with a language like Rust, which runs closer to the metal. But he also noted on X that “It's not exactly extra points for Elixir if frontier agents can't find the magic ‘go fast’ switches.” Elsewhere, observers noted that the Rust rewrite got a lot more post-coding attention than the other implementations of Go and Elixir, both of which seemed to be quickly wrapped up after the initial agent requests. “You're not benchmarking languages, you're benchmarking how much attention each port got,” one observer wrote on X. Golang advocates were likewise unamused. “The benchmark was unfair. More time was put into the Rust code while the rest were one-shotted,” one wrote on X. Someone else even made their own chart showing how much more the Rust code was tuned compared to the quick passes on the other languages. None of these rebuttals actually negates DHH’s advocacy of using agents to code. But clearly, skipping a manual review of the resulting work will still leave a lot of potential gains on the table. ®

events.title: Tokyo Stock Exchange to remove nearly 700 firms from Topix and add 35 in major reform
events.summary: After the reshuffle, the Topix index will be composed of 986 stocks, about 40% fewer than the current components. Tokyo Stock Exchange will cut nearly 700 firms from Topix and add 35, in its first major reshuffle to attract investors. Topix will shrink to 986 stocks, about 40% fewer than now, while the exchange continues trading and governance reforms. Trial Holdings, Workman and Tier IV will join; Pasona Group and Tsubaki Nakashima will leave. Removed stocks will fall to zero by July 2028. TOKYO – The Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) plans to remove nearly 700 firms from its main Topix index and add 35 companies in the first major reshuffle of its main index, as the exchange continues reforms to attract investors. After the reshuffle, the Topix index will be composed of 986 stocks, about 40% fewer than the current components, said JPX Market Innovation and Research, a unit of Japan Exchanges Group. The move comes as the TSE presses ahead with the reform of its trading platform, along with its push to improve corporate governance. The Topix is the main index tracked by large institutional investors, including the Government Pension Investment Fund, the world’s largest pension fund. Discount supermarket chain Trial Holdings, utility clothing and workwear retailer Workman, and autonomous driving startup Tier IV are among those joining the index. Human resources company Pasona Group and ball bearings maker Tsubaki Nakashima are among those being removed. The exchange will reduce the weightings of those stocks to be removed to zero by July 2028, JPX Market Innovation and Research said. The exchange will conduct the second round of its regular reshuffle in October 2027. REUTERS

events.title: Shell expects refineries to almost double the profit from every barrel of fuel made
events.summary: Record prices caused by global shortages amid shutdown of war-damaged refineries in Middle East and Russia Shell’s refineries are expected to make record profits on each barrel of fuel produced after shortages in the global market caused pump prices around the world to climb to all-time highs. In a trading update on Wednesday, the energy supermajor forecast profit margins of $42 a barrel in the July to September period, far above the margins of $24 a barrel in the second quarter. The forecast margins are also significantly higher than the previous record for petroleum products of about $28 a barrel, set in the early months of the Russia-Ukraine war. The margins reflect the steep increase in the price of refined fuels, including diesel, relative to the cost of the crude oil. A partial recovery of Gulf oil exports has allowed crude market prices to ease back to about $100 a barrel, while war damage to refineries in the Middle East and Russia has caused fuel prices to continue to climb. That gap should make larger profits possible for refineries, particularly those in the US and Europe. The Middle East crisis has already helped Shell to a profit of almost $10bn (£7.5bn) for the second quarter of 2026, more than double the figure for the same period last year and its second highest quarterly earnings on record. The market value of Europe’s biggest oil and gas company, now the second largest company on the UK’s FTSE 100 index, climbed to a record high of £36.23 a share at the end of last month. That share price was reached despite oil prices retreating from their 2026 peak of above $115 a barrel in spring to about $100. It was lifted by European gas prices, which doubled from the previous year over the summer, and record high diesel prices . Global oil prices were slightly lower in the third quarter of the year. Brent crude averaged $85.60 a barrel, compared with $97.05 in the second quarter, but still well above the $68.14 recorded in the third quarter last year. The diesel price premium over the global oil benchmark jumped above $100 a barrel for the first time, indicating record high profits from refining crude into fuels. Shell operates some of Europe’s largest refineries alongside the French energy company TotalEnergies, which has the continent’s largest refining capacity. TotalEnergies’ chief executive, Patrick Pouyanné, welcomed the opportunities created by the global energy crisis. He told an industry conference in London this week: “We’re doing really well by being integrated. Integration means your refineries in Europe, which you thought were liabilities, are suddenly becoming goldmines.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Europe’s benchmark gas price index more than doubled to €70.50 (£60) in August. The price of gas reached an average of more than €48 a megawatt-hour in the second quarter before leaping to almost €64/MWh in the third quarter. Shell’s gas production has been hard hit by the Middle East crisis, which led to severe damage to one of its key gas processing facilities in the Gulf, cutting its prewar gas production of 900,000 barrels ⁠of oil ​equivalent ‌per day (BOED) by a third. Shell said on Wednesday that it expected gas production to climb to about 740,000 to 780,000 barrels ⁠of oil ​equivalent ‌a day ‌after its acquisition of Canada’s ARC Resources, up sharply from its previous forecast of 570,000 to 630,000 BOED for the quarter. It produced about 631,000 BOED in the second quarter. The deal, which is expected to add about 370,000 barrels a day to Shell’s production of oil and gas, was completed in early September to add a month’s worth of production to its estimates for the quarter.

events.title: Your Next Great Read Might Be Certified ‘Organic’
events.summary: As scandals involving the use of artificial intelligence by professional authors pile up , a British startup has established a way for publishers to certify their books as “organic”—written by real people, no machines in sight. On Wednesday, Books by People confirmed it had received approval from the UK’s Intellectual Property Office to begin distributing a mark that indicates a published book has been authored by a human. The stamp, which looks like a thumbprint, will be displayed on the cover. “If people are going to be writing AI books or seeking it out for their own enjoyment, that’s their prerogative,” Esme Dennys, cofounder of Books by People, tells WIRED. “But if you want to read something that’s written by a person, you should be able to find that. We’re just trying to create that choice.” Previous book-labeling schemes, like Human Authored , have operated under an honesty system, where an author promises they haven’t used AI in the development process. To try to add more weight to its certification, Books by People asks for an authorship declaration, runs each manuscript through proprietary software, and manually examines early drafts and research materials supplied by the writer and editor for “indicators of humanity.” The organization is "looking at all the things that give us the best sense of whether a person wrote the work—whether the work was made during a natural process of drafting and redrafting,” says Dennys. Books by People will charge publishers a flat membership fee, plus an additional sum for every book they put forward for certification. Five publishers have signed up so far. The startup expects the new mark to feature on its first book by the end of the year. This year, the publishing industry has been caught up in a flurry of scandals involving the suspected use of AI by authors. A literary agent canceled a book deal reportedly worth $2 million; a publisher withdrew a novel from the shelves; readers alleged that a prize-winning short story had been generated with AI. Writers and publishers are not necessarily worried about being replaced by AI , industry insiders tell WIRED. They believe that few people will ultimately want to read machine-generated books. “You are essentially standing at the end of a conveyor belt, watching stuff fall off the edge. Once you know that, it prevents you from getting really emotionally invested in whatever falls into your hands from the belt,” says sci-fi author Ted Chiang, whose 1998 novella Story of Your Life was adapted into the Academy Award–winning film Arrival. “The knowledge of how something was created cannot be separated from your experience.” However, repeated scandals could shake public confidence in the unspoken rule of publishing: That every book that reaches the shelf has been authored by a real person who has not indulged in plagiarism. “Publishing has always relied on trust between the publisher, writer, and reading public. Cases where that trust is betrayed have been rare,” says Sam Jordison, codirector at independent publisher Galley Beggar Press, which intends to adopt the Books by People mark. “There’s almost a feeling of revulsion about the idea of reading an AI text that purports to be human. It feels like a con job.” Against that backdrop, the idea of a certification for human-authored books has received backing from various writers and editors. In a statement praising Books by People, Markus Dohle, former CEO of Penguin Random House, described human storytelling as “the lifeblood of our industry.” But while publishers might relish the chance to signal their commitment to “organic literature,” the routinization of AI detection is a double-edged sword for authors, who risk a false positive result spoiling their reputation . “We need to be quite careful that this doesn’t end up becoming a witch hunt,” says Tom West, CEO of the Publishers’ Licensing Services, which helps publishers to collectively license works to third parties. “Obviously, the devil is going to be in the detail.” New York–based startup Pangram , which has emerged as the leader in the field of AI detection, claims to be able to sniff out generated text with a 99.7 percent accuracy. But authors have questioned the reliability of its approach, which itself involves AI. In September, Jerry Falade, the debut author whose agent reportedly pulled the $2 million book deal, alleged that detection software had misconstrued his Nigerian dialect as evidence he had used AI. Pangram’s software scored the book as 97 percent AI-generated. “It takes months, even years to write a book,” Falade wrote in a recent essay . “It takes AI-detection software two minutes to ruin your life’s work.” (Pangram did not respond to a request for comment.) Others have warned against normalizing extreme scrutiny of authors.

events.title: COSMIC shuts the door on AI code as GNOME debates letting bug reports in
events.summary: System76 is banning AI-generated content from contributions to the COSMIC desktop. Some GNOME sub-projects also restrict AI-generated contributions, but one developer is urging them to make an exception for vulnerability reports. The COSMIC desktop project has changed its contributors' guidelines. The latest version now has a clear no-AI rule, insisting that contributors declare: "I have not included any LLM (also known as AI) generated content in this PR, including code, comments, and descriptions." In other words, you can teach yourself using AI, you can find bugs with AI, but if you want to submit your code for inclusion in COSMIC, you can't use AI to write the code, its docs or notes, or even the submission requests. This position is in keeping with some other desktop projects. For instance, the GNOME Calendar guide to contributing says: "This project does not allow contributions generated by large languages [sic] models (LLMs) and chatbots." GNOME Extensions also restricts AI-generated submissions, although it permits AI learning aids and code completion. Its review guidelines spell it out: "Extensions must not be AI-generated." COSMIC is one of the newest complete Linux desktop environments, but even so, it's been under development for years. The Register first reported on the effort nearly five years ago, meaning that it's older than ChatGPT, which debuted in late 2022 (it only feels so very much longer). COSMIC does use some GNOME components, and its default config looks not unlike GNOME, with a top panel and a dock-like launcher at the bottom. There are good reasons for that: the original System76 desktop called "COSMIC" was based on GNOME, quite heavily customized with GNOME extensions. Saying that, though, this new COSMIC is a very different beast. Its first stable release shipped with Pop!_OS 24.04 in late 2025. Although it looks similar, it's an entirely new, ground-up effort, written in Rust using the Iced toolkit. COSMIC itself is Wayland-only. GNOME is much older, larger, and more complicated. The project was announced in 1997, the year after the KDE project announcement. KDE 1.0 came out in 1998, and GNOME 1.0 in 1999. In part, GNOME was a response to KDE. KDE is built on the Qt toolkit, which was not fully open source. As such, in KDE's early days, Red Hat refused to include it in Red Hat Linux. Qt is aimed at C++ developers, so KDE was built in C++. Linux, like Unix, is built in plain old C and many Unix traditionalists scorned the much more complex C++. So GNOME was built in plain old C, using GTK, the toolkit built for the GIMP. In 1998, Red Hat Linux 5.1 included a preview of GNOME, and by Red Hat Linux 6.0 in 1999, GNOME 1.0 was the default desktop. GNOME is still the default desktop in RHEL to this day, and many GNOME developers' day jobs are at Red Hat. As we noted back in March, Red Hat management is noticeably enthusiastic about AI – although six months later, it was capping developers' AI spend. GNOME is largely written in C, which lacks automatic memory safety guarantees, although other languages feature too: GNOME Shell combines JavaScript and C, and some components are written in the GNOME-centric Vala programming language. Michael Catanzaro, GNOME developer, just published a blog post titled "The Era of Software Quality, or the Era of Ostriches?" which argues that the GNOME project must accept AI-generated bug reports. This is not a new subject for him. His post links to an earlier one from June, "Please Do Not Ban AI-Assisted Issue Reports." The following month, he announced a reduction in the disclosure deadline for issues reported to GNOME Security, from 90 days to 30, effective August 1. We recently reported on the 1,313 CVE identifiers listed in Debian's latest Linux kernel security advisory. AI is resulting in the discovery of vast numbers of bugs in the equally vast codebases of modern FOSS. GNOME is one of the biggest desktops in the Linux and BSD world, with much of its code written in memory-unsafe languages. As Catanzaro says: "No matter how much we try, GNOME developers will fail [to] write secure code when using unsafe languages like C, C++, or Vala: it's just too hard for even experienced developers to do properly." We are not arguing that Catanzaro is wrong. Given the stance toward AI of GNOME's biggest sponsor, it is entirely in keeping, and he makes a strong case. All we are noting is that this could in time prove to be the thin edge of a wedge with the weight of Red Hat behind it. First the project allows AI-generated bug reports. From there, it would not be a huge step to allowing AI-assisted triage. From there, to AI-assisted fixes. Once you're letting AI-assisted code in, then AI-assisted extensions may not seem so extreme, then core components, and in time, to the desktop itself. It would be wildly controversial, just as it already is in the KDE project. That doesn't mean it won't happen – in either project. Debian decided to allow it, and of course, the kernel itself does too. ®

events.title: Family offices branch out into private equity, infrastructure and alternative investments
events.summary: EQT, one of world’s largest private markets firms, sees more emphasis on diversification and flexibility Some financial analysts and wealth managers in recent years have suggested that the second- and third-generation leaders of family offices in Asia are moving away from the basic principles that helped to create and accumulate their existing assets, but that is not strictly accurate. Rather, just as the founding generation did, these investors look to assess available opportunities and adapt to circumstances as they build or adjust their portfolios to find the preferred balance between risk and reward. What has changed, though, particularly in the last couple of decades, is the range of options open to them. Previously, the focus would typically have been on making money in property, listed equities and direct business holdings, and then passing on those assets. Now, in tune with the times, there is much greater emphasis on international diversification, flexible structures and time horizons, and active ownership, while still maintaining a prudent, long-term approach. “In our interactions with family offices, we see that the second and third generations think slightly differently about managing wealth,” says Sueann Yeo, managing director and head of Asia-Pacific global wealth solutions for EQT, one of the world’s largest private markets firms. “When in your 20s to 40s, the mindset and expectations about capital preservation, growth and returns will not be the same as someone in their 60s or 70s. In particular, many of the younger generation are now thinking about private equity, infrastructure, alternative investments and different asset-allocation strategies.” Yeo says that a number of the more institutionalised family offices have been doing this for a long time. The change, though, is that many others are now setting up programmes to scale their allocations to these newer areas materially over a five- to 10-year period. Secondaries have evolved from a niche strategy into a core portfolio management tool for family offices, rather than simply an alternative route to private equity exposure. Global secondaries transaction volumes reached a record US$226 billion in 2025, up 41 per cent year-on-year, with momentum continuing into this year as first-half volumes exceeded US$120 billion, up 20 per cent year-on-year. Rather than framing secondaries as a faster-return alternative to primary commitments, Yeo describes the two as complementary: secondaries provide an additional way to access private markets, with differentiated portfolio characteristics, broader diversification and distinct cash-flow profiles. “There are a few elements to this: an increasing level of sophistication in the understanding of private assets; more attention to DPI [distributed to paid-in capital, a metric for measuring the cash returned to investors compared with the money they put into a fund]; and a more hands-on approach to strategic asset allocation and setting limits for each category.” Yeo points to the Wallenberg model as a reference point EQT draws on for its own investment approach – a model built around patient, multi-generational capital, active support for portfolio companies and reinvestment of returns to sustain long-term growth. She believes this style of long-term, engaged ownership offers a useful frame of reference for Asia’s family offices as they weigh how to balance risk and opportunity across generations. This kind of evergreen approach enables eligible individual investors and family offices to invest into the same strategies that previously only institutions could access. It allows investment in private equity without the operational complexity of managing capital calls, distributions and reinvestment decisions typical of close-end structures, while offering more flexible, though not unlimited, access to liquidity. “Family offices are warming up to the idea of having evergreen structures, which mirrors the content of classic closed-end private equity structures for institutional investors, but with more flexibility,” Yeo says. “EQT’s private wealth strategies comprise a mix of primary funds, co-investment deals and a cash portion with a soft lock period to manage the liquidity.” Eligible investors benefit from the immediate deployment with exposure to a diversified portfolio from day one, without the need for continual involvement or decision-making. Yeo emphasises that this is just one of many options available through the EQT Private Wealth platform, which embodies the principle of active ownership to create value for the private companies taken into its portfolio. This entails a focus on governance and careful use of the right levers to improve operating performance and revenue – but without the slash-and-cut type of management overhauls often seen elsewhere.

events.title: From reactive to proactive: How endpoint monitoring is fixing broken meeting rooms
events.summary: The role of meeting rooms is changing. Traditionally, they were formal spaces built around a large central table and inflexible physical setup, reserved primarily for board meetings, client presentations, or official status updates. The rise of hybrid work and advances in collaboration technology have made that approach increasingly obsolete. Employees now come into the office to connect, collaborate, and brainstorm with colleagues rather than to undertake the solo, focused work they can do better at home. The upshot is that many meeting rooms have transformed into fluid, digitized, data-enabled hubs. With modular partitions, movable furniture, and casual seating, they are designed to adapt to whatever task is at hand. As digital nodes, they also bridge the gap between remote and office workers, so remote and in-person participants get a consistent experience regardless of location. That shift is only possible because of the convergence between IT and audio-visual (AV) equipment, explains Yannic Laleeuwe, marketing director for Barco's ClickShare visualization, collaboration, and networking platform. Cameras, microphones, and wireless conferencing, collaboration and presentation tools, such as ClickShare can now connect to enterprise networks. That allows management through centralized cloud-based systems, so IT teams can monitor, update, secure and tune these systems in ways they could not before. "Historically, meeting rooms have sat in a gray zone between facilities management, AV and IT," Laleeuwe points out. "They were physical spaces first with technology added into them over time, so they were rarely managed by IT departments with the same level of telemetry as laptops, servers or network infrastructure." The impact of reactive tech support IT professionals could often tell whether a device was connected to the network, but struggled to see how the room was being used or whether it delivered a reliable user experience. That lack of visibility explains why meeting room tech support has often been reactive, with staff only intervening once something breaks. "A room was assumed to be working until someone complained that a call wouldn't start, the audio was poor, a display failed, or remote participants couldn't follow the conversation," Laleeuwe says. "Without reliable data on usage, performance and failure patterns, IT had limited ability to predict issues, prioritize investments or optimize rooms before users were affected." The situation had knock-on effects at various levels. For employees, faulty technology creates immediate friction: meetings start late, participation becomes difficult, and unsecured personal devices get pressed into service as a fallback. An additional challenge in a hybrid world is that meeting room technology acts as a bridge between remote and in-office colleagues, so when it fails, the meeting fails with it. For IT teams, poorly maintained technology produces operational inefficiency. Rather than working to make collaboration environments more effective, they end up firefighting individual incidents. For the business itself, a lack of activity data makes facilities planning considerably harder. "Some spaces may be over-engineered with technology that's barely used, while others are under-equipped for the way people actually collaborate," Laleeuwe points out. "This leads to wasted investment, inconsistent user experiences, and missed opportunities to design rooms around real behavior rather than just assumptions." The value of telemetry Endpoint monitoring technology, such as ClickShare's XMS Cloud Management Platform, changes that picture. Organizations can measure occupancy patterns and how their meeting rooms are used in practice, track equipment uptime, connection quality, and software and firmware status, and follow adoption levels alongside the volume and type of support incidents raised. The data helps IT professionals judge not only whether a room is operating effectively in a technical sense, but whether it is delivering the experience employees expect. As Laleeuwe explains: "Telemetry changes meeting room management from a reactive discipline into a proactive one. Instead of waiting for users to report problems, IT can identify patterns, spot underperforming rooms, detect device issues, plan maintenance and make investment decisions based on evidence." In other words, meeting rooms can be treated as managed endpoints, with IT monitoring, patching, securing, supporting, and assessing them against clear performance indicators. That matters because meeting rooms are now hubs where business-critical work happens, not just spaces where calls take place. "They influence productivity, employee experience, meeting equity, collaboration culture, and return on workplace investments," Laleeuwe adds. "When IT has better visibility and control, employees get more reliable rooms, IT teams reduce support overhead, and the business can make smarter decisions about workplace design, technology standardization, and future upgrades." IT shapes organization-wide collaboration While the benefits of such technology are clear, the approach requires IT teams to develop a broader range of skills than traditional device support. Endpoint management, networking, security, and lifecycle management all remain essential, but that expertise must now be combined with AV knowledge, an understanding of acoustics, data analysis, workplace experience design, and change management. This mix of skills "changes IT's role", Laleeuwe indicates, because teams are no longer just fixing what has broken. "They're helping shape how collaboration happens across the organization," she explains. "That means interpreting room data, understanding user behavior, working more closely with workplace, HR, facilities and sustainability teams, and influencing standards for how meeting spaces are designed and used." These skills are best developed through cross-functional collaboration and closer partnerships with AV specialists and vendors, Laleeuwe advises. Rather than regarding room analytics as isolated device data, she recommends treating them as part of a broader palette of workplace intelligence. That makes it easier to improve business performance by understanding how physical spaces, digital tools, people, and their daily tasks interact. AI takes meeting rooms to a new level The introduction of AI-driven meeting environments is expected to reshape meeting room experiences further still. Laleeuwe explains: "AI is moving beyond novelty features, such as basic transcription, and becoming part of the operational layer of collaboration. In the room, this can include intelligent camera framing, noise reduction, audio calibration, live transcription, translation, automated notes, action item tracking, room diagnostics and performance optimization." events.title: Jaguar unveils new electric car after 'woke' ridicule
events.summary: The Type 01's launch event was attended by celebrities including actor Florence Pugh Jaguar has revealed its new electric car two years after its controversial rebranding sparked a backlash with the firm accused of going "woke". The unveiling of the all-electric Type 01 is a gamble for parent company JLR, which has invested billions reinventing Jaguar and is facing mixed reactions over the new car's design and the brand's all-electric strategy. The car itself is an imposing four-door "Grand Tourer", with a long bonnet that deliberately harks back to Jaguar's emblematic 1960s E-Type. But it comes at a hefty price tag with a minimum cost of £130,000 in the UK and $130,500 in the US. The new model's electric motors are potent, producing about 1000 horsepower and allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds. JLR says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles. The company describes it as the "most technically advanced, powerful and aerodynamic Jaguar ever engineered". However, the unveiling of the Type 01 on Tuesday was met with mixed reactions on social media. "Looks like a Cybertruck and a Bentley Continental had an illegitimate child," Facebook user Ken Katch said, referring to the Tesla pick-up, known for its divisive design. Craig Kinnersley, who runs a luxury car consultancy, wrote on LinkedIn that the new design was an "unmitigated catastrophe" that looked like a hearse and lacked any "memorable Jaguar flourish". But car journalist Steve Fowler said the Type 01 looked "incredible" and made him "proud to be British". "Not everyone will like it - that's fine. Not everyone has to!" he wrote on X. Alistair Weaver from vehicle sales platform Edmunds said Jaguar deserved some credit for the Type 01's looks, despite it being "polarising". "If Jaguar designed a car that looked like anything else, it would have had no hope," Weaver told the BBC. But the firm faces an uphill battle in the US, where EVs are becoming less popular , he added. This launch was always bound to attract attention, after the company caused waves with the initial unveiling of its new direction. In 2024 Jaguar released a surreal advert, showing models in a range of bizarre and brightly coloured outfits. There was a new Jaguar logo - but no cars in the ad at all. Two weeks later, Jaguar's denim-clad design chief Gerry McGovern took to a Miami stage to show off a pair of radical concept cars , in Miami Pink and London Blue colour schemes. Concept cars are mock-ups built to demonstrate an idea, rather than to work when on the road. Acknowledging that they might prove controversial he quipped: "Jaguar has no desire to be loved by everybody". The pink concept car unveiled in 2024 The event, heralding Jaguar's future as a luxury all-electric marque , triggered a furious backlash in the press and on social media. Critics claimed JLR was betraying its heritage in favour of going "woke". Even the colour chosen for the launch was derided as "Barbie pink", as culture wars erupted around it. The reception appeared to catch JLR by surprise. The reinvention of Jaguar as a luxury electric brand was part of a wide-ranging strategy set out by the company in early 2023, in which it pledged to invest £15bn in new models and technologies. How Jaguar lost its way - long before that polarising advert Published 8 December 2024 'Trust and reserve judgement' on rebrand, says Jaguar Published 23 November 2024 At the time, Jaguar itself was struggling. The badge, which was once an intrinsic part of Swinging Sixties British cool, had lost its lustre. Where in the past it had supplied E-Types to Brigitte Bardot and Steve McQueen, it now struggled to sell upmarket saloons and SUVs to middle-ranking corporate executives, who generally preferred Audis and BMWs. "Jaguar's core demographic, despite the uproar, gave up on the brand years ago, so they effectively had nothing to lose," said Matthias Schmidt of Schmidt Automotive Research. The Type 01's design has been met with mixed reactions from car enthusiasts JLR wound down production of its old Jaguar models in 2024 and 2025. The "woke" row, while it may have made life briefly uncomfortable for the company's leadership, did at least keep the brand in the public consciousness. The GT is expected to be the first of three new electric designs from Jaguar. Since then JLR has parted ways with the agency behind the rebranding campaign, and the company also has a new chief executive. Jaguar had supplied E-Types to stars like Brigitte Bardot and Steve McQueen But the future of Jaguar itself still hangs in the balance. "I think it really is a last throw of the dice," says journalist Steve Fowler. "JLR has struggled to make serious money with Jaguar in the past, and that's what it's all about.

events.title: UK house prices flatline as rising mortgage costs weigh on market
events.summary: Average cost of home in September was £298,441, says Lloyds – about the same as year earlier and in August UK house prices flatlined in September, according to a leading index, as rising mortgage costs started to weigh on the market. The average cost of a home was £298,441, roughly the same as it was a year earlier and in the previous month, according to the tracker from Lloyds previously known as the Halifax HPI. Economists polled by Reuters had predicted a 0.1% monthly rise in prices, according to the median forecast, as well as a 0.2% annual increase. It came after house prices fell by 0.3% in August , the first decline in three years, as prospective buyers were hit by geopolitical uncertainty, combined with higher mortgage rates and stretched affordability. In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put prices up as a result of turmoil in the global bond markets, even though there has not been a change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year. Andrew Asaam, the mortgages director at Lloyds, said: “While the market overall has been fairly subdued, property prices have so far proved resilient during a period of higher mortgage rates, which has been driven by changing expectations around the future path of base rate.” On Monday the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage reached 6% for the first time in three years . Rising mortgage rates are bad news for borrowers whose fixed-rate deals are ending, as well as prospective buyers who are hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a home and the sellers who want the best price from them. It also adds to the squeeze facing consumers as a result of higher energy bills , linked to the Iran war, while rising prices elsewhere are raising concerns of a new cost of living crisis . Asaam said: “While higher mortgage rates and wider economic uncertainty are encouraging some people to take a more measured approach, new inquiries from prospective buyers are now at their highest since February.” He added that any movement in house prices was likely to remain modest. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Tom Bill, the head of UK residential research at the estate agent Knight Frank, said: “This year has been a story of rising energy prices and stalling house prices, as the unpredictable Middle East conflict unfolds and drives borrowing costs higher. This month’s budget adds to the uncertainty as buyers and sellers wonder which of the recurring tax rumours proves to be true.” The number of people applying for a mortgage to buy a property fell between July and September, as higher borrowing costs continued to affect prospective housebuyers’ budgets, according to quarterly figures from Stonebridge, one of the UK’s largest independent mortgage and protection networks. Mortgage applications for home purchases fell by 18.2% in the third quarter compared with a year earlier, Stonebridge found, while applications from first-time buyers slumped 18.6% over the same period. However, rising numbers of applications for remortgaging helped to slow the decline in overall mortgage activity.

events.title: Fears of NT business closures after delayed dry season and proposed visa cuts
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NT tourism sector calls for resilience fund to support struggling operators after difficult dry season Topic: Tourism and Leisure Industry There are fears many NT tourism operators won't survive the wet season after a difficult peak season this year and looming cuts to backpacker visas. ( ABC News: Michael Franchi ) Tourism operators in the Northern Territory's Top End have asked the federal government to establish a dedicated fund to help struggling businesses survive the quiet wet season months ahead. Sector representatives have warned proposed cuts to working holiday visas under the government’s new immigration plan could push businesses into financial collapse. Tourism operators and political leaders are urging the federal government to abandon its policy or create an exception for the NT. Tourism operators in the Northern Territory are advocating for a dedicated resilience fund to be set up to help businesses battling costly fuel, reduced flights and natural disaster recovery survive the upcoming wet season. Representatives from across the Top End tourism sector met in Darwin today for a roundtable with federal shadow minister for tourism, David Littleproud, to discuss their concerns for the industry. During the two-hour session, operators warned many small businesses and family-run tourism operators would struggle to survive the coming months following a difficult dry season period. NT tourism vendors face hundreds of thousands in flood damages After multiple major weather events, tourism vendors are looking at clean-up costs in the hundreds of thousands, with some businesses lost entirely. The rising cost of fuel, reduced flights and the impact of extreme weather earlier in the year which resulted in a delayed start to the tourism season were among the challenges raised at today's meeting. "We are seriously concerned that rising costs and a compressed tourism season will leave small and medium operators without the cash reserves to survive the coming Wet," Tourism Top End chair Chris Chaffe said. "These are local employers, family businesses and experiences that visitors come here for. Tourism Top End, which represents operators in the northern half of the NT, is urging the federal government to establish a dedicated fund to assist businesses without enough cash to survive the wet season. Chris Chaffe says local businesses and tourism operators in the Top End are struggling this year due to a delayed dry season. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) "That should combine tourism vouchers that generate additional travel and bookings, targeted wage support, coordinated payroll tax relief and tax payment arrangements, and interest-free loans for viable operators facing a temporary cashflow shortfall," Mr Chaffe said. "Small grants should also be available where taking on more debt is simply not a workable solution." Mr Chaffe said while immediate financial support was needed, policy changes were also necessary to tackle ongoing hurdles including the rising cost of flights and better management of Kakadu National Park, which is operated by the Commonwealth in partnership with traditional owners. "We need action before businesses close their doors," Mr Chaffe said. Closures of popular Kakadu attractions such as Twin Falls have been a concern for the NT tourism sector for years. ( Supplied: North Australian Helicopters ) Warning immigration cuts could bring NT 'to its knees' The roundtable came amid growing panic in the tourism sector over the federal government's recently announced immigration policy, which would see caps on working holiday visas . The changes announced last week mean that backpackers will have to enter a ballot if they want to remain in Australia for more than 12 months. The number of second-year visas will be capped at 45,000, while just 5,000 third-year visas will be issued, and in total Australia will welcome about 38,000 fewer second and third-year backpackers than it did in 2026. Tourism Top End executive Samantha Bennett said the changes would have "severe impacts" on the NT's tourism, agriculture and hospitality sectors. Samantha Bennett says the proposed changes to backpacker visas will have "severe impacts" on the NT's industries. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) "7,200 backpackers came through the NT in the last financial year," she said. "We need those workers who will come to the Territory in the three months we're busy." Mr Littleproud echoed the sector's concerns and reiterated his plea for Labor to scrap the working visa changes, saying they would "devastate" the industry.

events.title: Airfares to West still high with Mid-East war, premium for direct flights back to 2025 level: Report
events.summary: In 2025, direct flights from Asia-Pacific to the West were 18% more expensive than flights with a stopover in the Middle East, according to the report. Airfares from Asia Pacific to the West stay high because of the Middle East conflict, but the direct-flight premium has returned to 2025 levels: report Middle East airports operated only 66% of scheduled flights from March to August. Singapore's Changi Airport led ASEAN in economic impact in 2025. SINGAPORE – Airfares from the Asia-Pacific region to the West continue to be elevated by the persisting conflict in the Middle East that broke out on Feb 28 , according to a new report on air traffic disruptions. However, the premium for flying directly from Asia-Pacific to the West, compared with routes with a stopover at a major airport in the Middle East, has returned to the level seen in 2025. The report released on Oct 7 by the Airports Council International Asia-Pacific & Middle East, a trade association representing more than 600 airports, analysed the top 100 routes connecting Asia-Pacific countries to the West based on passenger traffic. In 2025, direct flights from Asia-Pacific to the West were 18% more expensive than flights with a stopover in the Middle East, according to the report. After the outbreak of the Iran war, direct airfares were around 30% more expensive in March and almost 50% more expensive in April. But such direct flights became cheaper than routes with a stopover in the Middle East in May and June because airlines that stop over in the region raised their prices and reduced their number of flights through that market, said Stefano Baronci, director-general of the Airports Council International Asia-Pacific & Middle East. Stefano Baronci, director-general of the Airports Council International Asia-Pacific & Middle East, expects airfares from Asia-Pacific to the West to remain elevated. Eleven major airports in the Middle East operated just 66% of their usual scheduled flights from March to August, according to the report. But the operational capacity of these airports has returned to more than 80% in August alone. Baronci also said the premium for flying directly from Asia-Pacific to the Middle East has since returned to the 2025 average. But in terms of actual pricing, he said: “Both direct flights bypassing the Middle East and flights via the Middle East continue to be higher than what they were in 2025, and this will continue to be the case.” He said the report had forecast a normalisation of airfares from Asia-Pacific to the West from September 2026 based on an assumption that Middle East airports would increase their capacity. But this “will probably be challenged by the reality”, he said. Some carriers have recently halted their flights to the Middle East because of geopolitical tensions. Earlier this month, Singapore Airlines and its budget arm Scoot extended their flight cancellations between Singapore and the Middle East until December. Hong Kong carrier Cathay Pacific has also suspended its flights to the Middle East until the end of January 2027. A separate report released on Oct 7 by the Airports Council International Asia-Pacific & Middle East also showed that Singapore’s Changi Airport contributed most to economic growth among airports in ASEAN in 2025. The airport directly contributed US$7.9 billion (S$10.1 billion) to gross domestic product, far ahead of the US$3.1 billion in contribution by all airports in Thailand and US$3 billion in Malaysia. Meanwhile, Singapore’s aviation sector contributed US$22 billion to its economy, considering indicators like trade, investment and productivity, which was also the highest seen in ASEAN. Taken together with its catalytic impact on tourism, the sector put US$47.8 billion towards the Republic’s GDP and supported 597,000 jobs in 2025. That was the second-highest socioeconomic value seen in ASEAN. Thailand led the chart because of the high value generated by tourism supported by the aviation industry. In terms of government revenue, aviation activity in Singapore generated US$3.1 billion in direct tax revenue in 2025, which was the highest of any ASEAN country. In comparison, the aviation sector in Malaysia contributed US$1.5 billion to government revenue, and that in Thailand, US$1.3 billion. Baronci said: “All the indicators show that Singapore is excelling, and this is demonstrated by the direct impact, where 42% of all direct aviation GDP across ASEAN is generated by Singapore. “In Singapore, you have high-value sectors. In Singapore, you have a high capital investment. In Singapore, you have strong human capital. In Singapore, you have a pro-business infrastructure. All of these fundamentally concur to have a bigger (contribution) than in other regions.” In all, the aviation industry supported 23.3 million jobs and contributed US$244 billion to GDP in ASEAN in 2025.

events.title: IMF chief urges countries to do more to curb debt and regulate AI
events.summary: The head of the International Monetary Fund says countries both rich and poor must take faster action to cut debt and counter growing inequality as their economies weather a triple whammy from the AI boom and shocks from wars in the Middle East and Ukr... Countries both rich and poor must take faster action to cut debt and counter growing inequality as their economies weather a triple whammy from the artificial intelligence boom, heavy borrowing and shocks from wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, the head of the IMF said Wednesday. “Some very tough political choices stare us in the face,” IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said in a speech in Singapore ahead of autumn IMF-World Bank meetings to be held in Bangkok next week. “My message to the world's economic policymakers next week will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action — you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said. At the meetings in Bangkok, finance ministers and central bank governors of 191 IMF-World Bank member countries will assess the state of the world economy and discuss strategies to support financial stability and sustained growth. So far, the hardest recent hits to global well-being have come from conflicts in the Middle East, Ukraine and elsewhere, Georgieva noted. But excessive debt is a growing burden for wealthy countries such as the U.S., Japan and Germany, as well as low-income countries that must choose between spending on public welfare or repaying onerous loans at a time of high interest rates, she noted. Georgieva pointed to risks associated with the rapid buildup of data center capacity to deliver artificial intelligence, which has helped push stock prices in many places to record highs, supporting strong economic growth despite high energy costs due to the Iran war. Investments in AI are likely to exceed the relative scale of spending on building railroads, electricity grids and telecommunications networks. “Love it, hate it or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy,” she said. Russian missile strike in Ukraine's capital kills at least 2 Ebola patient dies in Kenya after traveling from DRC to Nairobi Medical company announces program for 'AI-powered prescriptions' in Utah The AI building boom is underpinning robust corporate earnings as well as higher inflation. But there is a lag between the heavy investments involved and the arrival of AI's benefits, Georgieva said. “Should earnings fall short,” she said, “hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock.” Seven of the top 10 countries for AI-related trade are in the Asia-Pacific region, where the share of global economic activity has risen to 43% from 25% in 1991, the last time the meetings were held in Bangkok. While China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and other countries with strong tech sectors are benefiting from the AI boom, it is bypassing most others, Georgieva said, adding to economic inequality. AI also is raising energy demand, pushing prices for fuel, fertilizer, food and other key commodities still higher. She urged countries to rein in public spending and to raise the cost of borrowing as needed to control inflation, while protecting the most vulnerable members of their societies. Policies are needed to ensure AI is well regulated and to train workers, make labor markets more flexible, facilitate entrepreneurship and improve energy security, Georgieva said. events.title: Asia shares weaker, oil up as investors weigh Saudi-Houthi escalation
events.summary: The Japanese yen weakened, as the dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.1% to 102.06 following a 0.27% slide in the prior session. Asian shares fell slightly as investors grew cautious, while US stocks hit records and traders awaited Federal Reserve minutes for clues on future rate moves. Oil prices rose because of a Gulf of Mexico storm threat and Saudi-Houthi tension, even as more Middle East crude moved by tanker. Bond yields stayed high, weighing on the euro and US debt demand. India raised rates, and traders cut October Fed hike bets to 19%. SYDNEY – Asian markets were slightly weaker on Oct 7 as investor confidence showed signs of flagging, while oil prices rose due to a storm threat in the Gulf of Mexico and escalating Saudi-Houthi tensions. In Asia, MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares excluding Japan was down 0.5%, led by declines in Hong Kong and Singapore after US stocks ended higher. The index is up 0.9% so far in October . The S&P 500 hit a fresh record on Oct 6 , up about 0.6% on the day, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq gained 0.4%, also an all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.5%. In Asian trading, US crude ticked up 0.9% to US$90.2 a barrel; prices were little changed in the international session. Brent crude rose 1% to US$101.58 per barrel. The price rise came as commodity investors weighed supply constraints from a storm heading for North American oil-producing regions and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia against increased supplies of Middle East crude. Around ​12 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil and 2 million bpd of refined products have left the Middle East on tankers in the last seven to 10 days, commodities trading giant Vitol’s CEO Russell Hardy said on Oct 6 . US equities were showing signs of losing momentum as global bond yields resumed their ascent on Oct 7 . S&P 500 e-mini futures rose 0.1% for the fifth day of gains, but failed to surpass an intraday high set the previous session. Heavily sold French bond futures ticked down in Asia to retrace some of the previous session’s rebound as far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen pledged spending cuts and a reduction in the country’s budget deficit. Ten-year French yields fell more than 11 basis points (bps) on Oct 6 and the spread between French OATs and German bunds, which hit almost 160bps last week, according to LSEG data, narrowed to 132bps. “The magnitude of the move is striking given the 2027 election remains several months away and France’s deteriorating fiscal dynamics are hardly new,” said Laura Cooper, Nuveen’s head of macro credit and global investment strategist. “What has changed is sharply higher yields, leaving investors less willing to look through those vulnerabilities.” The resumption of investor concerns weighed on the euro, which slipped 0.3% to US$1.1229. US Treasury auctions to show depth of demand The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was up 3.8bps at 5.307% in Asian trade ahead of an auction of notes of the same maturity later in the session and a 30-year auction on Oct 8 . The auctions will show the depth of investor demand for US debt, analysts said. US longer-dated yields hit a 24-year high on Oct 5 amid a persistent sell-off since late August due to inflation and debt concerns. Australian shares were down 0.1% on Oct 7 , while Japan’s Nikkei stock index was off 0.8%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index was down 0.5% in afternoon trading, dragged lower by a decline of as much as 4.1% in the city’s biotech gauge. Mainland China’s financial markets remained closed for a holiday. Indian stocks slipped 0.5% as the Reserve Bank of India hiked interest rates for the first time in nearly four years to rein in rising inflation. The central bank raised its benchmark by 25bps to 5.5%, as expected by a majority of economists polled by Reuters. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.1% to 102.06 following a 0.27% slide in the prior session. The Japanese yen weakened 0.2% to 158.41 per US dollar. Sterling dipped 0.2% to US$1.3248. The Federal Reserve on Oct 7 will publish the minutes of its Sept 15 and 16 policy meeting, which will be scrutinised for potential rate moves over the next few months. Traders scaled back expectations of a Fed rate increase in October to 19% from about 50% a week earlier. Spot gold was down 0.6% at US$4,137.29 per ounce. REUTERS

events.title: Rainmakers: The drones used to seed clouds
events.summary: Rainmaker's drones were used over Alaska this year On 23 August, Cooper Freeman had no idea clouds above his head were being filled with a silver compound in order to cause rainfall. Neither did thousands of other residents in Homer, Alaska, who later discovered San Francisco start-up Rainmaker conducted an experiment in that region using cloud-seeding technology. The company claims it produced 19 million US gallons of water in the sky in three hours. This approach to weather modification, now more than 80-years-old, involves using planes and drones to disperse compounds such as silver iodide into clouds to form ice crystals. Those crystals eventually become large enough to fall as rain or snow, depending on the temperatures below. Essentially, cloud seeding speeds up the natural process of water vapor condensing inside of clouds. Gravity then pulls those crystals to the ground. The technology, though, needs ideal climate environments, such as mountainous or cold regions such as Alaska. Freeman, the Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, isn't just concerned Homer residents weren't widely alerted to these experiments. He's sceptical about what was shot into the clouds, and questions how safe it was for both residents and their habitat. "It doesn't appear that there was any downstream monitoring to verify that this silver iodide didn't impact the environment," he says. Freeman adds, "Having a company come in to do this seeding isn't going to solve our water woes, and it feels like a distraction from solving the urgent issues related to water conservation." Concerns are mounting about the challenges surrounding water security. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in July "our world is using freshwater faster than it can be replenished , external ", which echoes reports noting how the past five years have led to the driest period for global rivers , external in more than three decades. Cloud-seeding technology may be a drop in the bucket, as it doesn't create rainstorms. For example, Rainmaker's 19 million gallons equates to around 0.01 inch of rain across 100 square miles. Nevertheless, more than 50 countries , external are developing programmes to modify the weather and a surge of start-ups are developing systems to create rain. As well developed and promising as this innovative field has become, these businesses continue to face thorny questions on safety and efficacy, leading to novel approaches with both finding the right material to spray into clouds and how they do it. Augustus Doricko with a Rainmaker drone Augustus Doricko, the founder and CEO of Rainmaker, is quick to answer any questions on the consequences of how his company uses the silver iodide compound. It's clear he's been asked about chemical safety many times. He says Rainmaker releases this form of silver at 20 grams per flight, distributed across thousands of square kilometres. "The resultant increase in concentration on the ground is in the parts per quadrillion, way below the threshold laid out by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] on what is allowable." Rainmaker's flights use drones to soar into clouds because without clouds, "we can't do anything," he says, pointing to one of the key limits of cloud-seeding processes. Cloud-seeding sessions have to wait for clouds to form to try to coax them into precipitation. Their drones are outfitted with silver iodide flairs, and when lit the burning atomizes the water particles into a small enough size so they can stay suspended in the freezing cloud for hours, eventually turning into crystals and later rain. Rainmaker operates in states such as Idaho, Utah, Colorado and areas of the Middle East such as Jordan. Doricko says, "Jordan residents often only have water for hours per week from their utility because of how scarce water is, and it's a privilege to try to help this storied region." Cloud seeding's roots began in 1946 when researchers from the General Electric Research Laboratory used dry ice as the first seeding agent. A year later, silver iodide was found to be more effective than dry ice, which quickly turns into useless gas. While seeding agents caused more rainfall, they didn't move the needle much. In fact, sobering statistics point to how patchy this technology can be in what it pours on the ground. "With the right conditions, cloud seeding squeeze out about an extra five to 10% of precipitation," says Jon Meyer, an assistant state climatologist with the Utah Climate Center. What was encouraging, though, for the cloud-seeding sector was a landmark 2017 study that found how silver iodide worked as expected, one of the first reports to observe cloud seeding in action using radar and precipitation gauges. In the past several years, Meyer has been encouraged to see more companies such as Rainmaker bring innovation to an old industry.

events.title: UAE's 'very powerful' cyber defences can repel attacks, says Mistral AI boss
events.summary: The UAE 's “very powerful” cyber defences enable it to defend against threats, especially during geopolitical instability, the chief executive of French company Mistral AI said. The UAE's pursuit of technological sovereignty will help it establish reliable and secure cyber capabilities, Arthur Mensch told The National at the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi . “The UAE is under pressure, in particular, on the defence side,” he said. “Cyber capabilities are a must-have when it comes to having capable defence systems. “Sovereignty matters in that. It's important to be able to wield defence systems without having to ask for permission.” Mr Mensch's comments come after UAE authorities reported an increasing number of cyber attacks. Last month, the UAE's cyber security chief, Mohamed Al Kuwaiti, said the country is continuing to contend with daily online threats, with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps behind many of the attacks. Mr Al Kuwaiti said the country faced about 640,000 attacks on September 15 and that Iran remains “one of the main players” in the high-tech offensive, which is being exacerbated by the rise of AI. “Having very powerful cyber models deployed here in Abu Dhabi in a way where the deployment is fully under Abu Dhabi control is going to be quite important,” Mr Mensch said. Investing in UAE data centres Mr Mensch said Mistral AI would consider investing in UAE data centres, a move that would further solidify its co-operation with Abu Dhabi and boost the country's AI ambitions. “We may [invest in UAE data centres]. It's an interesting place for our AI buildout that is currently under way in this part of the world,” he said. On Abu Dhabi's efforts at data sovereignty, Mr Mensch said authorities and the wider industry had “very early on decided” that this aspect will be crucial for the deployment of AI. Data sovereignty is becoming vital for nations as it gives them legal control over the data within their jurisdictions. The most notable project to achieve this is the planned Stargate UAE data centre campus, a 5GW development valued at $30 billion . Mistral AI met more local organisations and companies at the summit, trying to “get a sense of what Abu Dhabi needs to build with AI ... [and] go in depth into the technological aspect of the asks”, said Mr Mensch, adding that the company has worked “extensively” with the oil and gas industry. Mistral AI has already forged partnerships with Abu Dhabi organisations , including AI major G42, to develop advanced platforms and infrastructure, and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence for research and development in AI foundation models, talent development and real-world AI solutions. In June, the company teamed up with UAE AI investment firm MGX and lender Bpifrance for the planned expansion of Campus AI in France, which aims to build a capacity of 3GW across Europe's third-biggest economy. “There is more that can be done ... on being able to have a compute capacity under full Abu Dhabi control; that's something where as a company we can help,” he added. AI accountability Fresh debacles have been hitting the AI industry, most notably AI models, supposedly in secure environments and built by names including OpenAI, Meta Platforms, Anthropic and Google, going rogue and infiltrating external sites. Mr Mensch was clear on where the responsibility should fall. At the same time, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman made a plea at the recent UN General Assembly for governments to do more to rein in AI. “Accountability for AI deployments, when they are hosted by AI companies, falls on the AI companies. This should be very, very clear. There's no way in which the accountability of what we're doing should be offset to governments,” Mr Mensch said. Governments, though, “are accountable for the adoption of the technology, and they should be accountable for how it's being used in the government itself”, he said. Mr Mensch also called for a tempered tone on the call for deceleration – or even acceleration – of the development of AI, as recent events have shown the potential disruption the technology can bring. “I'm very cautious about those warnings [to slow development down] because they serve their own interests very clearly,” he said. “The world we don't want to live in, which would be an extremely dangerous world, is the world where you have a duopoly of companies operated from the US serving the rest of the world,” he said, referring to the strength of the US AI industry, led by OpenAI and Anthropic, which is widely viewed as a counter to China's growing influence in the sector. On Tuesday, at AI Everything, Mistral AI launched its latest Mistral Large 4 AI model, which, it says, is among the fastest in the world and rivals the best open-source models from China. “We see no sign of slowing down when we look at how our model is being improved by the day,” Mr Mensch said.
