events.title: Thermal Complexity Grows With AI Chips And Photonics
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Photonics can speed up the movement of data using less energy, but the impact of heat, warpage, and other stresses needs to be fully understood up front. Understanding the transient behavior associated with multi-die assemblies is complex, but it opens the door to much more granular performance and thermal optimization. Tools that can accurately predict thermally accelerated aging are lacking today. Experts at the Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss the impact of heat on photonics, transient behavior, and system reliability, with Lang Lin, director of product management at Synopsys ; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco ; Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics at Vinci ; Chris Mueth, director of new markets management at Keysight EDA ; and John Ferguson, senior director of product management at Siemens EDA . What follows are excerpts of that conversation, which was held behind closed doors at the recent Design Automation Conference. This is the second of a three-part series. Part one is here . L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Lin; Vinci’s Radhakrishnan; Keysight’s Mueth; Siemens’ Ferguson. SE: Moving data takes power, which generates heat. So how do we keep data moving while still remaining within the power budget? Is the solution photonics? Even there, heat can cause issues. Mueth : Photonics has a lot of promise for reducing data center bottlenecks, but it can’t be scaled right now. Building a large mesh switch requires many components, and you have high losses. So you have to revisit the whole architecture for how things are done in photonics and do them differently, probably in a modular style that’s scalable. Another issue is heat sensitivity. You have to stabilize that. But even then, your photonic structure is going to have heaters in it because these have to be controlled. And if you have a large mesh switch, the amount of control you need is significant. So how do you calibrate your structures through that chip to get enough performance when you may have thousands of heaters that you have to control? If we can solve that problem, it will open things up a bit. But that still doesn’t get rid of the losses in the |photonics chips. That has to be solved with a modular, scalable architecture. SE: This leads to another issue, which is that you’re no longer dealing with just one type of processing element. What happens when you go from a GPU to a CPU? Do they both generate the same amount of heat? And is that, in turn, different when you have a high-intensity workload that’s short-lived? How do you cool everything down to keep temperatures consistent? Radhakrishnan : Co-packaged optics is trying to solve that problem, to some extent, bringing the silicon photonics into the package, keeping it small for EICs/PICs. They are trying to thermally isolate it. But if you try to simulate the whole thing, the part that will be missing is the transient nature, and that’s what’s really needed. If you try to keep something far off, then the heat is going to take more time to get there, and by the time the next wave comes on an ASIC, the heat will still be there. Even a very small change in temperature can shift the ring oscillator. What’s needed is the ability to simulate the whole thing together in a transient domain to make sure it’s going to function reliably and optically. Being able to simulate one part of a system in a transient domain is key to making sure co-packaged optics is viable and that we can push it forward. Mueth : That’s a good point. The difference in time constants really messes things up. And if you’re doing co-packaged optics, the EIC driver typically would be mounted near or on top of your PIC, so you have heat pollution, which steers your photonics. You’re introducing new stresses, and those stresses have a very big impact on the optical signals — maybe bigger than thermal. You have to know what those trade-offs are, and make sure you’re taking them into consideration so that you’re combining the best of both. Just by moving something, you can make things worse instead of better. SE: And how do you know your thermal sensors are functioning properly all the time? Mueth : You can do that in the calibration process. You can put a sniffing loop inside the photonic PIC, but it makes that incredibly complicated. Ferguson : We can try to move things to reduce some of the thermal that’s built up. But when you’re moving big elements, particularly like what we have in photonics, you’re introducing new stresses. Those have a very big impact on optical signals — maybe bigger than the thermal. So you have to know what those trade-offs are and make sure you’re taking them into consideration so that you’re combining the best of both. Lin : For silicon photonics, you can think about it as a type of analog circuit. When we deal with analog versus digital, the thermal behavior is very different. Digital transistors involve switching current. The current will supply the transistor’s on and off, so the Joule heating effect is not that bad. But for silicon photonics and analog devices, the DC current is always there, and there’s a big swing of signals. That creates current flowing through the interconnects, like a waveguide. It generates a lot of heat, and we need this heat for the CPO to work. That heat is needed to operate the EIC. But what if there are so many heaters together? How do you place them far enough away so that everything can operate, but not create hot spots within the heater area? Stress is another problem that has to be considered for silicon photonics to operate well. SE: Heat can cause warpage. If you put two warped chips together and they’re very thin, you may be able to flatten them, but at the same time you’ve probably lost some ability to dissipate heat due to thinner dies, right? Berg : Thermal variation on a PIC chip generally results in a mismatch of features — much more so than in EIC circuits. If you’re talking about multi-physics and digital twins and surrogate models affiliated with EICs, you essentially can triple that need in photonics ICs because they’re much more sensitive to warpage and thermal gradients. A laser is a heat source that potentially creates a reliability problem. To that end, photonics needs a thermal understanding and a multi-physics confirmation of not only the electrical, mechanical, and thermal, but optical as well. So now you’ve got four solvers that you potentially have to do. It’s a bit more complicated than the electronics, and that’s the reason why photonics has been the next big thing in the semiconductor world for the past 30 years. events.title: Blog Review: Oct. 7
events.summary: Siemens’ Karen Chow, Sheetal Veronica, and Kunjesh Agashiwala explore how CFETs and buried power rails come together to reduce the chip area needed, improve power efficiency, and help meet the high-performance needs of AI accelerators, data centers and mobile processors. Synopsys’ Thomas Andersen says the strongest results come when agentic AI can leverage the company-specific knowledge that makes each engineering organization distinct, such as its methodologies, design history, priorities, best practices, and accumulated experience. Cadence’s Reela Samuel considers what separates agentic AI from traditional and AI-assisted EDA workflows , noting that while individual operations in the loop are not necessarily new, what changes is how those operations can be coordinated. Keysight’s Stephen Douglas urges the industry to start rapid prototyping of the hardest 6G architectural questions as the window narrows to turn promising concepts into mature standards, interoperable products, and deployable systems. Arm’s Francisco Socal introduces AMBA C2C , which extends chiplet connectivity across AXI and CHI with scalable protocol subsets, interoperability, and flexible transport support for fully coherent, advanced heterogeneous compute. SEMI’s Saifi Usmani highlights finalists in the Startups for Sustainable Semiconductors program, which offer solutions from monolithic integrated voltage regulators to wafer defect inspection and characterization to a GPU-native physics simulation platform. Plus, check out the blogs featured in the latest Automotive, Security & AI newsletter : Infineon’s Karthik Rangarajan shows how distributed NVM supports high-endurance telemetry logging, functional safety, and time-sensitive networking where resilience is critical. Rambus’ Vincent van der Leest demonstrates how roots of trust are beginning to assume a broader role as platform security orchestrators. Cadence’s Kartik Hegde looks beyond RTL to a new representation that allows engineers to express intent more intuitively. Synopsys’ Brian Davenport outlines a development flow to ensure that hardware can do its job in the field without being vulnerable to attacks or leakage of private data. Siemens EDA’s Kartik Sahajpal and Prashant Dixit dig into integration and verification challenges in PCIe-over-UCIe systems, including how link-state transitions affect transaction behavior. Imagination’s Alex Pim examines time to first token and inter-token latency, and how they apply to the two main stages of LLM compute — prefill and decode. Keysight’s Marc Witteman contends that compliance with trade restrictions is no longer about proving where a device was built, but about how the product works. ( Supplied: Fei Chang ) Australia was one of the most popular travel destinations during China's week-long national holiday from October 1 to 7, according to a popular travel booking platform. The company reported passengers booking "longer and further trips beyond the region" this year. A Melbourne travel agent says many Chinese tourists now prefer "quality trips" in small groups or going on a road trip by themselves over big group tours. When Fei Chang and her husband landed in the Whitsundays for their holiday, they were shocked to find it filled with Chinese tourists. "At some tourist spots, it felt like I could almost speak Mandarin to everyone," she said. Ms Chang and her husband were among the Chinese tourists who visited Australia over the past week, during China's week-long national day holiday that ends today. This year, the timing of the three-day Mid-Autumn Festival public holiday together with Golden Week from October 1 to 7 gave people 13 days off. Fei Chang and her husband enjoyed visiting beaches in Sydney. ( Supplied: Fei Chang ) Australia was one of the most sought-after destinations for Chinese travellers, according to one of China's popular travel booking platforms Trip.com. The company said people were also taking "longer and further trips beyond the region" this year. International Air Transport Association (IATA) data showed that flight bookings from China to Australia for October 2026 were up 19 per cent compared to October 2025. There were also more than 2.2 million inbound and outbound passengers during the Mid-Autumn Festival, according to China's official immigration data, a 16.8 per cent increase compared to the same holiday last year. Zhang Cheng, a Melbourne travel agent and owner of Great Wall Travel Services, told the ABC that she had received a surge in bookings over the past week. Her agency takes bookings primarily from Chinese-speaking tourists. The number of Chinese tourists in Australia is yet to return to pre-COVID highs. ( Supplied: Fei Chang ) However, Ms Zhang was not sure how many of those tourists were from overseas and how many were from the Chinese-speaking community in Australia. "We are fully booked with two-day tours to the Great Ocean Road," she said. This week, Ms Zhang is taking a group of Chinese-speaking tourists to Canberra for one of the biggest horticultural shows in the Southern Hemisphere. Ms Chang says she was shocked to see so many Chinese tourists in Australia. ( Reuters: David Gray, file ) China was Australia's second-largest inbound tourist market in 2025, according to Tourism Research Australia. In 2025 , Australia saw 1.04 million visitors from China, a 17 per cent increase year-on-year. However, this was still below the 1.4 million visitors from China pre-COVID, in 2019. Ms Zhang said before the pandemic, people tended to travel in big groups. But they now prefer "quality trips" in small groups or going on road trip by themselves, she said. Chinese guided-tour groups sometimes operate under the Approved Destination Status (ADS) scheme, which is a bilateral agreement that facilitates group tours from China to Australia, organised by approved agencies. The program was paused during COVID and resumed in 2023. More than 300,000 tourists reportedly joined an ADS group tour in 2019 financial year, according to Austrade data. In the 2026 financial year, the number of visitors on ADS group trips dropped to 70,205.

events.title: Mint unveils new coins chronicling iconic Australian inventions
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Royal Australian Mint unveils new coins featuring celebrated Australian inventions A jaffle maker coin is part of the Royal Australian Mint's new Bright Ideas collection. ( Supplied: Royal Australian Mint ) What do a jaffle maker, a baby safety capsule and a black box have in common? Not only are they Australian inventions, but they will soon feature on $1 coins as part of the Royal Australian Mint's new Bright Ideas collection. The collection chronicles five of Australia's most decorated inventions, including the stump jump plough, jaffle maker, black box flight recorder, baby safety capsule and high-speed Wireless LAN (WLAN) technology. The Safe-n-Sound baby safety capsule was invented in 1984 as a safety precaution for infants. ( Supplied: Royal Australian Mint ) Mint chief executive Emily Martin said the coins gave Australians "a chance to stop, look again and celebrate the people who thought differently". "I've used four of the five inventions celebrated in Bright Ideas without necessarily stopping to think about the Australian ingenuity behind them," she said. The stump jump plough, designed in 1876, became a cornerstone of farming technology. ( Supplied: Royal Australian Mint ) One of the five coin designs features the stump jump plough, a piece of machinery that revolutionised the way farmers tended to their land. It was designed in 1876 by South Australian farmer Richard Smith and was adopted worldwide, hailed as a cornerstone of farming technology. In 1949, Dr Ernest Smithers invented the jaffle maker, which went on to become a classic culinary staple in many Australian kitchens. Appliance giant Breville later re-imagined the device into an electronic toaster, cementing its position in modern gastronomic Australia. The black box flight recorder, which is vibrant orange in colour, was invented in 1953 by an Australian scientist. ( Supplied: Royal Australian Mint ) A few years later, Defence scientist Dr David Warren invented the black box flight recorder, which collect data from cockpits and help investigators assess the causes of plane crashes. Adelaide trio Bill Bowtell, Bob Heath and Colin Nagel founded the Safe-n-Sound baby safety capsule in 1984 in response to flailing safety precautions for infants travelling in cars. The final invention featuring in the collection came about in the 1990s, when scientists from the CSIRO helped develop WLAN technology, which allowed devices to connect with each other without being tied to cables. The invention went on to pave the groundwork for Wi-fi. WLAN, a precursor to Wi-fi technology, was developed by the CSIRO. ( Supplied: Royal Australian Mint ) The collection has five $1 coins, each featuring one of the inventions. Also available for purchase is a $2 proof coin featuring all five of the inventions in its design. The coins will be available from Thursday, October 8, from the Royal Australian Mint in Canberra and participating newsXpress stores around the country. events.title: Iran war energy price shock large but contained so far, IMF chief says
events.summary: The head of the International Monetary Fund has said the energy price shock driven by the US- Iran war has so far been “large but contained”, but warned that energy demand could lead to further pressure. “Even if the war in the Gulf were to end soon, the problem of high energy prices would likely persist for some time,” managing director Kristalina Georgieva said in prepared remarks in Singapore ahead of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings. This year's gathering, held in Bangkok, comes as supply disruptions from the war in the Middle East pile on to inflationary pressures, potentially leading to higher interest rates for advanced economies. The Federal Reserve and European Central Bank have already begun to raise their key rates, with the Bank of England expected to join them next month. Higher energy prices and rising debt levels have also driven global borrowing costs to their highest levels in decades. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury, a benchmark for global borrowing costs, traded at 5.307 per cent as recently on Monday, its highest level since 2002. That pressure has also spread to markets in other advanced economies including in Japan, France, Germany and the UK. Oil producers in the Middle East are racing to establish alternative routes to bring their exports to the markets. The UAE is fast-tracking construction of its West-East Pipeline , which is expected to double export capacity through Fujairah by the time its expansion is completed in 2027. Saudi Arabia has rerouted its crude through the East-West Pipeline . The seven-day moving average for crude exports from the Gulf was 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared to the average 18 million bpd that passed through the region in the 12 months before the Iran war began, according to ship tracking firm Kpler. The latest figures included transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Ms Georgieva had credited the Gulf Co-operation Council's efforts to reroute energy supplies for preventing a larger shock to the global economy during a meeting with the bloc's finance ministers and central bankers in Bahrain last week. She also said the IMF anticipates the GCC economy will contract this year, adding that the region is expected to face a strong recovery next year, conditional on the normalisation of shipping. A separate report from the World Bank released on Tuesday said GCC economies will contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its April forecast. Meanwhile, continued supply disruptions in liquefied natural gas will hit buyers in Europe and Asia particularly hard, Ms Georgieva said, noting price pressures could further build with winter approaching and reserves dwindling. AI revolution is here In her address, the IMF chief also used her address to urge governments to embark on policies to unlock the productive gains under artificial intelligence . Ms Georgieva described the global economy as one being pulled in two directions, with the positive demand shock from AI partially offsetting the economic fallout from the US-Iran conflict. “Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries’ relative fortunes in the world economy,” she said. Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here, rapidly becoming a key driver of countries’ relative fortunes in the world economy IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva In the US, the AI buildout is shaping up to become the largest investment drive in the country's history. Analysts at Brookings anticipate AI investment in data centres, infrastructure, chips and other equipment will total $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032, or an average of 3.63 per cent of US GDP per year. The broad S&P 500 hit a fresh record-high of 7,800 on Tuesday driven by renewed AI enthusiasm. But with fears of an AI bubble also fomenting, Ms Georgieva said countries should adopt regulation and supervision as a “first line of defence” to prevent a far-reaching shock if AI earnings fall short. The Trump administration has recently adopted a defensive posture of AI amid a growing domestic backlash against the data centre buildout ahead of November’s midterm elections. US President Donald Trump has taken a light regulatory touch on AI advancement and repeatedly expressed his desire to beat China in the global AI race. Countries in the Gulf are seeking to advance large-scale acceleration of AI. The UAE targets to have AI contribute 20 per cent of its non-oil GDP by 2031. Ms Georgieva said AI could deliver up to a half percentage point of additional world growth – or “adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy” – annually. “Yet as this drives forward today’s AI economies, it largely bypasses most others, increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe,” she said.

events.title: Half the harvest, twice the bills: how drought hit farms
events.summary: The hottest summer on record, the longest drought, the worst harvest. West Country farmers are counting the cost of a "terrible summer", as one put it. The wheat harvest on Charles Day's family farm in Gloucestershire was cut in half. "It's just soul-destroying," he says. Dairy farmers had to rip open silage clamps stored up for the winter to feed the cattle as the grass failed. Sarah Godwin calculates it cost her family's Wiltshire farm "over £100,000". She says "it's shocking". I spent the summer watching farmers install showers for cows , watch their cauliflowers burn to a crisp in the heat, and search for apples in cider orchards reduced to a tenth of their normal crop. So now the harvest is home, just how bad was it? Charles Day's family farm in Gloucestershire lost half its wheat harvest to the drought Buy a loaf of bread and there's a good chance it started in the fields of Charles Day's family farm in north Gloucestershire. "I love harvest," the fourth generation farmer tells me. "It's a whole year's work coming to fruition." But 2026 was brutal. The crops were looking "fantastic" in April, he told me. Then in June, the rain stopped and "the sun just stole our yield". Throughout the crucial weeks of June and July, there was no rain at all. Wheat grains shrivelled instead of fattening, and the yield plummeted. Official figures estimate the total UK cereal harvest was the lowest on record , external , wheat down about three million tonnes, or 11% according to the Agricultural and Horticultural Development Board (AHDB). Anthony Hopkins, AHDB director of cereals and oilseeds, says: "At a time of high input costs, arable farmers in the worst-affected areas are really feeling the financial pressure right now." Shrivelled by drought, the UK wheat harvest was the lowest on record But in the South West, it was much hotter and the impact far worse. When the combines went out on Charles Day's family farm, they gathered a harvest "about 50% down, sometimes more". "It's just soul-destroying," he adds. Across the South West, Tom Collins, who speaks for the NFU in Wiltshire, says most cereal farmers had seen harvests down "at least 30%". Spring barley and beans were more than 50% down, he adds, particularly badly hit by the drought. "Most farmers will give this harvest 3 out of 10", he adds. "They're pretty depressed." Put some butter on your bread, or cheese, and that is probably from the West Country's other farmers - dairy producers. But unlike the wheat harvest, the amount of milk produced this summer barely fell. Total production is down just 4.5% , external , according to the ADHB. "That's because we have to feed our cows, and milk them, whatever the weather," explains Sarah Godwin. Her family raise dairy cows west of Chippenham, selling their milk to a major supermarket. Sarah Godwin calculates the drought cost her family's dairy farm more than £100,000 in extra feed for the cows The Cotswolds was badly hit by the drought, leaving grazing pastures brown and without any nutrition for the cows. So like many farmers, the Godwins had to open their sileage planned for the winter and buy in feed to boost their cows diets. "Altogether it cost us around £100,000," Godwin explains. "We also had a drop in production yields, that's around £20,000. "On top of that, cows suffered more lameness, lower fertility, more mastitis. They really did not enjoy the heat." The family spent £15,000 installing new sprinkler systems and huge fans to cool the cattle in their sheds when they sheltered from the heat outside. All vital for animal welfare, but more costs to the business. Tom Kimber said droughts and floods are becoming "far more frequent" on his Somerset farm Even the normally lush fields of Somerset withered in the heat. Tom Kimber's family have farmed near Charlton Musgrove in south Somerset, in the heart of England's most productive grazing land. They run 250 dairy cows on their own grass, cutting sileage for the winter months. By September, they would normally have three large clamps of sileage ready for winter. This year, they have only cut two, and had to raid one throughout July and August, to make up for the lack of grass. But sadly, Tom Kimber is getting used to what was once freak weather. "This is the fourth drought in eight years now, so you barely financially get over the last one and you're hit with another one. It's becoming far more frequent, these events. "It's incredibly difficult this constant lurching between one extreme to the other, that's what keeps you awake at night." Climate scientists are clear that weather like this is the new normal. "What we used to think of as extreme weather, we increasingly consider as normal," says Mike Kendon, a climate scientist at the Met Office. In Gloucestershire, Charles Day's family have a rare asset: a lake. Fed by a local river, it fills through the winter and then can be used in the summer.

events.title: Why parents need to be involved in the money conversation with their children
events.summary: (From left) Najwa Chua Ai Xin, UOB Heartbeat volunteer Ho Ying Ying and ST reporter Chor Khieng Yuit searching for frozen food on Najwa's grocery list during a July 22 shopping run. Shopping with real money helps children learn budgeting and financial decision-making through practical experience, as shown by a Primary 6 student managing a $50 budget effectively. Interactive activities like Curiosity Cove provide financial lessons but require parental involvement to make the learning meaningful and encourage discussions on needs versus wants. Digital tools like the Smart Buddy app help parents monitor children’s spending and foster daily conversations about money habits, enhancing financial literacy at home. SINGAPORE – Shopping with real money helps children become more financially savvy. This thought crossed my mind while volunteering on a shopping trip with UOB Heartbeat volunteers on July 22. I was paired with UOB’s Ho Ying Ying and Najwa Chua, 12, who has participated in these outings since she was eight. We began by reviewing the shopping list that Najwa had put together with her parents, before taking a short walk to FairPrice at Rivervale Plaza. Najwa went about getting the items on her list: bananas, grapes, 30 eggs, chicken and bread. Since the chicken was on sale, she picked up two packets. After all, her family loves curry chicken. However, she had to forgo her favourite Lay’s sour cream potato chips because they did not fit her budget. Instead, she opted for two packets of FairPrice house-brand chips, which were on sale. Najwa tried to keep a running tab in her head, but got overwhelmed as her shopping basket filled up, and she asked to borrow Ho’s phone to check the final sum. Her careful budgeting left her enough to buy a bottle of Thai sweet chilli sauce that her parents love. Her final bill came to $49.98, within the $50 she was allocated. It was clear that Najwa actively looked out for deals and knew which brands offered more bang for her buck. She shared that she had picked up budgeting skills and practical tips from the volunteers during previous shopping stints. A spokesperson from Children’s Wishing Well, the charity leading this financial literacy initiative, said that these hands-on experiences and interactions with the volunteers have helped Najwa become more confident in making spending decisions. Today, she knows how to manage her money and adapt her choices to stay within her budget – and not just on these organised shopping runs. Her mother has even entrusted her with the family’s weekly provisions, allowing her to head to the supermarket after school to buy the items on her own. Najwa Chua Ai Xin and her father Chua Peng Huat with her grocery purchases and receipt. Hearing how much Najwa has grown, I thought: “Why not try this out on my daughter?” She is in Primary 2 and will turn eight later in 2026. I started by increasing her daily allowance for school meals to $5, which she can use for both her morning snack and lunch. The experiment is still a work in progress. While her school has taught her about needs and wants, she still tries to justify her wants as a need. Once, she spent $2.50 at the bookshop on a mechanical pencil and pencil leads. When I asked why she bought them when she had normal pencils, she replied, “I need the mechanical pencil to write.” My daughter chose to spend on her perceived “need”. With only $2.50 left for the day, she spent $1.80 on two cheese sticks for her morning snack and decided to skip lunch – which to me is a “need”. Hoping to drive home the “needs versus wants” lesson through play, my husband and I decided to take our daughter to explore Curiosity Cove. During our visit, my husband observed that the financial literacy elements at Curiosity Cove are more of a sideline, and the educational concepts are relegated to “secondary amusement” for the children after they finish playing. Venturing outside Curiosity Cove, we spotted some activity stations around the Mandai area. One station focusing on needs and wants required children to build a virtual buggy. To do so, they had to decide which car parts they needed to buy and which parts they could skip. At the Super Savers Trail at Curiosity Cove, one of the outdoor stations taught children about needs versus wants. Another station touched on savings and interest. By shifting a marker on a slider board, children can see how interest grows as their savings increase – so the more they save, the more they earn. However, these displays would not automatically spur any meaningful discussion or learning unless parents step in to talk about the concepts, using the posters to convey the financial lessons to their children. A simple visualisation of how interest grows as children save more. Banks are offering digital tools to keep that dialogue going. Nelson Neo, DBS’ head of retail banking and head of POSB, noted that the Smart Buddy app enables parents to keep tabs on their children’s spending.

events.title: Woolworths fuel levy surcharge nearly triple pre-Iran war level
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Check-out pain fears as Woolworths increases freight fuel levy surcharge Woolworths has increased its freight fuel levy again amid high diesel costs. ( Supplied: Woolworths ) Woolworths has increased the fuel levy charged through its logistics network to food and grocery suppliers to almost triple its pre-Iran war level as diesel costs continue to climb. The fuel levy surcharges have increased for metro and regional areas, affecting some of the country's largest food and grocery manufacturers. This includes Primary Connect, Woolworths' logistics arm, which transports goods from suppliers to distribution centres and stores across the country. The business manages freight for more than 1,000 grocery producers, including brands such as Sanitarium, PepsiCo, Ingham's and Arnott's. The fuel levy for metro areas recently rose from 17.47 per cent to 19.88 per cent. In regional Australia, the levy increased from 44.20 per cent to 50.30 per cent. University of Sydney supply chain management professor Rico Merkert said the increases were not unusual when diesel prices rose sharply. "Fuel levies are commonly used in freight markets to manage fuel-price volatility," Professor Merkert said. "Many transport operators use surcharges that can be adjusted periodically rather than renegotiating contracts every time fuel costs move. "If diesel costs rise sharply, it is economically reasonable for freight providers and retailers to increase fuel surcharges to recover those additional operating costs." Rico Merkert says transport costs are only one component of the final retail price at the supermarket. ( Supplied ) Prior to the Iran war, the fuel levy Woolworths charged in metro areas was 7.28 per cent. Within weeks of the war, it had risen to 12.47 per cent. The regional fuel levy has jumped by more than 172 per cent since March, when it was 18.44 per cent. "We operate a large distribution network that includes independently owned and operated transport providers, and we are committed to supporting our transport partners, just as other industry players are doing," a Woolworths spokesperson said. "To ensure they can keep their trucks on the road and get products on shelves in stores, we increased our review of the fuel levy to twice monthly in March to reflect the challenges they still face." Experts believe the increase in freight costs are likely to be shared across the supply chain. "My prediction is that consumers and suppliers will get the worst end of the deal of the fuel surcharge increase," said Medo Pournader, senior lecturer of supply chain management at the University of Melbourne. University of Sydney professor Ben Fahimnia, who is also a specialist on the issue, said continually pushing rising logistics costs back onto suppliers is not a sustainable solution. "They have absorbed some of the costs initially and have tried to find savings elsewhere, but there is a limit to what businesses can absorb," Professor Fahimnia said. While Professor Merkert agrees, he believes the effect is unlikely to be one-for-one. "Higher fuel levies can eventually contribute to higher retail prices and hence inflation, but freight is only one element of the final shelf price, so consumers would not necessarily see a direct or proportional increase at the check-out," he said. Rising fuel prices have played a significant part in Australia's inflation rate, which recently jumped to 4 per cent in August. Transport was the second-largest contributor to the annual inflation figure as a result of higher automotive fuel prices. The odds of the Reserve Bank lifting interest rates in November have fallen sharply after the latest consumer price index (CPI) came in lower than expected, with headline inflation up 4 per cent in the year to August. On a monthly basis, automotive fuel prices rose 14.8 per cent in August, compared with a rise of 7.5 per cent in July. In a press conference after last week's monetary policy decision, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock warned businesses were preparing to pass on higher fuel costs if necessary. "The longer it [the war] lasts, if businesses were thinking, "Oh, look, it'll come off, I won't pass on costs," the longer it goes, the more likely it is that businesses will just try to pass through the cost increases," Ms Bullock said.

events.title: Logan mayor warns of backyard 'slums' as council slashes granny flat tax
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Logan City Council to slash granny flat infrastructure charges despite fears of backyard 'slums' Granny flats will be cheaper to build under the new infrastructure charges scheme. ( Supplied: Housing Industry Association ) Logan City Council has voted to halve its infrastructure charges on one-bedroom granny flats. Several councillors fear the change will incentivise landlords to create more backyard "slums". The new rules are expected to come into effect in November this year. Granny flats will be $13,500 cheaper to build in Logan after controversial new rules were passed by Logan City Council today. The council voted to halve its $27,000 infrastructure charge for one-bedroom secondary dwellings to incentivise new granny flats. Logan Mayor Jon Raven opposed the move, saying it would be exploited by landlords to fit more renters onto small backyard lots. He blamed laws introduced by the Queensland government in 2022 that allowed property owners to rent granny flats to non-family members. Jon Raven says granny flats should be for families, not property investors. ( ABC News: Lucy Loram ) Cr Raven said this was a "loophole" which allowed property investors to build more developments than they would otherwise be allowed to build. He said Logan's previous attempts to incentivise more secondary dwellings caused severe suburban overcrowding due to these laws. "We saw what happened with auxiliary units where you could put a two-bedroom secondary dwelling on the same site as a three-bedroom primary dwelling," Cr Raven said. "We got slums, and we can still see them in parts of the city today, because we can't remove them once they've been approved. "Savvy investors will find a way to exploit the discount as best as possible." Councillor Nathan St Ledger supported the move, saying more families wanted to move in together due to the growing unaffordability of housing. He said council's charges were "bloody expensive" and preventing more granny flats from being built. He said this would bolster the supply of affordable housing in Logan, even if much of it was run by unscrupulous property investors. "You've got rocks in your head if you think people aren't going to do it," Cr St Ledger said. "I completely understand the problem it could cause … but what about the residents who want to do the right thing?" Under Logan's current rules, infrastructure charges can be waived entirely if the granny flat is connected to the primary house and is used for family members. The changes are expected to commence in November this year. The motion passed with the support of eight councillors, with three opposing and one abstaining. The councillors who opposed were Mindy Rusell, Paul Jackson, and Cr Raven, with Teresa Lane abstaining. events.title: Coffee prices at some cafes rise by 10pc after RBA card surcharge ban
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Coffee prices at some cafes rise 10pc after Reserve Bank imposes card surcharge ban Topic: Business, Economics and Finance Hospitality businesses have raised prices in response to the surcharge ban. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross ) Cafes and restaurants have begun lifting prices in response to the RBA's surcharge ban. The ban was intended to lower prices, but the price hikes appear to be an unintended consequence. Former RBA official Luci Ellis says the ban is unlikely to have a significant impact on inflation. A ban on card surcharges has resulted in some cafe owners raising the price of their coffee. About 17 per cent of cafes are now charging more for a flat white, compared with prices prior to October 1, when the Reserve Bank's ban took effect. That is according to Small Flat White, an online platform that tracks coffee prices across more than 1,500 cafes. Typically, the increase was 50 cents, or almost 10 per cent of the coffee's price, which is much higher than the typical 0.5 to 1.5 per cent surcharge consumers used to pay on their credit or debit card transactions. Avtar Singh says most small businesses are operating on thin margins. ( ABC News ) Not every hospitality business has raised its prices in the immediate aftermath of the ban. Avtar Singh, owner of a Thai restaurant in Hobart, said he was currently absorbing the cost of the surcharges but eventually would have to raise prices. "The government needs to understand small businesses are already at a very thin margin," he told the ABC. "If you squeeze it any further, it'll come to a point where doing business is very, very difficult." Wes Lambert says the card surcharge ban has led to unintended results. ( ABC News ) Most cafes or restaurants have raised prices in some way, either by raising menu prices or increasing weekend or public holiday surcharges, said Wes Lambert, chief executive of the Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association. "Increasing prices can always affect demand, so that certainly is an unintended consequence that the RBA could not have predicted, because they believed that prices would only go up 0.1 per cent," he said. Mr Lambert said some businesses had started taking cash-only payments or accepting bank transfers. "They should have known better that inflation was going to remain pesky and that this ban would come online during a cost of living crisis and potentially should have delayed the ban during this high inflationary and high interest environment." The RBA has said the previous system was no longer working as intended, with surcharges increasingly difficult for consumers to avoid. The central bank has also said only about 16 per cent of businesses were surcharging and the ban was designed to reduce card acceptance costs, particularly for small businesses. Reforms unlikely to affect interest rates Luci Ellis says the changes will not have a significant impact on inflation. ( ABC News ) If the surcharge ban results in higher inflation, that effect would likely be temporary and have no effect on interest rates, according to Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis. "Previously surcharges were imposed to reflect the cost of accepting certain types of payment; that's now been bundled into the price, so some business have increased their prices, but that's a one-off, not inherently inflationary," she said. "Most of the reports we've seen of prices increasing … more than what the surcharge had been were in hospitality. "There are plenty of other inflationary forces going round, including the pass-through of high energy costs onto other prices that the Reserve Bank's going to be much more focused on." Surcharge bans are supposed to save consumers money but retailers say they're being forced to put prices up and are finding ways around the reforms. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver agreed. "The overall macroeconomic impact from higher prices flowing from the ban on surcharges may not be that significant," he said. Mr Oliver said many large businesses were already not charging surcharges. "It's really just an issue for small businesses, but there still may be some upwards boost to inflation, albeit minor," he said. "In theory, the RBA may just look through it as it's a one-off impact, but it may be hard to disentangle a general rise in prices from the impact of the surcharge versus other factors." The Reserve Bank declined to comment.

events.title: Capital Group secures ADGM licence to expand Middle East operations
events.summary: Capital Group, which manages $3.6 trillion in assets, has secured a licence from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Abu Dhabi's ADGM to operate as a regulated investment manager and expand operations across the region. The development comes after the company announced plans to set up its first Middle East office in Abu Dhabi in May, with Capital Group relocating associates from North America, Europe and Asia to support clients in the region. The company will now be able to conduct trading, investment management and distribution activities within Abu Dhabi's financial centre, it said in a statement on Wednesday. “Establishing a regulated presence in Abu Dhabi brings us closer to our clients and to the investment opportunities across the Middle East, a region where we have been active for many years,” said Benno Klingenberg-Timm, head of Abu Dhabi office and head of institutional for Europe and Asia at Capital Group. “From day one, we will have a meaningful presence, with on-the-ground investment, operational and client-facing capabilities,” he added. The move reflects “our confidence in the region’s long-term growth”, Mr Klingenberg-Timm said. Capital Group’s expansion adds to the growing number of global investment firms setting up in Abu Dhabi. ADGM , the largest international financial centre in the Middle East and Africa by number of active licences, has continued to attract global institutions, despite the Iran war. New Mountain Capital, an alternative investment firm based in New York, said on Tuesday it was opening an office in ADGM to strengthen its presence in the Middle East. Founded in 1999, New Mountain has about $60 billion in assets under management across its private equity, credit and net lease investment strategies. “We have been privileged to work with many leading investors in the region for years and establishing a local presence will allow us to deepen those relationships while building new partnerships over time,” said Adam Weinstein, president and chief operating officer. Last week, Eurazeo, a European asset manager with €40 billion ($45.2 billion) in assets under management, opened an office in ADGM . Global private markets firm Pantheon last week opened its first Abu Dhabi office in ADGM to expand its presence in the Middle East and tap growing demand from investors across the Gulf. A base in Abu Dhabi provides global investors and money managers with opportunities to expand regional operations and work closely with some of the world's biggest sovereign wealth funds, as well as large family offices and institutional partners. Other high-profile companies that the UAE capital has attracted in recent months include private credit lender Blue Owl Capital, tech-focused US company Vista Equity Partners, the world’s largest listed hedge fund Man Group, Barings, Bain Capital, Cantor and Swiss derivative investment company Adapt Investment Managers. Collectively, asset managers that established operations in ADGM in the first half of the year oversee more than $2.1 trillion in global assets under management. Capital Group’s “decision reflects the strength of Abu Dhabi’s financial ecosystem and ADGM’s growing position as a leading international financial centre for global institutions seeking long-term opportunities across the region”, said Ahmed Al Zaabi, chairman of ADGM.

events.title: Grocery runs on a budget and outdoor missions: How S’pore banks make financial literacy fun for kids
events.summary: UOB Heartbeat volunteers Derrick Sin (left) and Jane Lai (right) with Aaron Kishen Arun Pandian Pillai, 11, and Najwa Chua Ai Xin, 12. Singapore banks teach financial literacy to primary school children through hands-on programmes like shopping trips and interactive play spaces. UOB and OCBC participate in grocery shopping trips, helping children from lower-income families make budgeting and spending decisions. DBS offers educational play areas like POSB Forestlands, combining stories and activities to make money management fun, while involving parents in the learning journey. SINGAPORE – Every two to three months, Aaron Kishen Arun Pandian Pillai, 11, and his brother Leon Shrishen, nine, join UOB volunteers on shopping trips organised by Children’s Wishing Well. Each child gets a $50 FairPrice voucher, sponsored by the bank, to purchase groceries and household essentials under the Fresh Groceries for Every Student’s Home (FRESH) programme. Children’s Wishing Well started FRESH in 2019 to teach financial literacy to children and youth from low-income families. The charity also equips these children and youth with other essential life skills, such as career readiness and personal development, through its other enrichment programmes. To stretch their dollars, the children must compare prices, prioritise needs and make their own purchasing decisions. The initiative gives the children a chance to learn more about budgeting and apply what they have learnt in school about managing their expenses. It is one of a slate of hands-on programmes supported by local banks to reinforce the lessons on saving, spending and budgeting that children are taught in primary school. UOB has partnered Children’s Wishing Well on this initiative since 2022. The July 22 shopping trip that The Straits Times tagged along on was 11-year-old Aaron’s eighth outing with volunteers from UOB Heartbeat, the bank’s flagship volunteering programme. (Clockwise from left) Aaron Kishen Arun Pandian Pillai, UOB Heartbeat volunteers Lim Gene Harn and Derrick Sin and Aaron's brother Leon Shrishen Arun Pandian Pillai discussing how to de-conflict their shopping lists. Proclaiming himself the family’s “household planner”, he remarked: “My brother will buy the wrong brand, so I have to keep an eye on him.” Aaron managed his budget tightly that day, spending $50.02, including $3.91 on sweets – just under the $4 allowed for snacks. “My school organises workshops for us to learn,” Aaron shared. “I picked up budgeting and spending tips at the workshops, which I now apply to my shopping trips.” Besides the two brothers, there were eight other child beneficiaries, each paired with a UOB volunteer. Among them was Derrick Sin, vice-president of group retail (risk), who was a volunteer on the trip for the first time. Sin, who was paired with Leon, recounted how the young boy initially wanted to buy a bunch of grapes that cost nearly $10. Knowing it would use up a fifth of his total funds, he hesitated. But after further thought, Leon chose the healthy fruit option over an unhealthy Coca-Cola drink and gave up a few other items as well. “He was able to make that trade-off himself,” said Sin, who also observed how Aaron managed his own shopping expenses. When the older boy’s assigned volunteer forgot to track the price of each item in their basket, the 11-year-old stepped up and went to the counter to verify the tally. Watching Aaron take charge, Sin was impressed. He recalled thinking, “This boy really knows what he is doing.” Jane Lai, UOB senior vice-president of talent and development, noted that the children are forced to make choices during these shopping trips and consider what they must give up if they choose one item over another. The July event was her third time volunteering, and she was paired with eight-year-old Jariss . At one point, the girl felt torn between a Korean brand of instant noodles that cost more than $8, which her sister likes, and the cheaper Indomie alternative her family had asked her to purchase. She picked the more affordable option, leaving her enough cash for a $2 snack. UOB Heartbeat volunteer Jane Lai (left) pointing out the bleach on Jariss’ shopping list. Exposing children to real-life situations builds early financial awareness to ensure that they become savvy consumers, Lai said. She mused that she should have given her two children, now in their twenties, similar hands-on shopping experiences when they were younger. “In hindsight, I would have pushed a lot more of this (financial) discipline,” she reflected. “Protected kids like ours tend to be less resilient as they grow up.” To date, UOB Heartbeat volunteers have participated in about 50 grocery shopping sessions, which are organised twice a month, supporting more than 700 children.

events.title: Abu Dhabi to upgrade Tamm app as it pursues AI-native government goal
events.summary: Abu Dhabi plans to launch the latest version of the Tamm app in December as it pursues its goal of becoming the world’s first fully AI-native government, a senior executive has said. The refreshed Tamm 5.0 app, which would be introduced at the Gitex Global technology exhibition in Dubai, promises "increasingly intelligent" services, Department of Government Enablement director general Ruba Al Hassan told The National at the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. Those services are to also be more "proactive and personalised", but they still have to remain "simple and trusted", said Ms Al Hassan, who oversees strategic affairs and future foresight at the department. Tamm currently has about 4.7 million users, having grown by more than 1.5 million in just a year. About 90 per cent of its transactions are finalised within a day, the latest data from the DGE shows. Tamm 5.0 would be "another step" in the evolution from a digital government to an AI-native government, "moving towards a model where government increasingly understands context ... anticipates needs and helps people achieve things more easily", Ms Al Hassan said. The DGE did not reveal the specific changes to Tamm or new services that are to be introduced. "It’s time for the next phase, which is about making the experience even more seamless and reducing the effort required from residents, businesses and visitors," she added. The DGE remains "focused" on its goal of transforming the capital's government services into a fully AI-native platform by next year, Ms Al Hassan said. The agency is "moving with urgency, but building responsibly", she added. "We are already seeing that tangible progress across government, not only through individual AI applications, but through the foundations that make AI-native government possible," she said, referring to data, infrastructure, digital services, workforce capability and governance. "The question is not whether we can deploy AI faster, it’s whether we can create lasting value at scale, so we believe we are on the right path to do that." Abu Dhabi is boosting tech use across the emirate under its digital strategy, which focuses on five key enablers – one of them being the use of AI across public services. Despite the persisting challenges – especially issues involving AI models going rogue and compromising other websites – the DGE is seeking to ensure the safety and reliability of such systems. "We’re seeing a lot of noise in the global AI conversation. New models are constantly coming out, capabilities are getting better quickly and everyone’s focused on what might happen in the future," Ms Al Hassan said. "Our focus is slightly different. We’re interested in where AI delivers practical value today ... we also believe trust is critical. People need confidence that AI is being used responsibly, transparently and with clear human accountability." Educating users is also a key part of the DGE's mandate, she said. "As AI improves, the value of human judgment actually also increases. People need to know how to work effectively with AI, challenge AI outputs and make better decisions," she said. "When it comes to AI, the skill won’t be coding, it will be maintaining judgment." 'Most powerful generation' Meanwhile, Omar Al Olama, Minister of State for AI, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, described the present generation as the "most powerful in human history", while calling for more responsible use of AI. "The reason ... is because you have the intelligence of every single generation, every single human that has lived, that has actually produced something that has lasted ... the content and knowledge are at your fingertips," he told the conference. "And you don't just have raw knowledge. You're actually able to leverage intelligence to do something with it through agentic AI," he added, referring to the class designed to make autonomous decisions and act with minimal human supervision. "This is the time for a new ambitious generation ... people might not believe in your ideas, to wield these tools to create something that others can't see or don't believe is possible. It's a calling."

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Redmond explains how VMs die, but not when you can expect that to happen Microsoft is about to let Copilot loose on your file system 3 hours ago Dutch tax office ditches Microsoft 365 cloud for on-premises alternative 13 hours ago Microsoft extends the Outlook naughty step with two more file types 1 day ago Classic Outlook clings to stale search results as Microsoft works on a fix 1 day ago Windows 11 market share creeps upwards as cost of staying on Windows 10 set to double 2 days ago Microsoft has updated the lifecycle of an Azure instance, without offering any information on how long it takes for an instance type to expire. Redmond’s “enhanced lifecycle” landed in late September in a post that explains the four phases in the life of a cloudy VM: Current – VMs are recommended for new deployments, are available in many regions, and receive standard maintenance and support; Extended – Still supported, but may be subject to usage quotas and unspecified “changes to purchasing options and pricing.” Microsoft recommends planning a move to Current VMs. End of Life – VMs are still supported but are only available to existing customers and you may not be able to get more of the instances you want. Once VMs reach this stage, Microsoft wants you “actively” working to shift workloads onto Current or Extended VMs. Retired – Unsupported but not quite dead. Microsoft says VMs in this phase are no longer available and have been “deallocated” – Azure-speak for not having an IP address and being dormant, with data preserved. Customers can’t provision the instance types. Microsoft’s post explains that the company defined this lifecycle because it is “committed to helping you navigate these infrastructure transitions and take advantage of the next wave of innovation.” The post includes many mentions of “modernization” – the process of moving to Current Azure instance types. “As Azure continues to advance, our commitment is to make change predictable, transparent, and supported through clear lifecycle guidance, early visibility, and practical help to modernize with confidence,” the post states. The mention of “predictable” change led The Register to wonder if the lifecycle has a predictable cadence that means users can expect that instance types will remain in “Current” status for a certain number of years. We asked Microsoft if its Azure instance lifecycles are timed, and a spokesperson sent the following comment: “As Azure continues to innovate, we regularly evolve our infrastructure to give customers access to newer technologies and capabilities. As part of our updated Azure Virtual Machines lifecycle, we will continue to provide customers with advance notice when select older-generation VM series enter the End of Life stage. We’re giving customers time, guidance and resources to plan their transition to the current VM generations, while continuing to support Azure VMs through their lifecycle in alignment with the policies we published.” The spokesperson added that Microsoft customers are “notified directly about their specific VM retirements.” For what it’s worth, Microsoft publishes retirement announcements for Azure services . The company has also previously revealed it runs Azure servers for six years. It is unclear if the new Azure lifecycle is tied to that hardware retirement schedule. What is clear is that Microsoft wants Azure customers to regularly consider moving to its latest instance types. That’s a reasonable suggestion given that newer VMs will likely use more powerful processors. There’s also plenty of upside for Microsoft because more recent silicon typically offers more cores per die, and better performance-per-watt. Microsoft therefore gets greater processor density with lower energy consumption, which lowers its operating costs. Let’s see if Redmond’s lifecycle tweaks also see it pass on those savings.

events.title: Kenya confirms its first Ebola case and death in a man who traveled from Congo
events.summary: A Kenyan citizen who had been living in Congo before returning to Nairobi over the weekend has become Kenya’s first confirmed case of Ebola and the country’s first death from the disease in the fast-moving outbreak NAIROBI, Kenya -- A Kenyan citizen who had been living in Congo before returning to Nairobi over the weekend became Kenya’s first confirmed case of Ebola and the country’s first death from the disease in the fast-moving outbreak , authorities said Tuesday, sparking urgent contact-tracing efforts to try to contain the spread of the virus. The man had been residing in Congo for the past seven years and fell ill about a month ago. He was treated at various hospitals before traveling by road to Kampala, Uganda, where he boarded a flight to the Kenyan capital, arriving on Saturday afternoon, Health Minister Aden Duale said. Health authorities in Kenya have placed the country’s border points on high alert and are monitoring for possible additional cases. Duale said that the man had been isolated and treated at Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for the Ebola virus and died late Monday. Ebola is highly contagious and spreads in the human population through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The current outbreak was declared in mid-May, months after it had been spreading in a remote part of eastern Congo. At least 8,400 cases have been recorded, including more than 4,000 deaths, according to government data, making it the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in history. Kenya has never had an outbreak of Ebola, according to the Kenya Medical Research Institute. The country hosts a United States-funded isolation center for American citizens exposed to Ebola to quarantine for 21 days before traveling back to the U.S. The isolation facility faced legal battles and deadly protests by locals who feared it was exposing them to the virus. Kenya is the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in eastern Congo in mid-May. Uganda has recorded 20 cases and France one. Before Kenya reported its case, there had been no active cases outside Congo since Uganda declared its outbreak over in late August. Duale said that 28 contacts of the man who had returned on Saturday, including family members and health workers who cared for the patient, had been identified. Another 23 passengers on the flight and four crew members, who traveled on the same plane from Uganda, were being traced. The contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be released after testing negative for the virus, said the ministry’s director-general, Dr. Patrick Amoth. After the man arrived in Nairobi, his relatives took him in a private vehicle to Nairobi Hospital, where he was immediately isolated. He was buried on Tuesday afternoon in accordance with recommended public safety protocols. The minister said that Kenya had tested 267 samples at five laboratories across the country since May before this first case was detected. Former 'American Idol' contestant sentenced to life without parole for wife's murder Michael Douglas reflects on marriage 'time out' with Catherine Zeta-Jones Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys The World Health Organization on Tuesday said that it was working with Kenya to prevent the spread of the virus. “WHO has also delivered about 1,000 Ebola tests and 1,000 personal protective equipment kits to high-risk counties in Kenya,” a WHO statement said. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Tuesday commended the “rapid identification, isolation and testing of the patient” and said a high-level team had been dispatched to Kenya to offer support. In Congo, where the outbreak has spread to seven provinces, conditions are difficult. Responders have faced attacks on health teams, misinformation about the virus, a failure by locals to report symptoms and rebel violence that has limited access to treatment centers. While cases have slowed in Ituri province, the epicenter, the outbreak is spreading in emerging hot spots in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces. “It is like fighting a megafire. Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations,” Stéphanie Hoffmann with Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said in a statement. The World Health Organization has warned that it could surpass the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history, which erupted more than a decade ago and killed more than 11,000 people in West Africa. Chinedu Asadu contributed to this report from Abuja, Nigeria. events.title: Paramount and Warner Bros are now one Hollywood giant: Skydance
events.summary: Skydance-owned Paramount has closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros CHICAGO -- It’s official: Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery on Tuesday, ushering in a new Hollywood behemoth. The merger brings two of America’s oldest moviemaking studios together under a new name : Skydance. HBO Max, titles ranging from “Harry Potter” to “Sinners” and networks such as CNN now also find themselves under the same roof as Paramount+, CBS and the likes of “Top Gun” and “The Godfather.” All are under the helm of billionaire David Ellison and his new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz . “Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said. “We couldn’t be more excited to get to work.” Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount for $8 billion last year before setting its sights on Warner. What followed erupted into a tumultuous, roughly yearlong fight over the storied Hollywood giant. Including billions of dollars in debt, the acquisition amounts to nearly $111 billion. The now-combined Skydance marks one of the biggest tie-ups in media and entertainment history, further concentrating power in an industry already run by just a handful of big players. Politics also loomed over much of the process. The Ellison family has notably held a long relationship with Republican President Donald Trump, who said Tuesday that Skydance is “going to be a great company.” The early days of Paramount's quest for Warner turned into a messy bidding war. Months after disclosing it was open to selling all or part of its business, Warner initially struck a studio and streaming deal with Netflix in December. But Paramount said it also had made offers that Warner management “never engaged meaningfully” with. It soon launched a hostile counterbid . The Hollywood giants spent much of early 2026 in a heated back-and-forth over who had a stronger offer, with Warner leadership repeatedly backing Netflix as its preferred suitor. But Netflix bowed out after Paramount eventually upped its offer to buy all of Warner for $31 per share. Warner and Paramount inked a mutual merger agreement in late February. Hollywood was closely watching the fight over Warner's future. From awards shows to online petitions, A-list celebrities and other creatives made their voices known. In April, thousands of movie stars, writers, directors and other professionals announced their “unequivocal opposition” to the Paramount-Warner merger. An open letter — which was signed by long-outspoken critics of the deal like Jane Fonda and Mark Ruffalo, as well as Hollywood heavyweights from Denis Villeneuve to J.J. Abrams — warned of fewer jobs and “less choice for audiences in the United States and around the world.” Others lined up to back Paramount as Ellison reiterated his commitments to the movies. At CinemaCon, the company debuted a glossy mini movie about the studio directed by Jon M. Chu and narrated by Tom Cruise — who ended the spot atop the iconic Paramount water tower, with the words “the future is paramount and the future looks pretty great from here.” Director James Cameron also doubled down on his support of Ellison. The prospect of a new Warner owner also loomed over awards season, from #BlockTheMerger pins to more subtle nods in acceptance speeches. When accepting her Emmy last month, “Remarkably Bright Creatures” actor Sally Field — who also signed the open letter in opposition to the Paramount-Warner deal — stressed that “unique storytelling matters” and “we can’t let those voices be silenced, or compromised or merged.” Many industry critics were also outspoken when Netflix's studio and streaming deal was on the table, with a particular focus on the future of movies staying in theaters. Trump has regularly attacked reporting he deems unfavorable at CNN (most recently attempting to bar the outlet from the White House altogether). And over the course of the Warner buyout, his administration also chimed in about hopes for a new owner. Days after Paramount launched its hostile bid for Warner, Trump said CNN spread “poison and lies” and that it was “imperative” the network be sold. The White House took aim again at CNN in March, over the network's coverage of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told reporters that “the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.” Ellison has said editorial independence will be maintained at CNN. On Tuesday, he told reporters that the company had "not talked to any political leader of any party about news — other than to say that we want to be in the truth business and we want be in the trust business.

events.title: News anchor Richard Morecroft remembered as a 'great Australian'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Late veteran news anchor Richard Morecroft remembered for wit and generosity Late veteran news anchor Richard Morecroft is being remembered as a consummate professional and "a great Australian". The 70-year-old died "at a time of his choosing", a statement on Instagram said, after he received a cancer diagnosis earlier this year. "We are devastated to lose such a warm, generous and caring human and hope that all those who knew him, if only through their TV screens, will remember him fondly," the statement said. Morecroft graced television screens for decades as an ABC 7PM NSW anchor for almost 20 years, BTN presenter and host of Letters and Numbers on SBS. Doogue (left) and Morecroft presenting the news together. ( Supplied: Instagram ) Geraldine Doogue worked with Morecroft as co-host on The National in 1985, when her late husband Ian Carroll changed the half-hour 7PM television bulletin to an hour-long news and current affairs program. Doogue told 702 ABC Sydney that she was shocked by his death and said his professionalism was a big part of his legacy. "He was just terribly good to me and to my late husband ... during that really tumultuous year," she said. "I mean, he was very much for it. Richard, once he was in, he was in. He was a very loyal, he contributed massively." Veteran news anchor and television presenter, Richard Morecroft, is being remembered in tributes. ( Supplied: Instagram ) Doogue said he had a strong sense of what "an ABC authority ought to be" and modelled it "effortlessly". "He had quite a wit about him, but he fundamentally felt his role, I think, was to be that face of the ABC while he was doing this," she said. He also hosted wildlife and educational programs and wrote about nature and the environment. Morecroft eventually moved to the NSW south coast, which Doogue said he called "his cathedral", with his partner of 36 years, Alison Mackay. "He had this whole side in him that was artistic, very much involved with the natural world," she said. "He just thrived in that environment and gave enormously to [and was] very generous to all sorts of charities." Australian Story ABC presenter and friend, Leigh Sales, told ABC 702 Sydney Mornings she first saw Morecroft on TV while watching Behind the News at school in the 1980s. Sales says Morecroft spoke with her just after she started working at the ABC. Sales said when she moved from Brisbane to Sydney as a young reporter at 22, he checked in with her to see how she was settling in. Sales is often seen speaking with young journalists and producers, helping to foster the next generation. "I try really hard to be a good listener and to not be just telling people, 'Well, here's how I do it'," she said. "The other thing that I feel like I learned from him is it doesn't matter if you're the star, you muck in like one of the team and you're not better than anyone else." Richard Morecroft at the 2025 Sculpture in the Valley festival with festival director Stuart McCreery. ( ABC News: ABC Illawarra/Rory Macdonald ) Former ABC presenter Keith Conlon, who met Morecroft when they worked together at a student radio station in Adelaide in the 1970s, said his fellow broadcaster was always a "lovely, warm person". "We kind of invented community radio on the run, and Richard was one of those people who came through the door — he was an arts student [at University of Adelaide]," he said. "He wasn't one of those 'out there' types … Very articulate, very intelligent. Conlon said originally, Morecroft expressed interest in potentially becoming a teacher or an actor, but that it made sense he turned to news reading. "If you're a newsreader, you are in a way acting. You only run the gamut from A to B but you've got to try to lift that news off the page and give things a different nuance," he said. Conlon said Morecroft had "a twinkle in his eye". ( ABC News: Brant Cumming ) Conlon said he was "delightful" with "a twinkle in his eye". "He had a beautiful voice — just that lovely tone, but much more than that, he had a considered way of talking," he said. "He loved the language, he loved the sense of what we were talking about, and he was dedicated to doing those things right. He was a perfectionist. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement that Morecroft was a "great Australian". "Combining a consummate professionalism with an unyielding humanity, Richard was a figure of absolute trust, a warm and familiar presence who guided us through the good times and bad," he said. "He loved the arts and was deeply passionate about our natural environment.

events.title: Pakistan provides fuel aid to 9 million low-income people as Middle East war drives up prices
events.summary: Pakistan’s government is providing fuel subsidies to over 9 million low-income people as the U.S.-Iran war drives up energy prices ISLAMABAD -- Pakistan’s government has provided fuel subsidies to more than 9 million low-income people as the U.S.-Iran war drives up energy prices, officials said Tuesday. Information Technology Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja said the program was designed to ease the burden on millions of people as regional geopolitical tensions drove up global fuel prices. “We have ensured the process remains seamless and agile for citizens,” Khawaja said, describing it as Pakistan’s first nationwide use of technology to deliver targeted fuel subsidies. Rising petrol and diesel prices have added pressure on a cash-strapped nation already grappling with high inflation, pushing up transportation, food and other living costs and raising fears of anti-government protests. The program, approved by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif last month, offers fuel discounts to eligible motorcycle riders, rickshaw operators and owners of small cars, many of whom depend on their vehicles for work and daily travel. The subsidies were announced after Jamaat-e-Islami, Pakistan’s major Islamist political party, threatened to march on Islamabad to pressure the government to cut taxes on petrol and diesel. Fuel prices in Pakistan have risen by more than 50% since the war between the United States and Iran began earlier this year, adding to pressure on households already struggling with the cost of living. Sharif’s government says the subsidies are intended to help low-income motorists buy gasoline at prewar prices. Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Army to execute Fort Hood mass shooter by firing squad Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik said more than 9 million people are benefiting from the program, in which eligible motorists receive a token by text message and present it at a participating gas station, where staff verify their eligibility before applying the discount. According to the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication, the amount and frequency of assistance vary by vehicle type. Motorcycle and three-wheeler users qualify for a discount of 500 rupees ($1.79) a week, with a limit of four tokens a month. That brings their maximum monthly assistance to 2,000 rupees ($7.14). Owners of cars with engines of up to 800 cubic centimeters are eligible for a discount of 100 rupees (36 cents) per liter on up to 10 liters of gasoline (2.6 gallons) every 10 days. They can receive three tokens a month, saving up to 3,000 rupees ($10.71). Amir Shahzad, an Islamabad resident, said the subsidy was enough to cover his commute between home and work.
