events.title: Landowner pushes back against opposition to Goolwa's first McDonald's
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Regional Development and Planning If the application is successful, it will be Goolwa's first chain-based fast-food outlet. ( ABC News ) A property in Goolwa is under contract to the fast-food giant, subject to state planning approval. The landowner says a McDonald's in Goolwa will employ young people and bring increased competition for takeaway food. An application is expected to be made to the Fleurieu Development Assessment Panel soon. The landowner where Goolwa's first McDonald's could be built has pushed back against local opposition, saying residents have a "democratic right" to choose what to eat or drink. Mick McArdle's commercial property at Hutchinson Street is under contract to the fast-food giant, subject to approval of a development application expected to be lodged with the Fleurieu Development Assessment Panel soon. But it has faced vocal opposition, first from a volunteer group dedicated to protecting Goolwa's culinary and cultural heritage, and then from Alexandrina Council, which recently voted to oppose establishing chain-based fast-food outlets in the seaside town. The property is under contract and a development application is expected soon. ( 891 ABC Adelaide: Caroline Horn ) "I don't think that people should have the right to take away other people's democratic right to choose what they eat or drink," Mr McArdle said. "A lot of people actually like the idea of having a McDonald's here. Alexandrina Council last month voted in favour of Cr Peter Oliver's motion, which stated that 38 food outlets in the area, including restaurants, cafes, supermarkets and service stations, already offer food. The motion passed, but not unanimously. It followed lobbying by Cittaslow Goolwa, a volunteer group of about 250 members. Goolwa was the first Australian town to be accredited by Cittaslow International in 2007, a European movement that promotes quality of life and sustainability in towns and cities, and handed a "slow town" status . Cittaslow Goolwa vice-president Christine Putland said recently that the town already sold takeaway hamburgers and did not need to rely on a "multinational company" to create more . "Even if the franchises might be more local or state-based, it is still not growing out of the community," she said in August. A Cittaslow delegation travelled to Goolwa from Italy in 2007 to present the council with a certificate. ( Website: Cittaslow Goolwa ) But Mr McArdle, who has lived in the town since 1978 and runs an automotive repair business on the site, said a significant portion of the town's population of more than 8,000 wanted a McDonald's because it would give young people work, and create more competition for takeaway food. "Competition has to be good for the people in Goolwa; competition keeps the prices at a reasonable level," Mr McArdle said. "And one of the service stations where you come into town has golden fried chicken, pizzas, the whole lot. He acknowledged he had a vested interest in the situation, but pointed out members of Cittaslow Goolwa involved with food outlets did as well. "At the end of the day, if the development application ticks all the boxes as far as zoning and all that sort of stuff, then why should they [McDonald's] not be able to go in there?" Mr McArdle said. Advocates for Goolwa's heritage attractions say the site of a former automotive repair business has been targeted for a McDonald's. Alexandrina Council Mayor Keith Parkes said there were "definitely people in the town" who backed a McDonald's but "the vast majority didn't". "It would be interesting to know whether the people that are in favour are long-term residents or fairly new residents to the area," he said. He agreed that a McDonald's would require local staff. "However, the small businesses in the town at the moment and around the place, struggle to get staff as it is, particularly in the hospitality area," Mr Parkes said. Aside from a McDonald's at the top of the Fleurieu Peninsula at Aldinga, there is only one other McDonald's on the peninsula, which is located 17 kilometres to Goolwa's west at Victor Harbor. "It will be very interesting, when eventually all the information comes out in the open, just where we stand with who's for and who's against it, and their reasons," Mr Parkes said. He reiterated that any development application requiring a change of use for the site would not go to the council for consideration. It would go to the Fleurieu Development Assessment Panel — an independent body established under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016.

events.title: Licence granted for controversial mineral sands mine
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Avonbank Mineral Sands Project near Horsham granted licence by Victorian regulator WIM Resource dug a test pit, which it then grew barley and lentil crops on. ( Supplied: WIM Resource ) Resources Victoria has approved a mining licence for the Avonbank Mineral Sands Project in Dooen, near Horsham. The WIM Resource-operated mine was granted a 20-year licence to dig up materials used in everyday technology and renewable energy projects. WIM Resource says construction could start in late 2027, with the mine to be operational by 2029, pending finances, construction and environmental approvals. Victoria's mining regulator has granted a 20-year licence for a controversial mineral sands mine near Horsham in Victoria's west. Resources Victoria granted the licence to the WIM Resource Avonbank project in Dooen, 15 kilometres north-east of Horsham, licensing the company to mine heavy mineral sands including zircon, titanium and rare earth elements. The mine site will cover about 3,400 hectares, with the Chinese-backed company planning to mine around the clock for materials used in everyday technology and renewable energy infrastructure. The company said construction could begin late next year, with mining starting in 2029, pending finances and other construction and environmental approvals. "This is a major moment for Avonbank, but just as importantly, it is a major moment for the Wimmera Southern Mallee," said the WIM Resource executive team of Eddy Wu and Michael Winternitz in a statement. The company plans to operate the mine for 36 years, digging up 12.75 million tonnes of heavy mineral concentrate. It has done so in the face of stiff opposition from residents and the local council, which has previously labelled the company's attitude to community concerns "disgusting". "Going by my phone calls … I think there's some people absolutely devastated in the community," said Horsham Rural City Council Mayor Brian Klowss. Brian Klowss says the community remains unhappy with the mining company's plans. ( Supplied: Rural Press Club of Victoria ) The Victorian government's mining regulator said it approved the company's licence after determining it had an "appropriate program of work", which it could finance and complete. However, it rejected the company's request for a 38-year-licence. The Horsham Rural City Council has previously raised numerous concerns about the proposed mine, including dust issues, and concerns with use of the nearby intermodal freight hub and rehabilitation prospects of the land. Resources Victoria said mineral handling procedures, real-time onsite monitoring and the mine's operating hours would be finalised as part of the work plan assessment. The mine site is near Dooen, a rural village in the Wimmera region. ( Supplied: WIM Resource ) "This outcome is as a result of diligent assessment work by numerous agencies and departments at both the state and Commonwealth level," said Resources Victoria director for regulatory operations, Laura Helm. But Cr Klowss said many in the community felt their voices had not been heard, and that he was "dubious" about the site's rehabilitation plans. He said while some concerns had been considered, questions remained about real-time air monitoring and a potential mining licence for the nearby freight hub. "They're devastated about what it's going to do to our community," he said. Cr Klowss said he was told to expect a licensing decision in January, and that former planning minister Lily D'Ambrosio and current minister Sonya Kilkenny would not speak to council about the mine. "I'm actually probably curious to know why the decision was made now," he said. The ABC has contacted the Victorian government for a response. Victorian Farmers Federation (VFF) president Ryan Milgate said the licensing approval on the eve of an election was fundamentally at odds with the VFF's call for a pause on new critical minerals projects. The mine site will cover about 3,400 hectares. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) The Avonbank mine is one of 10 mineral sands projects planned for the Wimmera-Mallee and across the New South Wales border. WIM Resource said it estimated the project, when complete, would support 1,000 full-time local jobs, and that it would continue to work with traditional owners, councils, landowners, businesses and the broader community. The company also said it would provide a $40 million community benefit fund, progressively funded over the life of the mine, that would provide long-term investment for communities across the region. WIM Resource says the mine will support the community.

events.title: Musk’s SpaceX in talks to borrow US$40 billion to buy Nvidia chips
events.summary: SpaceX is seeking to raise about US$10 billion (S$12.8 billion) in bank loans and US$30 billion in investment-grade debt to pay for the chips. SpaceX is seeking US$40 billion, led by Apollo Global Management, to buy Nvidia chips, showing huge demand for AI computing power. The plan includes US$10 billion in bank loans and US$30 billion in investment-grade debt, with the deal expected to close in 2027. The report highlights rising costs and heavy AI spending, while SpaceX shares fell and Nvidia’s stock rose after the news. Elon Musk’s SpaceX is in talks with banks and investors to raise US$40 billion (S$51.1 billion) of debt to buy chips from Nvidia, sources familiar with the matter said, underscoring the insatiable demand among AI developers for more computing power. Pacific Investment Management is one of the investment managers looking at the deal, said the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the talks are private. SpaceX’s fund-raising discussions are in an early stage and could end without a deal being completed, they said. Musk’s AI, satellite and rocket conglomerate is seeking to raise about US$10 billion in bank loans and US$30 billion in investment-grade debt to pay for the chips, the Financial Times reported earlier, citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter. Apollo Global Management is leading the financing, in a deal that is expected to close in 2027, the newspaper said. Tech companies and artificial intelligence model developers are investing and borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to build and lease giant data centres full of chips to power AI systems. The worldwide expansion of computing capacity has sent the costs of everything from land to chips and power-generation equipment soaring, touching off a series of massive financing deals. Nvidia, SpaceX and Apollo did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Times’ report. SpaceX shares erased gains in postmarket trading following the FT’s report, falling 1.2% in US postmarket trading to $169.79. Nvidia’s stock rose fractionally. In September , Musk said Colossus 2, an AI computing cluster built by his xAI business, may more than double its current Nvidia chip count by the end of 2026 . It was the most detailed timetable that the trillionaire has given yet for expansion plans for the Memphis-area cluster. Colossus 2 now has 110,000 Nvidia GB200 chips and 440,000 GB300s, Musk said in a post on X. A further 220,000 GB300s are due to be operational next week, with another 220,000 expected in November, he said. An additional 220,000 may come online late December “if we get lucky”, he said. Musk’s xAI has recruited multiple Wall Street firms to test its Grok chatbot, including Apollo and Morgan Stanley. Apollo was among the US investment giants that Nvidia tapped for a high-profile partnership in August to source US$500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure. The coalition – which also includes Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs Group and KKR & Co. – said at the time that they would “create dedicated pools of capital at significant scale at attractive rates for Nvidia customers”. Executives indicated that it will focus on debt financing to provide access to compute for Nvidia’s largest customers and signalled that there were already many deals in the works that would qualify towards this commitment. events.title: NSW coalmine climate ruling a massive shake-up to Australia's coal and gas
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts High Court rules in favour of climate group in Hunter Valley coalmine case Tony Lonergan and Wendy Wales from the Hunter Valley community group which fought the case rally outside the High Court of Australia in Canberra. ( Supplied: Zoe Lonergan ) A landmark ruling in the High Court has found planning authorities are required to consider the emissions caused by burning fossil fuels overseas when approving projects. Three of the five judges found in favour of a Hunter Valley residents' group, which halted the Mount Pleasant mine expansion last year in the New South Wales Court of Appeal. The High Court case centred around the open-cut coalmine near Muswellbrook, which was approved for expansion by NSW planning authorities in 2022, before being halted through the community-led court battle last year. The extension of the Mount Pleasant coalmine would add roughly twice Australia's total annual greenhouse gas emissions to the atmosphere. ( Supplied: Nearmaps ) MACH Energy, which operates the mine and brought the High Court case, wants to extract a total of 444 million tonnes of coal from the site, almost doubling the amount currently produced each year, until 2048. Because the thermal coal is for export, the more than 870 million tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions caused by its combustion will occur in other countries. They are known as scope 3 emissions and are not accounted for in Australia's greenhouse gas inventory. Residents from the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG) have fought to block the expansion on the grounds that those "downstream" emissions will also cause climate-related harms locally and should have been considered as part of the planning process. In July 2025, the NSW Court of Appeal agreed that the project's global emissions would cause local climate change impacts and that the Independent Planning Commission's 2022 approval did not take this into account. MACH Energy wants to extract more than 440 million tonnes of coal from the site. ( Supplied: Climate Media Centre ) MACH Energy's appeal to the High Court sought to overturn that NSW Court of Appeal decision on the basis that scope 3 emissions from the project should be considered at a global scale through pre-existing obligations under the Paris Agreement. Three of the five High Court judges dismissed that appeal, finding that the NSW Independent Planning Commission needed to "consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable all greenhouse gas emissions, including Scope 3 emissions". Decision could impact other projects The case is expected to have national implications for the way fossil fuel project approvals take global emissions into account. Legal experts say the case is the first time the High Court has dealt with questions about who is responsible for greenhouse gas emissions and the harm they cause, and whether local planning authorities have a duty to consider how fossil fuel projects contribute to the climate crisis. In a week of floods and droughts across Australia, the government extended the life of one of the world's largest gas facilities. Anita O'Hart, the principal lawyer who fought the case for the resident's group, said it was a historic ruling for Australian environmental law "and for the communities who have been fighting for accountability in the fossil fuel approvals process". "The High Court has confirmed that planning authorities cannot ignore the chain of causation from a project's emissions," she said. "The Independent Planning Commission was required to consider those impacts, and that obligation is now binding across the NSW planning system." MACH Energy released a statement on its website acknowledging the court decision, which it said it would carefully review. "We advanced this appeal to obtain clarity on important questions regarding the scope of mandatory considerations in environmental decision-making," the company said. "Clear legal principles benefit proponents, regulators, communities and environmental organisations alike. The High Court has now provided that guidance." MACH Energy's Mount Pleasant coal mine can continue operating until the end of 2032. ( 7.30 Report ) The company noted that a permit provided by the NSW government in August would allow the mine to continue operating for another six years. "Our focus now is on working constructively with regulators, governments, local communities and other stakeholders to understand the practical implications of today's High Court decision" the MACH Energy statement said.

events.title: Why Darwin could become 'a major interconnection point' for global data
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Darwin could host multiple international subsea cables amid NT government's digital infrastructure push Topic: Urban Development and Planning The developments have been pitched for the Darwin suburb of Fannie Bay. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Development applications show Google and Inligo Networks want to connect subsea fibre-optic cables to infrastructure in Darwin's Fannie Bay. Telecom analysts and the government say the NT capital city is optimally placed to serve markets in south-east Asia and Australia's southern states. Darwin is becoming a "network ecosystem" of subsea cables, terrestrial cables and data centres, Mr Tan says, which has been embraced by the NT government. As data centres and fibre-optic cable networks proliferate globally, planning documents show two international subsea cables could soon dock in the Darwin suburb of Fannie Bay. An application lodged with the Development Consent Authority shows tech giant Google plans to connect its "Bosun" subsea cable to infrastructure on the corner of Atkin Drive and Conacher Street. Subsea cables are fibre-optic wires which run along the ocean floor, transmitting data to onshore landing stations and facilitating intercontinental internet traffic. The planning application does not detail what the telecom infrastructure at the site will be. The proposed development is located near the Darwin Ski Club, at the corner of Atkin Drive and Conacher Street. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) If approved, Bosun will travel through telecommunication conduits — connected to the Fannie Bay site — to Christmas Island , where there is onward connectivity to Singapore. Bosun forms part of Google's Connect Australia initiative , a network of fibre-optic cables connecting Darwin and Perth to the east coast and trans-Pacific cable networks. On the parcel of land directly opposite the proposed Bosun site, multinational subsea cable company Inligo Networks is building Darwin's first "open" cable landing station. According to designs published by Inligo, the station will comprise a single-storey building and is set to harbour part of Inligo's Asia Connect Cable System (ACC-1). Designs for the building planned by Inligo Digital Australia's open cable landing station at Fannie Bay. ( Supplied: Inligo ) Once complete, ACC-1 will connect Darwin to four Indonesian cities, East-Timor, Singapore, the Philippines, Guam and the US mainland. It will also connect to Inligo's Unite Cable System — a network linking Darwin, Adelaide and Melbourne, granted major project status under the former NT government. The facility's "open" status means it will be accessible to multiple telecommunication companies and service providers looking to use one of the cables for their networks. Darwin is on track to host five international subsea cables in the coming years, with major tech firms seeking to exploit the city's proximity to south-east Asia and the Pacific. The NT's first international subsea cable, Vocus's Darwin-Jakarta-Singapore Cable system (DJSC), went online in July 2023 following a government investment of nearly $8 million. The lot is typically used by Darwin Ski Club patrons for overflow parking. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Hawaiki Nui 1, a subsea cable stretching from Singapore to Sydney via the Indo-Pacific, is being developed by digital infrastructure company BW Digital. Meanwhile, Meta's gargantuan Project Waterworth is on track to stretch around the world — from the United States' east to west coast — will also connect to Australia via Darwin. Marvin Tan, a senior research analyst from telecom research group TeleGeography, said Darwin is optimally placed to serve markets in south-east Asia and Australia's southern states. Marvin Tan says Darwin's geographic proximity to south-east Asia means it can service international markets wanting to bypass the South China Sea. ( Supplied ) "Traditionally, cables reached the eastern parts or the western parts of Australia, but now you can simply tap into Darwin and the terrestrial network to reach both," he said. Mr Tan also noted Australia's geopolitical stability and robust legal system, which he said make it an optimal location for data centres and, subsequently, subsea cable development. Google plans to connect its Bosun subsea cable to infrastructure in Fannie Bay. ( Supplied: FYFE/Google Earth ) Darwin specifically gives international proponents of data centres and subsea cables an opportunity to bypass the South China Sea. "Instead of going from Singapore to Japan and the United States, you can go south to Darwin and then back to the US, like with Project Waterworth and ACC-1," Mr Tan said.

events.title: Big Red Bash says 2027 will be the outback festival's last hurrah
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Big Red Bash organisers say 2027 is final year of the Birdsville festival Thousands of caravans lined up around the stage, beside the Big Red sand dune in 2024. ( Supplied: Matt Williams ) The Big Red Bash will be held one last time in Birdsville in 2027. The outback festival has been a major tourism drawcard for 13 years. The festival site is still underwater, but organisers are confident the site will be dry by mid next year. The Big Red Bash has been a major event in outback Queensland for more than a decade, but organisers say next year will be the festival's last hurrah. "To make a call like this after 13 years, it's a very hard thing to do," festival founder Greg Donovan said. "We built this festival over many years; we built it from our heart, but this decision is one we've had to make with our head. It's so sad to know next year will be our last one. Flooding in front of the Big Red sand dune in 2026. ( Supplied: Ben Fullagar ) "Our family and many other people put their hearts and souls into making this the great event that it is." Birdsville is 1,500 kilometres west of Brisbane, where Queensland, South Australia and the Northern Territory meet. Mr Donovan said that while event costs had increased in recent years, expense wasn't the main challenge. The event was cancelled this year after widespread flooding inundated the site at the Big Red sand dune. Big Red sand dune surrounded by water in May, 2026. ( ABC Western Qld: Heidi Sheehan ) In 2025, a scaled-back version was held, with a John Williamson concert at Big Red. In 2023 and 2024, rainfall caused havoc for organisers and festival-goers. "All of those challenges add up ... maybe it's time to bow out graciously and celebrate what has been an amazing festival," Mr Donovan said. The Big Red site is still flooded after significant rainfall across outback Queensland and the Northern Territory earlier this year. But Mr Donovan is confident the site will dry over the summer months, based on the Bureau of Meteorology's evaporation data. Rain and mud made things difficult for the festival organisers and attendees in 2023 and 2024. ( ABC Western Qld: Peter Quattrocelli ) The festival has attracted crowds of between 8,000 and 12,000 people in previous years, cementing it as one of the most significant tourism drawcards for outback Queensland. Locals believe its absence will be a major blow for outback tourism, as tourists often stop in small towns to boost the western Queensland tourism economy. "It's a bit devastating for us out here; it's something we look forward to to boost our economy," Diamantina Shire Council Mayor Francis Murray said. "It's going to have an effect on our businesses that are already doing it tough, that's for sure" Birdsville business owner Jenna Brook said the Big Red Bash had helped put Birdsville on the world stage. "It brings a huge number of people to Birdsville and surrounding towns that wouldn't come," Ms Brook said. The Nutbush dance record attempt is a fixture at the Big Red Bash. ( ABC Western Queensland: Heidi Sheehan ) "To lose that is a huge hit to businesses. The final Big Red Bash will be held in July 2027 with artists including Missy Higgins, Hoodoo Gurus, Jessica Mauboy, Leo Sayer, The Living End, Birds of Tokyo and Shannon Noll. events.title: Anthropic reconfigures its cool kids security program
events.summary: Only a week after warning about the perils of competitor Z.ai's GLM-5.3 model and its advanced cybersecurity capabilities, Anthropic has expanded its Cyber Verification Program (CVP) – or rather, reconfigured it. "For the past six months, we’ve enabled trusted access through two programs: Project Glasswing and the CVP," the AI biz said. "Now, we’re integrating these programs into one expanded offering, designed to give more security organizations access to the capabilities they need to protect their systems." Project Glasswing and CVP launched in April 2026 alongside the debut of Mythos, the company's highly capable and equally hyped frontier model. Project Glasswing gave partners early access to Mythos so they could scour their systems for vulnerabilities before attackers beat them to it. VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity was not particularly impressed with CVEs identified by Project Glasswing, noting that fewer than 0.5 percent of the 225 Anthropic-linked vulnerabilities he tracked were being exploited in the wild. And Anthropic's own warning last month about the risks posed by GLM-5.3 somewhat undermines the idea that there's anything special about its own Mythos model. Even so, Anthropic says that its security program has allowed its partners to spot at least 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities between April and July 2026. And the biz claims that its own open source scanning efforts revealed an additional 5,500 verified vulnerabilities between April and October. "Of these verified vulnerabilities, more than 33,000 have so far been rated as critical- or high-severity," Anthropic said. "This is likely an undercount, as it is based on survey data from only a subset of Glasswing partners. As such, we expect the true impact to be at least five times higher." When these might get patched is unclear. The company's own figures indicate that of 5,674 true positive vulnerabilities, 3,014 are high severity, and 1,522 are critical severity, yet only 516 have been patched. Given industry boasting about the cybersecurity prowess of AI models, generating a fix, testing it, and deploying it ought to be nearly automatic at this point. But the gap between identification and remediation suggests there's a lot of slack in the system that needs to be ironed out. Two programs into one with three tiers Now Anthropic's two programs, one intended for organizations and one for individual security professionals, have been merged and reconfigured into three tiers. The AI biz has not explained why, but its stated intent is to tie model capabilities to specific tasks: Defense Access, Red Team Access, and Specialized Access. Depending on the tier, participants will encounter more or fewer blocks on security-related tasks. As a measure of program participation value, Anthropic said that based on five attempts at 10 CyScenarioBench challenges, those without CVP access got blocked on every attempt. Defense Access is intended for security teams at companies, nonprofits, universities, and government organizations that focus on system defense. In this tier, Claude Opus 5.5 faced refusals in 46 of 50 attempts and succeeded four times. Red Team Access is for penetration testing and offensive cyber evaluation, and participants will still face model refusals for model interactions that would cause physical harm or mass disruption. Specifically, Claude Opus 5.5 completed 34 of the 50 tasks with Red Team Access safeguards enabled, a rate similar to what would be expected from Specialized Access. Specialized Access sounds like a rebranding of Glasswing – it's "reserved for a limited set of verified organizations that are authorized to test safety systems that could impact people’s lives or disrupt markets, such as flight operating systems, power grids, telecom networks, interbank transfer infrastructure, and government administrative networks." Those granted admission to this exclusive tier will face the fewest model refusals, not counting anyone using abliterated open-weight models that have had their guardrails suppressed. For the next month or two, program participants will need to allow their data to be retained by Anthropic as part of its AI safety requirements. But soonish, the company's Enterprise Frontier Safeguards program will offer zero data retention. Organizations already granted zero data retention while using Claude Fable 5.1 or Claude Mythos 5.1 can participate in CVP under those same terms.®

events.title: Google teams with nuclear power giant to give reactors a tune-up
events.summary: Google on Tuesday struck a deal with Constellation Energy for 3,590 megawatts of future energy supply, including nearly a gigawatt of new nuclear capacity, as the search and advertising giant tries to find enough energy to power its datacenter ambitions. The 20-year power purchase agreement will see Constellation, the largest purveyor of atomic energy in the US, bring an additional 890 megawatts of nuclear capacity online by making "targeted investments at multiple nuclear plants." We understand those investments will go toward upgrades to at least 11 existing nuclear plants across Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey through a process known as uprating. "By modernizing and upgrading turbines, steam generators, and digital control systems at operating plants, uprates deliver substantial capacity gains without the multi-year timelines or interconnection bottlenecks associated with greenfield construction," the power company explained in a statement. The other 2,700 megawatts the deal covers will come from other unspecified sources. Constellation expects to spend $4.3 billion to fulfill its side of the deal, and plans to complete its first uprated reactor by 2028. Google is on track to spend as much as $205 billion on datacenters and compute this year, but all that money is wasted if it can't secure power to make its servers and GPUs work. The hyperscaler is far from the only one scrambling to secure adequate power to keep its AI ambitions from starving. Microsoft also tapped Constellation to reignite the Three Mile Island Unit 1 reactor – you know, the one that didn't partially melt down back in 1979. That reactor is expected to come online as early as next year. Meta is also making noise about nuclear. The Social Network is working with Constellation to save a doomed nuclear plant in Illinois. Earlier this year, Meta revealed that its nuclear and clean energy commitments now total 6.6 gigawatts, though it's worth noting that figure depends heavily on the successful rollout of small modular reactors, an unproven form of miniature nuke plant. ®

events.title: "You suck": Emmer unloads on Senate Republicans
events.summary: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) is saying out loud what House Republicans have been grumbling about for much of the year: They're fed up with the Senate. Why it matters You won't ever hear Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) or Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) talk about their Senate counterparts like this. "There are no Democrats. There are no Republicans. They are just senators," Emmer told donors last week at a closed-door fundraiser Axios attended for Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.). Emmer said Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) "is doing the job that he thinks he's supposed to do. There's a certain fraternity sorority that is the U.S. Senate." The intrigue: Emmer had a blunt message for senators who repeatedly say they can't pass House GOP priorities: "Don't just keep telling me 'Don't have the votes. Don't have the votes.' You suck." Emmer said he once thought as a House member that he should stay out of the filibuster debate. Now, he thinks his colleagues should "get rid of the darn filibuster." A Senate GOP aide retorted that what would "suck" would be losing the majority and that Republicans should be targeting Democrats instead of attacking their own side. Driving the news: Emmer's comments are the most critical yet from a House GOP leader, but sum up the mood inside the conference. More than a dozen Republicans paralyzed the House floor this summer in an effort to force Senate action on the SAVE America Act, the GOP's signature election bill that's become a major source of tension between the two chambers. "We're frustrated with the Senate," Emmer told Axios in an interview after the fundraiser. "We feel like we've been doing everything we were hired to do, and a lot of it goes over to the Senate and it just sits there." House Republicans put their votes "up on the board," Emmer argued, while senators "try to avoid" taking tough votes. The big picture: House GOP leaders often say they've "done their job" when asked about unfinished business. But there's a clear implication in that phrase: The Senate hasn't. Johnson has pointed to the backlog across the Capitol — including when he defended sending the House home early last month by noting that hundreds of House-passed bills were awaiting Senate action. The speaker blames Democrats for that, but his complaints have put the spotlight on Senate GOP leadership. Zoom in: Congressional Republicans spent much of the summer on completely different wavelengths over reconciliation 3.0 , which doesn't require any Democratic votes. Johnson pushed the Senate to take up the House's reconciliation framework, declaring in July that the Senate would pass it before leaving for August recess. "That'd be news to me," Thune said at the time about Johnson's floated timeline. The Senate left town without any action on reconciliation 3.0. "They can say all day long, you know, 'It's going to be hard.' Everything's hard. Give me a lecture about how hard things are. That's what I do every day. They've got to figure out a way to get it done," Scalise told Axios of his colleagues in the Senate in July. The bottom line: Emmer stopped short of saying Senate Republicans have been a bigger obstacle to the GOP agenda than Democrats. But he said two things frustrate lawmakers in the House when it comes to Senate Republicans: 1) They don't say what changes would get them to yes; and 2) they don't put themselves on the record when the answer is no. "Put your money where your mouth is. Put your vote up on the board, and let's see where you really are," Emmer told Axios.

events.title: House GOP leaders admit redistricting fell short
events.summary: House GOP leaders are now openly acknowledging that their mid-decade redistricting push didn't work out as well as they'd hoped. Why it matters: Republicans kicked off the redistricting wars hoping new maps would give them a bigger cushion against the historical headwinds facing the president's party. That advantage is looking a lot smaller than they envisioned. Driving the news: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) told Axios that Republicans won't win all 13 seats they'd hoped to gain from new maps. "We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats. That's correct. We're not," Emmer told Axios aboard a plane Thursday between campaign stops in North Carolina and Virginia. Emmer echoed House Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), who told Axios last month that Republicans were unlikely to sweep all 13. Zoom in: Emmer said he'd be "surprised" if Republicans sweep all five newly drawn seats in Texas and "shocked" if they win all four in Florida . But he said Republicans are certain to pick up newly drawn seats in Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee. At a fundraiser for Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.) on Thursday, Emmer told donors that Republicans could also offset losses with pickups in Maine and potentially North Carolina, Ohio, New Mexico and Washington. Even assuming Republicans lose five seats because of redistricting in California and Utah, pickups elsewhere give the party a path to come out ahead, Emmer told donors. State of play: Redistricting still gave Republicans an edge, just smaller than they once thought. The Cook Political Report now projects Republicans will net around four seats from redistricting alone, down from the double-digit gains Republicans once hoped to squeeze from new maps. Democrats' maps in California and Utah — in response to a new Texas map — offset the GOP gains. Some newly drawn Republican pickup opportunities have become more competitive than expected. The bottom line: Democrats need to net just three seats to win the House, and the broader battlefield is moving in their direction. Cook shifted 15 House races toward Democrats last month, while Sabato's Crystal Ball moved 11 races toward Democrats days later. Many of the most competitive races are now in districts President Trump carried in 2024.

events.title: The next step in factory automation: Machines that adapt with AI
events.summary: Discover what’s coming to Microsoft Ignite, Nov 17-20, 2026. Register now. Physical AI in manufacturing: From intelligent machines to coordinated operations There are nearly 5 million industrial robots operating in the world’s factories today, a number that grew nearly 10% in a single year. Almost all of them execute instructions written in advance by someone who anticipated the conditions they would meet. That approach has defined industrial automation for six decades. Physical AI is moving intelligence into the work of manufacturing itself. Robots, vehicles, production systems, and connected infrastructure can now perceive changing conditions, reason over context, and act within defined boundaries. Automation delivered precision, productivity, and safety by executing known instructions. Physical AI extends that foundation by helping systems respond to more variation in the conditions around them. At the International Manufacturing Technology Show (IMTS) 2026, standing on the main stage in Chicago, Illinois, I framed the opportunity around a practical question: how do manufacturers turn intelligence that works in one machine or process into a capability they can deploy, govern, and improve across the enterprise? Physical AI closes the loop between intelligence and action Physical AI is intelligence operating in the physical world through machines, systems, and people. It works through a continuous loop: Perceive : Read machines, environments, and operational signals. Reason : Interpret that context and determine the next best action. Act : Execute through machines, systems, and people, then use the result as feedback for the next cycle. Connected operations gave people visibility. Industrial AI added reasoning over patterns and outcomes. Physical AI closes the loop by acting in the physical world, measuring the result, and improving the next cycle. When AI moves from recommending on a screen to acting in the physical world, value and risk both become physical. Operating limits, identity and security, observability, validated fallback, and human approval and override must be designed into the system. Physical AI is creating value across the industrial lifecycle Manufacturers are already applying these capabilities from engineering through live operations. At the engineering end, KUKA is making industrial robots easier to program and deploy. With iiQWorks.Copilot, users can describe a task, generate code, simulate the workflow, and deploy it. For simple tasks, programming can be up to 80% faster. Krones is using AI agents and physically accurate digital twins to speed filling simulations. Runs that took three or four hours can now take five minutes or less. In live operations, ARUM is bringing the same shift into the machining center. TTMC Brain turns a conversation into a machining program and reduces numerical control programming from 177 steps to two. ABB is applying live industrial data to predictive maintenance and real-time optimization. Across its customer base, ABB reports up to 20% higher critical-asset reliability and up to 60% less unplanned downtime. These examples address two constraints on scaling automation: the engineering effort needed to deploy it and the reliability needed to keep it running. What physical AI changes for operations leaders In my conversations with manufacturers, the challenge is increasingly orchestration. A successful machine or workcell is only the first step. Leaders have to connect that capability to the way the enterprise operates, decides, and scales. Physical intelligence changes three enterprise models: The operating model moves from site automation to network coordination . Lines, plants, fleets, and field environments can operate as one connected system. The decision model moves from manual planning to agent-assisted operations . People set intent, policy, approval, and override while agents interpret context and coordinate work within those boundaries. The technology model moves from disconnected tools to one governed environment . Data, controls, platforms, and cross-vendor systems must work together across cloud and edge. Those shifts depend on two connected loops. One accelerates physical systems innovation: teams simulate conditions, train and adapt models, validate behavior and failure modes, and iterate before deployment. The other operationalizes physical intelligence: teams orchestrate work, execute across machines and people, govern what happens, and optimize performance across systems and fleets. Agentic orchestration connects the two. Operational feedback returns real-world conditions, interventions, failures, and outcomes to the next simulation and validation cycle. Repeatability matters more than any single deployment. A successful machine or workcell becomes an enterprise capability when its data, integration, governance, and operating model can be reused across lines, plants, and fleets. Otherwise, the organization scales exceptions instead of capability. AI governance in manufacturing belongs in the operating architecture Identity, policy, monitoring, security, and accountability must travel with the capability from one machine or site to the next. Operational, engineering, and business context must inform the same decisions across cloud and edge. For global manufacturers, that architecture must also support sovereignty, data residency, and operational technology security across sites and regions. Leaders need visibility into what the system can do, why it acted, and when a person must approve, intervene, or override. A consistent trust model lets teams deploy, manage, observe, and improve capabilities across mixed environments without rebuilding the controls at every site. For more on Microsoft’s industrial AI platform, read Microsoft named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Global Industrial AIoT Platforms . Manufacturers do not need to automate an entire plant to begin. A practical starting point is one operational problem where the outcome matters and the boundaries are clear. Choose a workflow with measurable value, such as quality inspection, maintenance triage, machine programming, or process optimization. Map the data and operating context required to make a sound decision. Define what the system may recommend, what it may execute, and where a person must approve or intervene. Then design the deployment so that the successful pattern can be reused across another line, site, or fleet. For examples of how manufacturers can scale high-value use cases, read Step into the Factory of the Future . Physical AI will be measured in the operation: faster engineering, safer work, more reliable assets, and systems that improve under clear human authority. Start with one consequential workflow. Define its boundaries. Build so success can repeat. Turn shop-floor signals into coordinated action across your factory.

events.title: CDC: Monitoring Russian plague risk, "prepared" for any threat
events.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says it is monitoring reports of a suspected pneumonic plague case in Russia and says it is prepared for any threat that emerges. Why it matters: Pneumonic plague is the most dangerous form of plague and is almost always fatal unless if left untreated. The latest: President Trump told reporters Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to discuss the suspected plague case and would speak with him "very soon." Asked what U.S. intelligence was saying about the situation, Trump said officials were in "very deep discussions" and that "we'll be able to report about it, probably tomorrow." Catch up quick: Darya Shipilova , a worker at a Russian anti-plague institute, died after reports that she may have been exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. Russian authorities say testing has not linked her death to plague or to pathogens she handled at work. However, at least five hospitals in the area remain in quarantine and almost 200 people who had contact with Shipilova have been placed under medical observation as a precaution. What they're saying: "We are working across the U.S. government to assess developments as additional information becomes available," the CDC said in an X post Tuesday. "At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely." Context: The CDC said the plague is a dangerous bacterial disease that can be treated with antibiotics, especially when caught early. Pneumonic plague can spread between people through respiratory droplets during close contact. The CDC says "rapid identification and treatment of infected individuals, and monitoring of potentially exposed individuals" are important for keeping people safe. State of play: The concerns have drawn attention on social media and from government officials and the White House. President Trump acknowledged Monday that he is aware of the situation. "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday, but said he hadn't spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about it yet. "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can." The Department of Health and Human Services and the State Department are also monitoring the situation. What we're watching: Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Russia Tuesday to share more information about Shipilova's death, per Reuters . ​Rubio told reporters: "I ​think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously ⁠share more information with the world." Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from President Trump.

events.title: Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI's, study says
events.summary: The rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI, the two leading US AI model makers, is no contest when it comes to assessing which one gives you more value for your subscription money, according to industry research firm SemiAnalysis. Following changes to OpenAI's $200 per month subscription plan that effectively halved its value, SemiAnalysis looked at the various subscription plans offered by AI companies, because that's still the main way that individuals and small businesses buy AI services. AI subscriptions are heavily subsidized – customers get far more tokens for their money than they would paying metered API rates. And SemiAnalysis argues that it's necessary to delve into subscription pricing to evaluate AI shops financially because subscription usage consumes a disproportionate amount of company compute resources. Claude subscriptions, the biz claims, take up about 42 percent of Anthropic's inference compute while generating just 10 percent of its revenue. And those subscriptions provide considerable value. "Anthropic is an overwhelmingly better deal, offering ~5x the API-equivalent value across the board," SemiAnalysis claims in reference to mid-tier models GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5. "You could argue that this is unfair for [OpenAI] because 6.1 Sol is much cheaper per token than Opus 5.5, but the gap is still massive even if you switch to comparing the number of tokens." OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. SemiAnalysis' calculation relies on measuring token output rates, converting those into tokens per 5-hour usage window and per month, and then computing the API-equivalent value. Company researchers contend that API-equivalent value is the best figure for capturing the value of a subscription plan, though they allow that other measures like raw token volume may be more appropriate in some instances. API-based comparisons can be slow to account for the rapidly shifting capabilities of models that come to market. The debut of a new open source model, for example, can alter what's possible at a given price. For those with access to subscription plans, the subsidized prices clearly offer real value, so much so that there's an underground market for reselling tokens from pooled subscription accounts in many parts of the world. But there are other ways to measure AI value. Artificial Analysis, for example, tracks cost per task – the estimated dollar cost of completing a specific task. By that yardstick, GPT-6.1 Sol ($0.72) is far more affordable than Claude Opus 5.5 ($5.98), at least for those paying API rates. But that ratio may not be true for different tasks – benchmark performance may not reflect your workload. As measured by tokens, Claude Pro ($20 per month) provides 2.9 billion tokens per month, compared to ChatGPT ($20/mo) at 1 billion tokens per month, according to SemiAnalysis. But models may use more or fewer tokens than others for the same task, and when the output is functional, like code, AI output may achieve a similar result across different models but with differing degrees of efficiency. Anticipating AI costs gets more complicated for businesses, which can't count on subscription subsidies and may not have experience with AI cost management. In a July report, McKinsey said 93 percent of enterprises exceeded their AI budgets. "I think all businesses are seeing their AI costs rise," said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of AI agent biz Skydive, in an interview with The Register. Since the beginning of the year, he said, AI has been getting better at solving certain business problems, and companies have started deploying AI more widely, then noticing their token bills going through the roof. "The labs typically subsidize their prosumer plans with subscription pricing massively," said Amin. "And I think it's part of their marketing funnel because more people are able to use the tools, get familiar with the tools, and then bring those tools to work." But for larger companies, he said, two problems arise. You have more employees than can fit on a subsidized plan and, at scale, costs add up fast. "A huge way that enterprises solve this is being able to make a workload work well on the frontier and then quickly switch it to an open source model that they control and that they can serve at a much lower fraction of the cost," he said. "And so for us internally we were able to drop our AI costs 75 percent plus just by moving them all to Skydive Glide, which is our model router that for the given workload tries to find an equivalent open source model that can handle that workload without a quality drop. And so today we run a lot of our workloads on GLM-5.3 Flash." Amin said that companies adept at AI cost management maintain evaluation benchmarks that reflect their workloads. Companies use those metrics to test new models as they come out in whatever AI harness they're using, to ensure consistency. Looking ahead, he said, he expects companies will trust more of that work to service providers. "So what this means is that if you deploy an agent on top of us, we capture in the background the data of how that agent's actually running in production," he said. "And then we use that to construct the eval data set on the fly." ® Updated Oct 6 at 2322 GMT to clarify that Skydive is the platform that sells the agents, while Anything is the umbrella parent company.

events.title: Programmable Memory Controller Eases Adoption of New DRAM Techniques (ETH Zürich, CISPA, NYU)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at ETH Zürich, CISPA , and New York University published a technical paper titled “Terracotta: Enabling the Adoption of New DRAM Techniques via a Flexible DRAM Interface and Memory Controller.” “DRAM continues to limit the performance, energy efficiency, and robustness of modern systems. Many prior works propose DRAM techniques that support in-DRAM computation, improve memory access latency and parallelism, and enhance DRAM maintenance and reliability. However, adopting each new technique requires repeated modifications to the rigid DRAM interface and memory controller, hindering its deployment. Our goal is to reduce these repeated modifications. We observe that the DRAM commands and memory controller structures of many DRAM techniques are similar. Our key idea is to use these similarities to compose a set of primitives for implementing diverse DRAM techniques. We propose Terracotta, a new framework with two flexible components: (i) custom command extensions that let DRAM vendors define new commands within a single, standardized interface, and (ii) a programmable memory controller that system designers can program to support new DRAM techniques post-silicon. Together, these enable deployment by configuring the memory controller instead of modifying the interface and controller. ” Find the technical paper here . October 2026. events.title: CDC ‘closely monitoring’ suspected pneumonic plague case
events.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is “closely monitoring” developments in a suspected case of pneumonic plague that led to the death of a researcher in Russia. “At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC posted on X . Paul Friedrichs, a retired military medical officer who worked as the inaugural director of the White House Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy under former President Joe Biden, said Russian officials could help alleviate the worst fears if they disclosed what the researcher was working on, when she developed symptoms, and when she was treated with antibiotics. “What would really make me have trouble sleeping at night is if they continue to refuse to release really basic information,” Friedrichs said, adding that one key piece of information that should be released is the genomic sequence of the pathogen that killed the researcher. “It is understandable that people will assume the worst in a scenario when it would be so easy to disprove that the worst is occurring.” Still, the biosecurity expert cautioned against projecting onto the Russians how the US would handle a biosecurity incident. “The Russian culture and the Russian government bring security forces into all sorts of things that we would never, in normal circumstances, think about involving security agencies or military forces” in, Friedrichs said. “Assuming that their actions would look like ours, and then assuming because their actions don’t look like ours, it must be something nefarious — that’s a bad assumption.” — David Lim

events.title: A brutal winter heating bill is coming for some homes
events.summary: Americans could pay far more to heat their homes with oil this winter than last, a new analysis reviewed by Axios shows, as volatile energy markets and the Iran War deepen the affordability crisis. Why it matters: Heating bills are eating into household budgets before winter sets in, with stark divides between fuel types. By the numbers: Families that heat with oil could pay about 50% more this winter than last, according to estimates from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), up from its 31.3% projection in mid-September. The average cost of heating a home with oil is expected to rise by about $878, costing over $2,600 this winter. By comparison, the Energy Information Administration's Winter Fuels Outlook released Tuesday projects electricity bills will rise 4% nationally, while natural gas bills will fall 9% and propane spending will drop 3%. EIA expects a smaller increase on heating oil than NEADA, projecting a 21% increase in household expenditures. Northeastern households will feel the pain most acutely: about 82% of home heating oil is consumed in the region, where some states lack robust natural gas pipelines, according to NEADA data. Just 3% of U.S. households use oil as their primary heat source, compared to about 45% using natural gas and 43% using electricity, EIA's report says. The big picture: Heating oil prices are rising as global oil markets falter because of the wars in Iran and Ukraine and as refinery activity declines. "Those trends really reflect the worst-case scenario of this war, and they are going to feel it this winter, and it's unfortunate," Mark Wolfe, executive director of the NEADA, tells Axios. What they're saying: Because of the cost, some families will cut back on food or medicine, borrow from payday lenders, or turn the heat down to unsafe levels to cover their heating bills, Wolfe says. " With low-income families, sometimes states will move money around to help them, but they'll go without, " Wolfe says. Between the lines: States can put more money toward heating assistance, but they have fewer tools to protect heating-oil customers than households served by regulated gas and electric utilities, Wolfe says. States can require utilities to offer discounts, affordability programs or winter shutoff protections, but they generally don't apply to independent heating-oil dealers. Zoom in: Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey declared a State of Energy Emergency Monday over rising winter energy costs, unlocking nearly $150 million in relief and expanding assistance to middle-class households that heat with oil. Rhode Island has also declared an energy affordability emergency and directed $28 million in reserves toward winter electric-bill relief, and Maine Gov. Janet Mills announced $40 million in automatically applied electricity discounts for low-income residents. Zoom out: The energy affordability crisis is compounded by the Trump administration's attempts to dismantle the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP. The administration fired LIHEAP's federal staff at the Department of Health and Human Services in April 2025 and proposed eliminating funding for the program. LIHEAP is still running, but state administrators are operating without dedicated federal staff. The White House referred Axios to HHS, which said it "will carry out its responsibilities for funding Congress has made available" and that "HHS has the staff and capacity to distribute these funds in a timely manner." The bottom line: Winter is coming, and Americans need to prepare for both the cold — and the prices — to bite. Go deeper: How to save money on your electric bill this winter

events.title: S&P500, Nasdaq reach record closing highs as focus pivots to earnings
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Oct 6, before the closing bell, in New York City. - US stocks hit record closes as oil steadied and Treasury yields eased, shifting attention to third-quarter earnings. - The S&P 500 and Nasdaq reached all-time highs, while the Dow stayed about 5% below its August peak. - AI-linked shares and strong company news lifted markets, as traders cut bets on another Fed rate hike and watched inflation risks. NEW YORK - US stocks ended higher on Oct 6 as crude prices steadied and US Treasury yields eased, offering some reprieve from concerns that have preoccupied investors in recent weeks, and allowing markets to turn their attention to the approaching third-quarter reporting season. The broad rally pushed the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq to all-time closing highs. The blue-chip Dow remains just over 5% shy of its record closing level reached on Aug 5. When oil prices stabilise or move lower, “that causes yields to move down because there’s less anxiety about energy-driven inflation, which in turn is helping lift stocks higher”, said Oliver Pursche, senior vice-president at Wealthspire Advisors in New York. “This has been the narrative of the market for the last couple of weeks.” Six of the “Magnificent Seven” group of AI-linked megacap firms advanced, bolstering gains, while small-caps lagged their larger-cap counterparts. The AI trade is very much alive, with the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index gaining ground. Expenditures on AI-related infrastructure were reflected in international trade data, which showed imports of capital goods rose by 4.4% in August. The Commerce Department’s report showed the US trade deficit grew by 13.7% as imports rose to a record high. On monthly and annual bases, imports have grown by 4.3% and 28.4%, respectively, reflecting robust domestic demand that could exacerbate inflation pressures, particularly amid war-related supply constraints. Even so, financial markets are currently pricing in a diminishing probability of 19.4% that the US Federal Reserve will implement its second consecutive rate hike at this month’s monetary policy meeting, down from 50.9% a week ago, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. Fed rate hike bets have been responsive to oil prices, which have surged amid the Iran war, threatening to morph into broader price pressures. But supply worries eased after the Group of Seven countries reached an agreement to release emergency diesel and crude stockpiles, helping to stabilise front-month WTI and Brent crude futures. “We don’t expect (the Fed) to do anything at the next meeting,” said Tim Ghriskey, senior portfolio strategist at Ingalls & Snyder in New York. “But I think they’re in a gradual hiking cycle.” “High oil prices have hit a broad range of consumers,” Ghriskey added. “That’s one of the reasons for the recent Fed hike.” The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 253.14 points, or 0.49%, to 51,521.04, the S&P 500 gained 45.00 points, or 0.58%, to 7,818.95 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 122.48 points, or 0.45%, to 27,599.79. Of the 11 major sectors in the S&P 500, all but healthcare gained ground, with utilities leading the way. Third-quarter earnings season kicks off next week, with a number of high-profile financial firms expected to report on Oct 13. Analysts currently expect annual S&P 500 earnings growth of 30.6%, in aggregate, for the July-to-September period, led by an expected 114.7% jump in energy earnings, followed by a 66.5% estimated surge in tech results, according to LSEG. Marvell Technology climbed 5.8% following the chip designer’s 2028 revenue forecast hike due to strong demand for its data center chips. Chipmaker AMD gained 2.8% after CEO Lisa Su said it plans to substantially increase its chip supply in 2027 to meet booming AI demand. Constellation Energy jumped 12.3% after Alphabet entered into a 3,590-megawatt power deal with the company. Option Care Health soared 32.7% after drug distributor McKesson and private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice agreed to buy the infusion therapy provider in a deal worth about US$5.8 billion (S$7.4 billion), including debt. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.93-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. There were 258 new highs and 219 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 2,394 stocks rose and 2,378 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.01-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 23 new 52-week highs and 2 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 61 new highs and 182 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 16.50 billion shares, compared with the 17.51 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

events.title: Permanent daylight saving time could be a public health time bomb
events.summary: President Trump is pushing hard for the US Senate to make daylight saving time permanent so, among other things, golfers can stay on the course longer, but it may not be such a bright idea. New research out of Canada suggests that, even if Americans would get an extra hour of daylight in the evening, the ill health effects of permanent daylight saving time could outweigh the benefits. A paper published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal on Monday reviewed evidence on the health effects of permanent daylight saving time (pDST) as several Canadian jurisdictions move to stop changing their clocks. It finds that the opposite approach - adoption of permanent standard time (pST) - would actually be better for people’s health. Sorry, night owls and after-work social butterflies, but the science simply isn’t with you on this one. “Permanent DST preserves later evening light that may facilitate commuting, recreation, social participation, and some economic activity, but it also prolongs darkness on winter mornings,” the authors note. Prolonged morning darkness doesn't really jibe with the inner workings of the human body and light’s essential role in regulating the circadian rhythm. Sure, no one wants to drive home from work in the dark, but we really need morning light to get us functioning properly. Our circadian rhythms, the authors explain, actually run on a slightly longer schedule than a full day - 24.2 hours. For that reason, we rely on natural sunlight to keep us synchronized with the world around us. Morning light is some of the most important, the authors note, because it jump starts that rhythm, wakes us up and gets us moving. Evening light, on the other hand, delays the circadian rhythm, messing with our sense of “social time” and making it tougher to get to sleep and wake up rested in the morning. The effects of later evening light can show up in sleep, mood, education, and work productivity, the authors noted, and we don’t even need pDST to see some of those associations - we can just look at time zones. Move from east to west in the US or Canada and you’ll get some considerable differences in when the sun rises and sets in a particular time zone - in some cases, sunrise and sunset can differ by more than an hour of clock time across a single time zone. In one study cited by the Canadian analysis, residents on the western side of US time zones, where the sun sets later, got around an hour less sleep a week. The study also estimated that an additional hour of sleep per week was associated with around 5 percent higher long-term earnings. Similar results turned up in a German study, the team noted. Another study found that workers on the western end of US time zones ended up working fewer hours, too. On the educational front, an extra hour of sunlight before school was associated with higher math and reading scores in a Florida study “comparable in magnitude to meaningful class-size reductions.” “Ending biannual clock adjustments may eliminate transition harms that last a few weeks, but the health effects of permanent time are likely to be chronic,” the authors noted. “The preponderance of health evidence favors pST, which would align with the recommendations of sleep and chronobiology societies worldwide.” This isn’t the first time researchers have concluded such. British sleep scientists concluded much the same in 2024, which led to their recommendation to permanently kill DST in favor of a permanent shift to Greenwich Mean Time. That isn’t stopping the US from plowing ahead with plans for pDST, though. The Senate passed a measure to enshrine DST in 2022, but the House never acted on it. This time around, the House has passed its own bill to enact pDST, but the Senate is dithering, leading President Trump to go so far as to post the personal cellphone number of one Republican holdout on social media, Senator Tom Cotton (R-AR), who is opposed to the measure. “No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Cotton explained in a post on X following Trump’s doxxing. He’s right, too: The US has twice enacted pDST - once during World War II, which ended after the war, and again in 1973 as an energy saving measure. Congress curtailed the experiment later in 1974 following public backlash over dark winter mornings. The US isn’t alone in trying and failing at enacting pDST, either, as the Canadian paper points out. Russia adopted pDST in 2011 and reversed it in 2014. Chile tried and reversed it as well. In those cases, the reasons for reversing course varied, but concerns included dark winter mornings, disrupted sleep and body clocks, safety, and public dissatisfaction. It’s unclear whether the US government’s latest attempt at enacting pDST will succeed despite political resistance and scientific evidence that it’s a bad idea, but the researchers sure seem to hope not: They note that, if the US makes such a change, Canada will likely be pressured to conform. At the end of the day, we might all be better off just dealing with a couple of clock changes and some short-term sleep disruption. ®

As alleged in the SEC’s November 2024 complaint , from at least January 2021 through October 2023, Leech placed trades and then routinely delayed allocations until near or after futures markets set daily settlement prices, allowing him to observe price movements and disproportionally allocate hundreds of millions of dollars in realized and unrealized first‑day gains to favored portfolios and a similar amount of realized and unrealized first‑day losses to disfavored portfolios. Without admitting the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Leech consented to entry of a final judgment, subject to court approval, that would order him to pay a $3 million penalty, impose an officer-and-director bar and permanently enjoin him from violating antifraud provisions of federal securities laws. Leech also agreed to a forthcoming associational bar against him. In June 2026, the Commission instituted settled public administrative proceedings against Western Asset, ordering the firm to pay a $100 million civil penalty and establishing a Fair Fund to distribute money to affected investors in the disfavored portfolios. “The conduct by Leech and Western Asset was an egregious breach of fiduciary obligations to their clients,” said Brent Wilner, Associate Director of the SEC’s Los Angeles Regional Office. “Together, the resolution with Leech, if approved by the court, and the SEC’s prior settlement with Western Asset will return $103 million and provide meaningful relief to harmed investors, and reinforce that advisers must put clients first, every time.” Also in June 2026, Leech pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court in the Southern District of New York to obstruction of justice charges related to false and misleading testimony he provided to the SEC during its investigation; sentencing will take place in the coming weeks. The SEC acknowledges the assistance of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York and the FBI. events.title: Google backs 'existing nuclear plants' as data centres strain US energy grid
events.summary: Google has said that its data centre growth , fuelled by the artificial intelligence boom, led the company to reach a power-purchase agreement involving the upgrade of six nuclear plants in the US. An essay posted to Google's corporate news detailed the agreement made with Constellation , which operates the "largest fleet of nuclear facilities in the US". Through the PPA, Google says it is essentially enabling more than "1.5GW of new nuclear capacity for the US energy system from increasing the power output of existing reactors and bringing dormant facilities back online". Technology companies continue to come under criticism in the US over the rise in data centre construction. The centres cause energy demand to surge in some areas and lead to an increase in electricity prices for consumers. "As our data centre investments in the US continue, so does our commitment to revitalise the nation’s energy supply, support local jobs and economic opportunity, and bring new reliable electricity capacity to strengthen US grids at no cost to other ratepayers," Google said. The company said that as part of the PPA, Constellation had agreed to use the technology company's agentic AI "workflows across its core operations to accelerate uprate planning, streamline construction and optimise plant output". Nuclear criticism Google is the latest among Big Tech firms to support nuclear reactors in the US, although the moves have not always been welcomed. Critics say that many of the reactor deals include large loans from the US government, meaning citizens are paying for nuclear energy centres. On Monday, the US Department of Energy announced the latest such deal "of up to $4.2 billion" to modernise nuclear plants in Ohio and Pennsylvania. "By getting more power out of the nuclear plants we already have, we can deliver more affordable, reliable, round-the-clock energy for American families and businesses," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said. There are also concerns about safety. Constellation's PPA with Microsoft in 2024 involved the rehabilitation of one of the Three Mile Island reactors in Middletown, Pennsylvania. In March 1979, the core of TMI Unit 2 was partially exposed, prompting a temporary partial evacuation of the area and a lengthy clean-up around Middletown that continues to this day. Although it is Unit 1 of TMI, closed in 2019, that is being rehabilitated, energy safety groups have continued to express concern. And in Covert, Michigan, efforts to restart the Palisades nuclear reactor, which closed in 2022, are also under way. The owners of Palisades, Holtec International , had hoped to restart the reactor by this year, but a series of incidents have cast doubt on that goal. In September, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission confirmed that it was investigating an incident related to a "tipped fuel assembly" that occurred while the reactor was being fuelled. On Tuesday, however, Google did not appear concerned about the potential for opposition as it promoted its endeavour with Constellation. "This builds a more affordable energy future for everyone," the company said. It said it was providing guaranteed revenue that Constellation "needs to invest in upgrades for 11 of their nuclear reactors, while ensuring other grid customers bear none of the associated costs".
